text: In one novel by this author, a boy tricks his friends into whitewashing a fence in St. Petersburg, Missouri. A sequel narrated by that boy's friend Huckleberry Finn follows a journey down the Mississippi River with the escaped slave Jim. For 10 points, name this American author of "The Adventures of Tom Sawyer," who wrote under a pen name.

This man's first inaugural address declared that "the only thing we have to fear is fear itself." He created programs like the Civilian Conservation Corps and Social Security as part of the New Deal. Elected four times, he led the United States for most of World War II. For 10 points, name this president, nicknamed "FDR."

This organelle contains folds called cristae and an inner space called the matrix. Its own circular DNA is cited as evidence for the endosymbiotic theory. Most of a cell's ATP is produced here through oxidative phosphorylation. For 10 points, name this "powerhouse of the cell."

Allotropes of this element include graphite, diamond, and buckminsterfullerene. Its isotope with mass number 14 is used in radiometric dating. With atomic number 6, it forms four covalent bonds and is the basis of organic chemistry. For 10 points, name this element with chemical symbol C.

This painter's "Irises" and "Café Terrace at Night" were completed in the final years of his life. After an argument with Paul Gauguin in Arles, he cut off part of his own ear. His works include a series of sunflowers and "The Starry Night." For 10 points, name this Dutch Post-Impressionist.

This country's Great Barrier Reef lies off its northeastern coast, and its red center contains the monolith Uluru. Its capital is Canberra, though its largest city is Sydney. Kangaroos and koalas are native to this country. For 10 points, name this island country and continent in the Southern Hemisphere.

This hero was driven mad by Hera and killed his own family, then performed penance for King Eurystheus. His tasks included cleaning the Augean stables, capturing Cerberus, and slaying the Nemean lion. For 10 points, name this Greek hero, the son of Zeus and Alcmene, called Hercules by the Romans.

According to the Book of Exodus, this man was hidden as a baby in a basket among the reeds of the Nile. He confronted a burning bush and called down ten plagues upon Egypt. He later received the Ten Commandments on Mount Sinai. For 10 points, name this prophet who led the Israelites out of Egypt.

Euclid proved that there are infinitely many examples of this type of number. His argument multiplies any finite list of them together and adds one. A number of this type has exactly two positive divisors, one and itself. For 10 points, name this type of number, examples of which are 2, 3, 5, and 7.

In binary, this number is written as 10, and it is the base of that number system. It is the only even prime number, and the square root of this number is irrational. It is the smallest prime, and a pair of anything has this many members. For 10 points, give this number, the successor of one.

text: The lawyer Mr. Jaggers and the convict Magwitch appear in one novel by this author, which features Pip and the jilted Miss Havisham. Another of his novels features Sydney Carton, who sacrifices himself during the French Revolution, and opens with "It was the best of times, it was the worst of times." For 10 points, name this Victorian author of "Oliver Twist" and "A Tale of Two Cities."

This man took power in the coup of 18 Brumaire in 1799 and promulgated a civil code that bears his name. He crowned himself emperor at Notre-Dame in 1804 and was defeated at the Battle of Leipzig and, after returning from Elba, at Waterloo. He died in exile on Saint Helena. For 10 points, name this French emperor.

Johann Loschmidt estimated a related constant for the number of molecules per volume of gas. This quantity is named for an Italian scientist who proposed in 1811 that equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of particles. For 10 points, name this number, approximately 6.022 times ten to the twenty-third, the number of particles in one mole.

Rosalind Franklin's Photo 51 provided crucial X-ray diffraction evidence for the structure of this molecule. Erwin Chargaff showed that its adenine and thymine, and its guanine and cytosine, occur in equal amounts. James Watson and Francis Crick described its double helix in 1953. For 10 points, name this nucleic acid that stores genetic information.

This composer wrote six concertos dedicated to the Margrave of Brandenburg and a set of preludes and fugues titled "The Well-Tempered Clavier." He served as Kantor of the Thomaskirche in Leipzig and wrote the Mass in B minor and the Goldberg Variations. For 10 points, name this Baroque German composer of the "Toccata and Fugue in D minor."

The Aswan High Dam on this river created Lake Nasser. Its two main tributaries are the White and Blue branches, which meet at Khartoum. It flows north through Sudan and Egypt and empties into the Mediterranean through a large delta. For 10 points, name this longest river of Africa, whose valley hosted ancient Egyptian civilization.

This man was born in Lumbini as a prince, and left his palace after seeing an old man, a sick man, and a corpse. He practiced extreme asceticism before achieving enlightenment under a Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya. His first sermon at Sarnath set out the Four Noble Truths. For 10 points, name this founder of Buddhism.

This thinker wrote that an evil demon might deceive him about everything, and he doubted all he could in order to find a foundation for knowledge. His "Meditations on First Philosophy" and "Discourse on Method" argue for mind-body dualism. For 10 points, name this French philosopher who wrote "I think, therefore I am."

This economist described a division of labor in a pin factory, using it to explain how specialization improves productivity. He argued that individuals pursuing their own interest are led as if by an "invisible hand" to benefit society. For 10 points, name this Scottish economist who wrote "The Wealth of Nations" in 1776.

This scientist explained the photoelectric effect by proposing that light comes in quanta, work for which he won the 1921 Nobel Prize. He explained Brownian motion in his annus mirabilis of 1905, the year he published his special theory of relativity. His general theory of relativity describes gravity as the curvature of spacetime. For 10 points, name this physicist who wrote "E equals m c squared."

text: This author's epic includes a character who tells of Francesca da Rimini and Paolo being blown about by a whirlwind, and another who describes Count Ugolino gnawing on a skull. In it, the Roman poet Virgil guides the narrator through nine circles, while Beatrice leads him through Paradise. For 10 points, name this Florentine author of the "Divine Comedy."

In this author's best-known novel, the patriarch José Arcadio Buendía founds the village of Macondo, and a plague of insomnia strikes the town. The story ends when the last Buendía deciphers Melquíades's parchments. A pioneer of magical realism, he won the 1982 Nobel Prize. For 10 points, name this Colombian author of "One Hundred Years of Solitude."

A traitor named Ephialtes revealed a mountain path that let the Persians outflank the defenders in this battle. King Leonidas stayed behind with 300 Spartans and a force of Thespians and Thebans. Xerxes's invasion forces overwhelmed the defenders at this 480 BC pass in Greece. For 10 points, name this battle, a famous last stand.

The Judiciary Act of 1789 and William Marbury's undelivered commission as a justice of the peace were at issue in this case. In it, Chief Justice John Marshall wrote that a law contrary to the Constitution is void. For 10 points, name this 1803 Supreme Court case that established judicial review.

Ludwig Boltzmann's tombstone is inscribed with an equation defining this quantity as a constant times the logarithm of the number of microstates. Rudolf Clausius coined its name. The second law of thermodynamics states that this quantity in an isolated system never decreases. For 10 points, name this measure of disorder, symbolized S.

This mathematician scribbled a note in the margin of a copy of Diophantus's "Arithmetica" claiming a marvelous proof that was too large for the margin. His little theorem states that a to the p, minus a, is divisible by prime p. For 10 points, name this French mathematician whose "last theorem" was proved by Andrew Wiles in the 1990s.

This architect designed the Casa Batlló and Casa Milà, and the undulating bench of Park Güell. His unfinished masterpiece in Barcelona has towers with Nativity, Passion, and Glory facades. For 10 points, name this Catalan architect of the Sagrada Família.

This god sacrificed an eye at Mímir's well in exchange for wisdom, and he hung for nine nights on Yggdrasil to learn the runes. His ravens Huginn and Muninn gather news for him, and his eight-legged horse is Sleipnir. For 10 points, name this one-eyed leader of the Aesir who is killed by the wolf Fenrir at Ragnarok.

The Serengeti plains and the volcano Kilimanjaro lie in this country, which includes the island of Zanzibar. Its largest city is Dar es Salaam, though its official capital was moved to Dodoma. For 10 points, name this East African country, formed by the union of Tanganyika and Zanzibar, whose neighbors include Kenya.

A metronome and later a bell were sounded before food was delivered in experiments by this researcher, who measured the salivation of dogs. His work on classical conditioning revealed that a neutral stimulus can evoke a conditioned response. For 10 points, name this Russian physiologist who won the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

text: In this novel, a pig named Wilbur is saved from the butcher when a spider spins words such as "Some Pig" and "Radiant" into her web. The girl Fern first rescues Wilbur as a runt, and he later wins a special prize at the county fair. For 10 points, name this E. B. White children's book named for its spider.

The Sorting Hat places students into houses such as Gryffindor and Slytherin at this school, where Hagrid is gamekeeper and Albus Dumbledore is headmaster. Hermione Granger and Ron Weasley are friends of the title character of the series set there. For 10 points, name this British author of the Harry Potter books.

Friar Laurence marries the two title characters in secret, and a feud between the Montagues and the Capulets ends in tragedy when Tybalt kills Mercutio. A famous scene takes place on a balcony, and both lovers die in a tomb. For 10 points, name this play by William Shakespeare set in Verona.

In this novella, the ghost of Jacob Marley warns a miser that he will be visited by three spirits. The spirits show him his lonely past, his clerk Bob Cratchit's family, and the sickly Tiny Tim. For 10 points, name this Charles Dickens story about Ebenezer Scrooge, set at the holiday it names.

In this epic poem, the hero blinds the Cyclops Polyphemus, resists the song of the Sirens, and is delayed for years by the enchantress Circe. After ten years of wandering, he returns to Ithaca and defeats the suitors of his wife Penelope. For 10 points, name this epic attributed to Homer, a sequel of sorts to the Iliad.

This author, whose real name was Theodor Geisel, wrote "The Lorax" and "Green Eggs and Ham." His rhyming books feature a mischievous cat in a striped hat and a grumpy creature who tries to steal Christmas. For 10 points, name this author of "The Cat in the Hat" who used a pen name.

This man served as the third president and doubled the size of the country with the Louisiana Purchase. He lived at Monticello and founded the University of Virginia. For 10 points, name this man who was the principal author of the Declaration of Independence.

The archaeologist Howard Carter discovered this ruler's nearly intact tomb in the Valley of the Kings in 1922. Found inside were a famous golden funeral mask and a nested set of coffins. For 10 points, name this young Egyptian pharaoh of the 18th dynasty, nicknamed "King ___."

This 1773 protest was organized by the Sons of Liberty in response to the Tea Act. Men disguised as Mohawks boarded three ships and threw 342 chests of tea into the water. For 10 points, name this event in a Massachusetts harbor that helped lead to the American Revolution.

Born Araminta Ross in Maryland, this woman escaped slavery and made about thirteen trips back to the South. She guided enslaved people to freedom along the Underground Railroad and was called "Moses." For 10 points, name this abolitionist.

This man crossed the Rubicon in 49 BC, defeated Pompey, and became dictator of Rome. He formed the First Triumvirate with Crassus and Pompey and wrote about his campaigns in Gaul. For 10 points, name this man stabbed by senators including Brutus on the Ides of March in 44 BC.

This period began with the stock market crash of October 1929. Dust storms ruined farms in the Plains, banks failed, and about a quarter of Americans were out of work. For 10 points, name this decade-long economic downturn that led to the New Deal.

Heat from the Sun drives evaporation in this process, and water vapor then condenses into clouds. It falls as rain or snow and flows back to the oceans through rivers and groundwater. For 10 points, name this cycle that moves water between the sky, land, and sea.

This man's "Principia" laid out the laws of motion and universal gravitation. He invented calculus independently of Leibniz and showed that white light is made of many colors. For 10 points, name this English scientist who, according to legend, was inspired by a falling apple.

This Russian chemist arranged the elements by atomic weight and left gaps for undiscovered ones such as gallium and germanium. He published his table in 1869. For 10 points, name this man who created the periodic table.

Galileo discovered four large moons of this planet: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto. A storm larger than Earth, called the Great Red Spot, rages in its atmosphere. For 10 points, name this largest planet of the Solar System.

Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents were once joined in this single landmass, whose name means "all land." It split into Laurasia and Gondwana about 200 million years ago. For 10 points, name this ancient supercontinent.

This bone is the strongest and the longest in the human body. It runs from the hip to the knee and is protected by large muscles including the quadriceps. For 10 points, name this bone of the upper leg, also called the thigh bone.

Archimedes approximated this number using polygons inscribed in and circumscribed about a circle. It is irrational, so its decimal expansion never ends or repeats. For 10 points, name this number, about 3.14, equal to a circle's circumference divided by its diameter.

This artist's notebooks include designs for flying machines and a drawing of a man with outstretched arms in a circle and square called the Vitruvian Man. He also painted "The Last Supper." For 10 points, name this Renaissance artist who painted the Mona Lisa.

This composer continued to write music after becoming almost completely deaf. His Fifth Symphony opens with four notes that go "da da da DUM," and his Ninth Symphony includes the "Ode to Joy." For 10 points, name this German composer of the "Moonlight Sonata."

This Spanish painter went through a Blue Period and later co-founded Cubism with Georges Braque. His huge anti-war mural shows the bombing of a Basque town. For 10 points, name this artist of "Guernica."

This composer was a child prodigy who toured Europe's courts as a boy with his sister Nannerl. He was born in Salzburg and wrote "Eine kleine Nachtmusik" and an unfinished Requiem. For 10 points, name this Austrian composer of "The Magic Flute."

This fisherman was called Simon before Jesus renamed him, and he walked on water briefly before sinking. He denied Jesus three times before the rooster crowed. For 10 points, name this apostle regarded by Catholics as the first pope.

Its followers observe the Five Pillars, including fasting during Ramadan and making a pilgrimage to Mecca known as the hajj. Its holy book is the Quran, which it holds was revealed to the Prophet Muhammad. For 10 points, name this monotheistic religion, whose followers are called Muslims.

This god wields the hammer Mjolnir and drives a chariot pulled by two goats. He fights the world serpent Jormungandr, and the day Thursday is named for him. For 10 points, name this Norse god of thunder, a son of Odin.

According to Hesiod, Hephaestus molded this first woman from clay on the orders of Zeus. She was given a jar, or box, that she opened, releasing evils into the world and leaving only hope inside. For 10 points, name this woman of Greek myth.

This man asked probing questions in a method named for him and was the teacher of Plato. He was tried in Athens for corrupting the young and impiety. For 10 points, name this philosopher who was sentenced to die by drinking hemlock.

This Austrian founded psychoanalysis and described the id, the ego, and the superego. He wrote "The Interpretation of Dreams" and developed the practice of free association. For 10 points, name this psychologist from Vienna.

Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay first reached the summit of this mountain in 1953. It sits in the Himalayas on the border of Nepal and Tibet. For 10 points, name this tallest mountain above sea level in the world.

The Colorado River carved this landform over millions of years, exposing layers of rock up to a mile deep. It is in Arizona and is roughly 277 miles long. For 10 points, name this enormous canyon, a national park and a popular destination for rafters.
Computers use this number system because transistors have two states, on and off. A single digit in it is called a bit. For 10 points, name this base-two system that uses only the digits 0 and 1.

Johannes Gutenberg introduced this machine to Europe around 1440. It used movable metal type, and its first major product was a Bible. For 10 points, name this invention that made books much cheaper to produce.

text: In this novel, Winston Smith works at the Ministry of Truth rewriting records and is later tortured in Room 101. The Party uses Newspeak and telescreens, and its leader is the face on posters that say he is watching. For 10 points, name this George Orwell dystopian novel named for a year.

Thornfield Hall is the setting for much of this novel, in which a governess is hired to teach a girl named Adèle. She later discovers that her employer, Mr. Rochester, has hidden his first wife Bertha Mason in the attic. For 10 points, name this Charlotte Brontë novel named for its title heroine.

Hester Prynne is forced to wear an embroidered "A" in this novel, and the minister Arthur Dimmesdale is the secret father of her daughter Pearl. Her husband takes the name Roger Chillingworth. For 10 points, name this Nathaniel Hawthorne novel set in Puritan Boston.

A group of schoolboys is stranded on a deserted island in this novel, where they use a conch to call meetings. The boy Piggy is killed, and the hunter Jack rebels against the elected leader Ralph. For 10 points, name this William Golding novel.

The explorer Robert Walton relays the story of Victor in this novel, which Mary Shelley began during a ghost-story contest in Geneva. Victor brings a creature to life and then abandons it. For 10 points, name this novel whose title is often wrongly given to the monster.

This poet lived in Amherst, Massachusetts, and published very few poems during her life. Her poems use dashes and slant rhyme, as in "Because I could not stop for Death." For 10 points, name this reclusive American poet whose nearly 1,800 poems were found after she died in 1886.

The wrath of Achilles after his quarrel with Agamemnon is the central subject of this epic. Patroclus is killed wearing Achilles' armor, and Achilles then kills Hector. For 10 points, name this Homeric epic of the Trojan War.

King John was forced to accept this document at Runnymede in 1215 by rebellious barons. It limited royal power and promised that no free man could be imprisoned except by the lawful judgment of his peers. For 10 points, name this English charter.

Crowds searching for gunpowder and prisoners attacked this Paris fortress and prison on July 14, 1789. The governor, Bernard de Launay, was killed. For 10 points, name this building whose storming marks the start of the French Revolution.

This Venetian merchant traveled to China with his father and uncle and served at the court of Kublai Khan. His account of his journeys was dictated to Rustichello da Pisa. For 10 points, name this explorer, author of "The Travels."

John F. Kennedy announced a naval quarantine of an island after U-2 planes photographed missile sites there. Nikita Khrushchev eventually agreed to remove the missiles in October 1962. For 10 points, name this Cold War confrontation named for the country where the missiles were placed.

James Watt's improvements to the steam engine and the invention of the spinning jenny by James Hargreaves were important in this period. It began in Britain in the late 1700s and moved work from farms and workshops to factories. For 10 points, name this era of mechanization.

Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott organized this 1848 meeting in New York, where a Declaration of Sentiments called for women's right to vote. For 10 points, name this first women's rights convention, held in a town in the Finger Lakes region.

This man was tutored by Aristotle and succeeded his father Philip II as king of Macedon. He defeated Darius III at Gaugamela and rode a horse named Bucephalus. For 10 points, name this conqueror who died in Babylon in 323 BC after building a huge empire.

Helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, and radon are the members of this group. They sit in the far-right column of the periodic table and are chemically unreactive because their outer electron shells are full. For 10 points, name this group of gases such as the one in neon signs.

The Calvin cycle is the light-independent stage of this process, which takes place in chloroplasts. The light reactions occur in the thylakoid membranes and use chlorophyll. For 10 points, name this process by which plants convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose.

This scientist discovered polonium, which she named for her native Poland, and radium. She won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903, sharing it with her husband Pierre and Henri Becquerel, and the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1911. For 10 points, name this pioneer of radioactivity.

The boundary of this object is called the event horizon, and nothing inside it can escape, not even light. Stephen Hawking predicted that it should slowly lose mass through radiation. For 10 points, name this object, such as Sagittarius A*, with a singularity at its center.

The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is a boundary where new crust forms in this theory, and the San Andreas Fault is a boundary where plates slide past each other. Subduction zones surround the Pacific in the so-called Ring of Fire. For 10 points, name this theory that Earth's outer shell is broken into moving slabs.

This English physician noticed that milkmaids who caught cowpox seemed to be protected from smallpox. In 1796 he inoculated a boy named James Phipps. For 10 points, name this man who developed the first vaccine.

Leonardo of Pisa introduced this sequence to Europe in his book "Liber Abaci" using a problem about rabbits. Each term is the sum of the two before it, as in 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. For 10 points, name this sequence, whose ratios approach the golden ratio.

This man helped break the Enigma code at Bletchley Park during World War II. He proposed an abstract machine now named for him and a test of whether a machine can imitate a human. For 10 points, name this British mathematician and computer scientist.

This composer, nicknamed "the Red Priest," taught at a Venetian orphanage for girls called the Ospedale della Pietà. He wrote hundreds of concertos, including a set of four violin concertos named for the times of the year. For 10 points, name this Baroque composer of "The Four Seasons."

This Dutch painter's "The Night Watch" depicts a militia company, and his "The Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Nicolaes Tulp" shows a dissection. He made many self-portraits and was known for dramatic contrasts of light and dark. For 10 points, name this artist of the Dutch Golden Age.

The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan commissioned this building as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal. It stands on the banks of the Yamuna River in Agra and is made of white marble with four minarets. For 10 points, name this mausoleum, one of India's most famous landmarks.

This Spanish painter was a leader of Surrealism and sported an upturned mustache. His works include "The Persistence of Memory," which has melting clocks, and "Swans Reflecting Elephants." For 10 points, name this artist.

In Egyptian mythology, his brother Set tricked him into a coffin and later cut his body into pieces, which his wife Isis gathered. He became lord of the underworld, and their son Horus avenged him. For 10 points, name this Egyptian god of the dead.

This German monk is said to have nailed his 95 Theses to the door of the Wittenberg church in 1517. He was condemned at the Diet of Worms in 1521 and later translated the Bible into German. For 10 points, name this leader of the Protestant Reformation.

This man founded a school called the Lyceum and wrote the "Nicomachean Ethics" and the "Poetics." He was a student of Plato and tutor to Alexander the Great. For 10 points, name this Greek philosopher who developed formal logic.

Simon Kuznets developed the national accounts that led to this measure. It is computed by adding consumption, investment, government spending, and net exports. For 10 points, name this measure of the value of a country's output, abbreviated GDP.

This Swiss psychologist proposed four stages of cognitive development: sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, and formal operational. He studied his own children and developed the idea of object permanence. For 10 points, name this child psychologist.

This river begins in the Andes of Peru and flows across Brazil past the city of Manaus. It discharges more water than any other river and is surrounded by the world's largest rainforest. For 10 points, name this South American river.

Lake Itasca in Minnesota is the source of this river. The Missouri and Ohio rivers are its major tributaries, and it empties into the Gulf of Mexico south of New Orleans. For 10 points, name this river that forms the boundary of many states.

text: This novel takes place on June 16, 1904, a date now celebrated as Bloomsday. Its chapters loosely parallel the episodes of the Odyssey, and its Dublin wanderers include the advertising canvasser Leopold Bloom and the young teacher Stephen Dedalus. For 10 points, name this James Joyce novel, whose title is the Latin name of its mythic model.

Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are sent to spy on the title character of this play, who later holds a skull and recalls the jester Yorick. A play-within-a-play called "The Mousetrap" is staged to "catch the conscience of the King." For 10 points, name this Shakespeare tragedy that includes the line "To be, or not to be."

This author's only novel published in his lifetime has a narrator who lives in a basement lit by 1,369 light bulbs. The narrator is told by a Brotherhood that he can serve as a spokesman, but he finally retreats underground. For 10 points, name this author of "Invisible Man."

In this Old English poem, a hero cuts off the arm of Grendel in the hall Heorot. He later kills Grendel's mother in an underwater lair, and in old age he dies fighting a dragon. For 10 points, name this epic whose title character is a Geat prince.

Mr. Lockwood narrates part of this novel, in which Nelly Dean tells of the Earnshaw family. A foundling named Heathcliff loves Catherine, who marries Edgar Linton at the neighboring Thrushcross Grange. For 10 points, name this novel set on the Yorkshire moors by Emily Brontë.

This author wrote of a man who is turned into a giant insect in a novella called "The Metamorphosis." His novels "The Trial" and "The Castle" feature characters trapped in baffling bureaucracies. For 10 points, name this Prague-born writer whose last name has become an adjective for nightmarish systems.

The crew of the Pequod includes the harpooneer Queequeg and the mate Starbuck. Its captain loses a leg to the title creature and swears vengeance, but the ship is destroyed, and only Ishmael survives. For 10 points, name this Herman Melville novel about a white whale.

Article 231 of this 1919 agreement made Germany accept responsibility for the war. It was signed in the Hall of Mirrors and limited the German army to 100,000 men. For 10 points, name this treaty that formally ended World War I with Germany.

Thucydides wrote the history of this conflict, in which he included Pericles' funeral oration. It included a disastrous Athenian expedition to Sicily and ended with the fall of Athens in 404 BC. For 10 points, name this war between Athens and Sparta.

This statesman edited the Ems Dispatch to provoke France into war in 1870. He practiced "Realpolitik" and oversaw the unification of Germany under Prussia. For 10 points, name this first chancellor of the German Empire, the "Iron Chancellor."

Toussaint Louverture led a slave uprising in Saint-Domingue that grew into this event. After his capture by the French, Jean-Jacques Dessalines declared independence in 1804. For 10 points, name this revolution that created the first Black republic in the Americas.

The Freedmen's Bureau was created during this period, which also saw the passage of the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments. It ended after the Compromise of 1877 led to the withdrawal of federal troops from the South. For 10 points, name this period after the Civil War.

Commodore Perry's arrival in 1853 helped end the isolation that led to this event. In 1868 power was restored to the emperor, and the country rapidly industrialized and built a modern army. For 10 points, name this transformation of Japan named for the "enlightened rule" of Emperor Mutsuhito.

Mehmed II captured Constantinople for this state in 1453. Under Suleiman the Magnificent it besieged Vienna, and its elite infantry were called Janissaries. For 10 points, name this empire centered in Istanbul that lasted until 1922.

This scientist's equation describes how the wave function of a quantum system changes with time. He devised a thought experiment in which a cat in a sealed box is both alive and dead until observed. For 10 points, name this Austrian physicist.

In eukaryotes, this series of reactions occurs in the mitochondrial matrix, where acetyl-CoA is oxidized and NADH and FADH2 are produced. It is named for the biochemist Hans Krebs. For 10 points, name this cycle, also called the citric acid cycle.

This principle was proposed by Werner Heisenberg in 1927. It states that certain pairs of quantities, such as position and momentum, cannot both be known precisely at the same time. For 10 points, name this principle of quantum mechanics.

This principle says that when a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts to counteract the change. Adding more reactant, for example, shifts the reaction toward products. For 10 points, name this principle of chemical equilibrium named for a French chemist.

This astronomer used Cepheid variable stars to show that the Andromeda "nebula" lies outside the Milky Way. He found that galaxies recede at speeds proportional to their distance. For 10 points, name this American astronomer for whom a space telescope is named.

This Swiss mathematician solved the Königsberg bridge problem, founding graph theory, and solved the Basel problem. He introduced the notation f(x) and popularized the symbols e and i. For 10 points, name this prolific mathematician.

Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing a method of editing genes named for these repeating DNA sequences. It uses a guide RNA and the enzyme Cas9 to cut DNA at a chosen site. For 10 points, give this acronym for a gene-editing tool.

The Large Hadron Collider at CERN was used to find this particle in 2012. Its associated field gives other elementary particles their mass. For 10 points, name this boson predicted by Peter Higgs and others.

The premiere of this composer's "The Rite of Spring" in 1913 in Paris is said to have caused a riot. He also wrote the ballets "The Firebird" and "Petrushka" for Diaghilev's Ballets Russes. For 10 points, name this Russian composer.

This Mexican painter created many self-portraits, including ones with a necklace of thorns and a wounded deer. She was married to the muralist Diego Rivera and lived in the Blue House in Coyoacán. For 10 points, name this artist of "The Two Fridas."

Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque developed this movement, which broke objects into geometric facets seen from several angles at once. "Les Demoiselles d'Avignon" is often seen as a precursor, and its two phases are called analytic and synthetic. For 10 points, name this early 20th-century art movement.

This Austrian painter was a founder of the Vienna Secession and used gold leaf in his "Golden Phase." His works include "Judith and the Head of Holofernes" and a painting of two lovers embracing. For 10 points, name this artist of "The Kiss."

In this Hindu scripture, a warrior hesitates to fight on the field of Kurukshetra. His charioteer, who is an avatar of Vishnu, teaches him about duty and devotion. For 10 points, name this part of the Mahabharata, a dialogue between Arjuna and Krishna.

In this Mesopotamian epic, a king of Uruk befriends the wild man Enkidu and fights the monster Humbaba. After Enkidu dies, the king seeks out Utnapishtim to learn the secret of immortality. For 10 points, name this epic of the Babylonians and Sumerians, named for its hero.

This philosopher wrote the "Critique of Pure Reason" and spent his life in Königsberg. He argued that one should act only according to a maxim that one could will to be a universal law. For 10 points, name this German thinker who formulated the categorical imperative.

This thinker wrote "Thus Spoke Zarathustra" and introduced the idea of the Übermensch. His works "Beyond Good and Evil" and "The Gay Science" include the declaration that "God is dead." For 10 points, name this German philosopher.

This thinker collaborated with Friedrich Engels on "The Communist Manifesto" in 1848. His multivolume "Das Kapital" analyzed capitalism through concepts such as surplus value. For 10 points, name this German philosopher and economist.

This British economist argued in "The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money" that governments should use deficit spending to fight depressions. He was a delegate at the Bretton Woods conference. For 10 points, name this namesake of an economic school.

This American linguist wrote "Syntactic Structures" in 1957. He proposed that humans have an innate capacity for language, often called universal grammar. For 10 points, name this MIT professor and political critic.

Ferdinand de Lesseps oversaw the construction of this waterway, which opened in 1869. It links the Mediterranean to the Red Sea and spares ships a trip around Africa. For 10 points, name this Egyptian canal.

This lake in Siberia is the deepest in the world, at over 5,000 feet. It holds about a fifth of the planet's unfrozen fresh water and is home to the freshwater Baikal seal. For 10 points, name this Russian lake.

text: This painter killed a man in a brawl in Rome and fled to Malta. He used dramatic contrasts of light and dark called tenebrism, as in his Judith Beheading Holofernes. His Calling of Saint Matthew hangs in the Contarelli Chapel in San Luigi dei Francesi. For 10 points, name this Italian Baroque master.

This Spanish court painter made a portrait of Pope Innocent X and the Rokeby Venus. His masterpiece shows the Infanta Margarita surrounded by attendants, with the artist himself standing at an easel. For 10 points, name this painter of Las Meninas who served Philip IV.

This French painter caused scandals with a nude woman gazing at the viewer in Olympia and with a picnic scene showing a naked woman beside clothed men. His last major work shows a barmaid at the Folies-Bergère. For 10 points, name this artist of Luncheon on the Grass.

This Post-Impressionist from Aix-en-Provence painted many views of Mont Sainte-Victoire. He also painted The Card Players and several groups of bathers. His method of building form from planes of color influenced the Cubists. For 10 points, name this painter.

This Frenchman worked briefly with Van Gogh in Arles, then left for Tahiti. His paintings include Where Do We Come From? What Are We? Where Are We Going? and use flat areas of bold color. For 10 points, name this Post-Impressionist who painted Tahitian women.

This Austrian artist was a founder of the Vienna Secession and used gold leaf in his portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer. His painting of a couple embracing, with patterned robes, is called The Kiss. For 10 points, name this Symbolist painter.

This Italian painted the fresco The School of Athens in the Vatican's Stanza della Segnatura. He also made the Sistine Madonna and worked in Rome under Pope Julius II. He died in 1520 at age thirty-seven. For 10 points, name this Renaissance painter.

This Flemish painter used oil glazes to produce intensely detailed pictures. His Ghent Altarpiece was made with his brother Hubert. A convex mirror in the background of his Arnolfini Portrait reflects the room. For 10 points, name this Early Netherlandish painter.

This Flemish Baroque painter ran a huge workshop in Antwerp and painted full-figured nudes and swirling allegories. He made the cycle of the life of Marie de' Medici and The Descent from the Cross. For 10 points, name this artist.

This Spanish painter made a harrowing image of an execution by French soldiers, The Third of May 1808. His late Black Paintings include Saturn Devouring His Son. His series The Disasters of War depicts atrocities. For 10 points, name this artist of The Naked Maja.

This French Romantic painter showed a bare-breasted woman waving the tricolor flag over a barricade in Liberty Leading the People. His Death of Sardanapalus is filled with color and violence. For 10 points, name this rival of Ingres.

This French painter depicted the murdered revolutionary Jean-Paul Marat in his bath. His Oath of the Horatii is a prime example of Neoclassicism, and he later served as Napoleon's court painter. For 10 points, name this artist of The Death of Marat.

This movement was announced in a 1924 manifesto by André Breton. Its artists such as Max Ernst and René Magritte tried to express the unconscious through dreamlike images and automatic drawing. For 10 points, name this movement associated with Dalí.

This Belgian painter's The Treachery of Images shows a pipe with a caption saying it is not a pipe. He also painted a man in a bowler hat with an apple obscuring his face in The Son of Man. For 10 points, name this Surrealist.

This Norwegian painter made multiple versions of a figure on a bridge clutching its face as the sky turns blood red. He also painted Madonna and The Sick Child. His works helped found Expressionism. For 10 points, name this artist of The Scream.

This Catalan artist painted Harlequin's Carnival and made a series of works called Constellations. His biomorphic Surrealist paintings feature stars, eyes, and playful black lines on bright backgrounds. For 10 points, name this Spanish artist of The Farm.

This Latvian-born American painter produced large canvases with floating blocks of color for the Seagram Building and a chapel in Houston. He is a leading figure of Color Field painting. For 10 points, name this artist of the Rothko Chapel.

This artist enlarged panels from comic books, using Ben-Day dots and bold outlines. His works include Drowning Girl and Whaam!, which depicts a fighter plane firing at another. For 10 points, name this American pop artist.

This African-American painter made sixty panels about the Great Migration in a series with short captions. He also painted scenes of Harlem and studied at the Harlem Art Workshop. For 10 points, name this artist of The Migration Series.

This American painter's portrait of Virginie Gautreau, titled Madame X, caused a scandal at the 1884 Paris Salon. He painted high-society portraits in London and Boston. For 10 points, name this artist of Carnation, Lily, Lily, Rose.

This Italian sculptor carved The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa and designed the baldachin and colonnade at Saint Peter's. His marble Apollo and Daphne appears to capture a mid-transformation. For 10 points, name this master of Baroque sculpture.

This English Romantic painter showed a warship being towed to its last berth in The Fighting Temeraire. His Rain, Steam and Speed depicts a train on a bridge. His later paintings dissolve forms in light. For 10 points, name this artist.

This group formed in 1848 and rejected the formulas taught by the Royal Academy. Its members included John Everett Millais, who painted Ophelia, and Dante Gabriel Rossetti. They wanted to return to the clarity of art before the Italian Renaissance. For 10 points, name this British brotherhood.

This Dutch painter made The Garden of Earthly Delights, a triptych with a paradise panel, a middle panel full of nudes, and a panel of hell with monstrous creatures. His other works include The Haywain. For 10 points, name this artist.

This Flemish painter portrayed peasants in works such as Hunters in the Snow and The Peasant Wedding. He also painted The Tower of Babel. His sons were also painters. For 10 points, name this artist, sometimes called "the Elder."

This early twentieth-century movement is named after a critic's description of its artists as "wild beasts." Henri Matisse and André Derain used pure, unnatural colors in works such as Woman with a Hat. For 10 points, name this movement.

This eighteenth-century French style favored pastel colors, curves, and playful scenes. Fragonard's The Swing and Boucher's paintings of Madame de Pompadour are examples. It followed the Baroque. For 10 points, name this lighthearted style.

This Florentine painted frescoes in the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua. His figures show weight and emotion, breaking with the flatter Byzantine style. He also designed the campanile of Florence's cathedral. For 10 points, name this painter often called a forerunner of the Renaissance.

This anti-art movement began at Zurich's Cabaret Voltaire in 1916 in reaction to World War I. Its works mocked bourgeois values and used nonsense, collage, and chance. Hugo Ball and Hans Arp were participants. For 10 points, name this movement.

This French artist scandalized the 1913 Armory Show with Nude Descending a Staircase, No. 2. He submitted a signed porcelain urinal as Fountain and coined the term "readymade." For 10 points, name this Dada artist.

text: This Hungarian pianist wrote the Hungarian Rhapsodies and invented the symphonic poem. He was a famed virtuoso who caused near-hysteria among fans, a phenomenon called "Lisztomania." For 10 points, name this composer of Les préludes.

This composer was a child prodigy who wrote an overture to A Midsummer Night's Dream at age seventeen. He revived interest in Bach's Saint Matthew Passion. His sister Fanny was also a composer. For 10 points, name this German composer of the Wedding March.

This Italian composer wrote the operas Rigoletto, La traviata, and Aida. His Requiem is considered a dramatic work, and "La donna è mobile" is from one of his operas. For 10 points, name this composer of Otello and Falstaff.

This Czech composer spent three years in the United States and wrote his Symphony No. 9 "From the New World." He also wrote the Slavonic Dances and the opera Rusalka. For 10 points, name this composer.

This Austrian composer wrote symphonies of huge scale, including the Resurrection and the Symphony of a Thousand. He also wrote Das Lied von der Erde and Kindertotenlieder. For 10 points, name this Bohemian-born conductor and composer.

This Norwegian composer wrote incidental music for Ibsen's play Peer Gynt, including "In the Hall of the Mountain King." He also wrote a famous piano concerto in A minor. For 10 points, name this composer.
This Finnish composer wrote the tone poem Finlandia, which became a symbol of national identity. He also wrote seven symphonies and The Swan of Tuonela. For 10 points, name this composer.

This Russian pianist and composer wrote four piano concertos, including the Second, and the Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini. After leaving Russia in 1917 he settled in the United States. For 10 points, name this Romantic composer.

This Soviet composer wrote fifteen symphonies, including the Leningrad Symphony. He had a complicated relationship with Stalin's government and wrote the opera Lady Macbeth of the Mtsensk District. For 10 points, name this composer.

This French composer wrote a work that begins with a snare drum rhythm and slowly builds with a single repeated melody. He also wrote Pavane for a Dead Princess and orchestrated Pictures at an Exhibition. For 10 points, name this composer of Boléro.

This Hungarian composer collected folk songs with Zoltán Kodály. He wrote Concerto for Orchestra and the opera Bluebeard's Castle. His six string quartets are central works of the twentieth century. For 10 points, name this composer of Mikrokosmos.

This Italian composer wrote The Barber of Seville and an overture to an opera about a Swiss archer, William Tell. The final part of that overture is used as a theme for The Lone Ranger. For 10 points, name this composer.

This French composer wrote an opera set in Seville about a gypsy factory worker, which includes the "Habanera" and the "Toreador Song." He also wrote the L'Arlésienne suites. For 10 points, name this composer of Carmen.

This French composer wrote a suite for chamber orchestra that includes movements on the elephant, the swan, and fossils. His Symphony No. 3 has a part for organ. For 10 points, name this composer of Danse macabre and Carnival of the Animals.

This Russian composer wrote a piano suite inspired by an exhibition of paintings by his friend Viktor Hartmann. He also wrote the opera Boris Godunov and the tone poem Night on Bald Mountain. For 10 points, name this member of The Five.

This French composer wrote Symphonie fantastique, a work with an idée fixe representing the artist's beloved. He also wrote the opera Les Troyens and a treatise on orchestration. For 10 points, name this Romantic composer.
This African-American composer's "Maple Leaf Rag" became a hit in 1899. He also wrote "The Entertainer," which was used in the film The Sting. For 10 points, name this "King of Ragtime."

This trumpeter led a quintet that made Kind of Blue in 1959, with John Coltrane on saxophone. He pioneered cool jazz and later electric jazz fusion with Bitches Brew. For 10 points, name this jazz musician.

This American singer was nicknamed the "First Lady of Song." She was known for her scat singing and for songbook albums of Cole Porter and George Gershwin. For 10 points, name this jazz vocalist who recorded "Summertime" with Louis Armstrong.

This singer-songwriter wrote "Blowin' in the Wind" and "The Times They Are a-Changin'." He went electric at the 1965 Newport Folk Festival and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2016. For 10 points, name this artist of Highway 61 Revisited.

This type of piece features a soloist playing against an orchestra, usually with three movements: fast, slow, fast. Examples include Beethoven's Emperor and Tchaikovsky's one for violin. For 10 points, name this kind of work.

This woodwind instrument has a single reed and a cylindrical bore. Benny Goodman was a famous jazz player of it, and Mozart wrote a famous concerto for it. For 10 points, name this instrument whose lower register is called the chalumeau.

This string instrument is held between the knees and played with a bow. Yo-Yo Ma plays it, and Bach wrote six unaccompanied suites for it. It is tuned a fifth lower than a viola. For 10 points, name this instrument.
This form of unaccompanied, monophonic sacred song was codified in the Middle Ages and named for a pope. It is sung in Latin without harmony by monks. For 10 points, name this type of chant.

In a concerto, this is an unaccompanied passage for the soloist, often improvised in the classical era. It usually comes near the end of a movement, before the orchestra returns. For 10 points, name this showy passage.

This English Baroque composer wrote the opera Dido and Aeneas, which includes "When I am laid in earth." He worked in the Chapel Royal and wrote Come Ye Sons of Art. For 10 points, name this composer.

This Italian composer's L'Orfeo from 1607 is one of the earliest operas still regularly performed. He wrote the Vespers of 1610 and worked at Saint Mark's in Venice. For 10 points, name this composer.

This Viennese composer was called the "Waltz King." He wrote the Blue Danube and the operetta Die Fledermaus. His father, who wrote the Radetzky March, shared his name. For 10 points, name this composer.

This American composer and conductor wrote the music for West Side Story and led the New York Philharmonic. He also wrote Candide and the Chichester Psalms. For 10 points, name this man who gave televised Young People's Concerts.

text: This peak in the Sierra Nevada is the highest in the contiguous United States, at over fourteen thousand feet. It lies on the border of Inyo and Tulare counties in California. The town of Lone Pine sits at its eastern base. For 10 points, name this mountain.

This deep alpine lake on the California-Nevada border is known for its clear blue water. It lies in a basin of the Sierra Nevada and has ski resorts such as Heavenly nearby. Emerald Bay is on its southwestern shore. For 10 points, name this lake.

This Kentucky national park protects the longest known cave system in the world. Its passages have been explored for more than four hundred miles. Visitors tour its chambers such as the Rotunda. For 10 points, name this cave.

This New Mexico national park in the Guadalupe Mountains has a huge chamber called the Big Room. Millions of bats emerge from its entrance at dusk. It is named for a nearby city. For 10 points, name these limestone caves.

Clingmans Dome is the highest point in this mountain range on the Tennessee-North Carolina border. The Cades Cove valley lies within it. Blue mist often hangs over its slopes. For 10 points, name this part of the Appalachians whose national park takes its name.

John Muir called this range the "Range of Light." It stretches along the eastern edge of California and includes Yosemite and Sequoia national parks. Its eastern face rises steeply above the Owens Valley. For 10 points, name this mountain range.

This volcanic mountain range runs from northern California through Oregon and Washington. It includes Mount Rainier, Mount Hood, and Mount Shasta. It is part of the Pacific Ring of Fire. For 10 points, name this range of the Pacific Northwest.

This river of the northwestern United States flows through Idaho's Hells Canyon and past Lewiston. It begins in Wyoming near Jackson Hole and joins the Columbia River in Washington. Shoshone Falls is on it. For 10 points, name this river.

This river flows south from the Adirondacks past Albany to New York Harbor. The Palisades and West Point lie along it. It is named for an English explorer who sailed on it in 1609. For 10 points, name this river.

This waterway opened in 1825 and connected Albany to Buffalo. It was nicknamed "Clinton's Ditch" for the governor who championed it. It made New York City the nation's leading port. For 10 points, name this man-made channel linking the Hudson River to Lake Erie.

Brooklyn and Queens are on this island, which stretches east from New York City. It includes the Hamptons and Montauk Point on its eastern end. Fire Island lies off its south shore. For 10 points, name this large island of New York State.

This chain of barrier islands off North Carolina includes Kitty Hawk and Roanoke Island. The lost colony of Roanoke was here, and the Wright brothers flew nearby. Hurricanes frequently erode its narrow sands. For 10 points, name these islands on the Atlantic coast.

This range in South Dakota and Wyoming is sacred to the Lakota. Gold was discovered there in 1874, leading to the town of Deadwood. Crazy Horse Memorial is carved into one of its mountains. For 10 points, name these hills.

Eroded buttes and pinnacles with colorful strata mark this national park in South Dakota. Its name was given by the Lakota. Bighorn sheep and prairie dogs live on its grasslands. For 10 points, name this dry landscape.

This highland region in Missouri, Arkansas, and Oklahoma is a forested plateau, not a true mountain range. Branson and a large reservoir on the Osage River are in it. Its caves and springs are typical of karst terrain. For 10 points, name this region of the central United States.

This large shallow lake in south-central Florida drains into the Everglades. A dike built after hurricanes in the 1920s surrounds it. Its name comes from a Seminole word for "big water." For 10 points, name this lake.

This river rises in the San Juan Mountains of Colorado and flows through Albuquerque and El Paso. It forms part of the border between Texas and Mexico. It reaches the Gulf of Mexico near Brownsville. For 10 points, name this river.

Sandstone buttes such as the Mittens rise from the desert floor in this Navajo Tribal Park on the Utah-Arizona border. Many Western films by John Ford were shot there. For 10 points, name this red-rock landscape.

This Wyoming rock formation, a column of igneous rock, was declared the first national monument in 1906. Its sides are fluted columns. It was featured in the film Close Encounters of the Third Kind. For 10 points, name this tower.

This Oregon lake fills the caldera of Mount Mazama, which erupted about 7,700 years ago. Wizard Island rises from it. It is the deepest lake in the United States. For 10 points, name this national park lake.

El Capitan and Half Dome rise above this California valley. Ansel Adams photographed its waterfalls, and John Muir campaigned to protect it. Glaciers carved its granite walls. For 10 points, name this national park in the Sierra Nevada.

This chain of volcanic islands stretches west from the Alaska Peninsula toward Russia. Dutch Harbor is a major fishing port there. Japan invaded Attu and Kiska in World War II. For 10 points, name this archipelago.

This fault runs through California for hundreds of miles, where the Pacific Plate slides past the North American Plate. Slippage on it caused the 1906 earthquake in San Francisco. For 10 points, name this transform fault.

This large region of the western United States has no outlet to the sea, so its rivers drain into salt flats and lakes. It includes most of Nevada and part of Utah. Bristlecone pines grow in its mountains. For 10 points, name this high desert.

This desert covers much of southern Arizona and northwestern Mexico. The tall saguaro cactus grows there, and it has two rainy seasons each year. Phoenix and Tucson are in it. For 10 points, name this desert.

This line in the Rocky Mountains separates rivers that flow toward the Atlantic and Gulf from those that flow toward the Pacific. It follows peaks from New Mexico to Montana. For 10 points, name this feature, whose Triple Divide Peak is in Glacier National Park.

This point is the only place in the United States where four states meet. They are Utah, Colorado, New Mexico, and Arizona. A monument marks the spot on Navajo land. For 10 points, name this location.
Seneca and Cayuga are among these long narrow lakes in central New York, carved by glaciers. Ithaca sits at the south end of one. The region is known for wineries. For 10 points, name these lakes.

This capital of Colorado is called the Mile High City because its elevation is about 5,280 feet. It lies where the Great Plains meet the Rocky Mountains. Coors Field is there. For 10 points, name this city.

The Space Needle, built for the 1962 World's Fair, rises over this city in Washington State. It lies between Puget Sound and Lake Washington. Pike Place Market is there. For 10 points, name this city.

This lake north of New Orleans is crossed by a very long causeway. It is brackish and connects to the Gulf of Mexico through passes. Its name honors a French minister. For 10 points, name this Louisiana lake.

text: This river rises in the Black Forest of Germany and flows past Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest, and Belgrade. Its delta in Romania is a wildlife reserve. It empties into the Black Sea. For 10 points, name this second-longest river in Europe.

This river begins in the Swiss Alps and flows north past Basel, Cologne, and Rotterdam to the North Sea. Its Middle Rhine gorge is famous for castles and the Lorelei rock. Barges carry heavy cargo along it. For 10 points, name this European river.

This longest river in Europe flows through Russia past Kazan, Nizhny Novgorod, and Volgograd. It ends in a large delta on the Caspian Sea. It is called "Mother" in Russian folk tradition. For 10 points, name this river.

This river is sacred to Hindus and flows past Varanasi. Its tributary, the Yamuna, joins it at Allahabad. Its delta, shared with Bangladesh, empties into the Bay of Bengal. For 10 points, name this river of northern India.

This river in central Africa crosses the equator twice. The capitals Kinshasa and Brazzaville face each other across it. It is the deepest river in the world. For 10 points, name this river, which empties into the Atlantic Ocean.

This waterfall on the Zambezi River lies on the border of Zambia and Zimbabwe. David Livingstone named it for a British queen. Its local name means "the smoke that thunders." For 10 points, name this falls.
This is the largest lake in Africa, shared by Uganda, Kenya, and Tanzania. John Hanning Speke named it in 1858. It is the main source of the White Nile. For 10 points, name this lake.

This lake in southern Siberia is the deepest lake in the world and holds a large share of the planet's unfrozen fresh water. Irkutsk is nearby. The nerpa seal lives only here. For 10 points, name this lake.

The cities of Baku and Astrakhan lie on this largest inland body of water, which has no outlet to the ocean. Kazakhstan, Iran, Turkmenistan, Azerbaijan, and Russia surround it. It is famous for its sturgeon, source of caviar. For 10 points, name this body of water.

Odessa and Varna are ports on this sea, which connects to the Mediterranean via the Bosphorus. The Danube empties into it. Constanta in Romania and Batumi in Georgia are ports on it. For 10 points, name this sea between Europe and Asia.

The shore of this salt lake, between Israel and Jordan, is the lowest land elevation on Earth. Swimmers float easily on it because it is so salty. Scrolls were found in caves at Qumran near it. For 10 points, name this sea fed by the Jordan River.

This sea separates Africa from the Arabian Peninsula. Its northern end splits into the Gulf of Suez and the Gulf of Aqaba. Eritrea and Saudi Arabia lie on its coasts. For 10 points, name this sea that Moses parts in the Book of Exodus.
The Strait of Hormuz links this body of water to the Gulf of Oman. Kuwait, Bahrain, and Qatar lie on it. Iran lies on its northern coast. For 10 points, name this gulf, rich in oil.

Knossos, the palace of the Minoan civilization, is on this largest Greek island. Its capital and largest city is Heraklion. In myth, King Minos kept the Minotaur in a labyrinth here, and Zeus was said to have been raised in one of its caves. For 10 points, name this island south of the Aegean Sea.

This desert in northern Chile is considered the driest non-polar desert on Earth. Parts of it have gone without rain for years. Its nitrate deposits once caused wars. For 10 points, name this desert west of the Andes.

This semi-arid sandy region covers much of Botswana and parts of Namibia and South Africa. The San people have lived there for thousands of years. The Okavango Delta lies in it. For 10 points, name this southern African desert.

Each year, huge herds of wildebeest and zebras migrate across this ecosystem in northern Tanzania. Its name comes from a Maasai word meaning "endless plains." Ngorongoro Crater lies nearby. For 10 points, name this national park and plain.
This island nation in the North Atlantic sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Its capital is Reykjavik. It is known for geysers, glaciers like Vatnajokull, and volcanoes. For 10 points, name this country.

Palermo and Catania are cities on this largest island in the Mediterranean Sea. Mount Etna is a volcano on it. The Strait of Messina separates it from the Italian mainland. For 10 points, name this island south of Italy.
This high plateau north of the Himalayas is sometimes called the "Roof of the World." Lhasa lies on it. Many major Asian rivers begin there. For 10 points, name this plateau, located mostly in China.

These mountains run north to south through Russia and are the traditional boundary between Europe and Asia. Yekaterinburg lies at their eastern foot. Rich mineral deposits have been mined there. For 10 points, name this range.
This range separates the Iberian Peninsula from the rest of Europe. The tiny country of Andorra lies within it. Its high point is Aneto. For 10 points, name these mountains between Spain and France.

Olduvai Gorge and Lake Tanganyika lie within this long fault system in East Africa, where tectonic plates are pulling apart. It extends from the Red Sea region south to Mozambique. Many early hominid fossils have been found along it. For 10 points, name this trough.

Challenger Deep, the deepest known point in the oceans, lies in this feature of the western Pacific. It lies near the island of Guam. The Trieste carried two men to its bottom in 1960. For 10 points, name this deep trench.

This lake on the border of Peru and Bolivia is one of the highest large navigable lakes in the world. The Uros people live on floating islands made of reeds. It lies on the Altiplano in the Andes. For 10 points, name this lake.

This waterfall in Venezuela is the tallest in the world. It plunges from the flat summit of Auyan-tepui. Its English name honors a pilot who landed his plane on the plateau above it. For 10 points, name this falls.

The Drake Passage lies just south of this headland, the southernmost tip of South America's Tierra del Fuego archipelago. Sailors have long feared its storms and high waves. It belongs to Chile. For 10 points, name this cape.
Bartolomeu Dias rounded this cape in 1488 and called it the Cape of Storms. It is near Cape Town, South Africa. Its later name inspired hope of a sea route to India. For 10 points, name this cape.

This narrow strait connects the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara. It passes through Istanbul and is crossed by several suspension bridges. It forms part of the boundary between Europe and Asia. For 10 points, name this strait.

This region at the southern end of South America is divided between Argentina and Chile. Perito Moreno Glacier is in it. Its steppe is home to guanacos and penguins. For 10 points, name this windswept region.

The cone of this volcano in Japan is nearly symmetrical and rises to about 3,776 meters. It last erupted in 1707. Climbers ascend it in summer, and snow covers its peak. For 10 points, name this sacred mountain west of Tokyo.

text: This Serbian-American engineer developed the alternating-current induction motor and the coil that bears his name. He worked briefly for Thomas Edison before partnering with George Westinghouse. The unit of magnetic flux density is named for him. For 10 points, name this inventor.

This Scottish scientist noticed in 1928 that a mold had killed bacteria in a dish at Saint Mary's Hospital in London. The mold was Penicillium. He shared the 1945 Nobel Prize for the discovery of the first true antibiotic. For 10 points, name this man who discovered penicillin.

This French chemist developed a vaccine for rabies in 1885 and treated a boy named Joseph Meister. He disproved spontaneous generation and championed germ theory. A process that heats liquids to kill microbes is named for him. For 10 points, name this scientist.

This German physicist discovered X-rays in 1895 in Wurzburg. He made an image of his wife's hand showing her bones. In 1901 he received the first Nobel Prize in Physics. For 10 points, name this scientist.

This Swedish chemist and engineer invented dynamite in 1867. His will left money for prizes in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature, and peace. He owned an armaments company. For 10 points, name this man for whom a set of annual prizes is named.

This American inventor patented the cotton gin in 1793, which sped the separation of seeds from cotton fibers. He later promoted interchangeable parts in making muskets. He graduated from Yale. For 10 points, name this man.

This automaker introduced the Model T in 1908 and started a moving assembly line at Highland Park in 1913. He offered workers a five-dollar day. His company was based in Dearborn, Michigan. For 10 points, name this American industrialist.

This Austrian friar studied traits in pea plants in the garden of his monastery in Brno. His 1866 paper described dominant and recessive factors. His work was largely ignored until about 1900. For 10 points, name this founder of genetics.

This British mathematician helped break the Enigma cipher at Bletchley Park during World War II. He proposed an abstract computing machine in 1936. A test for machine intelligence is named for him. For 10 points, name this man.

This woman, a daughter of Lord Byron, wrote notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, including what is considered the first computer program. She was an English mathematician. A programming language is named for her. For 10 points, name this Countess of Lovelace.

This British scientist at CERN proposed a system of linked hypertext documents in 1989. He wrote the first web browser and server. He created HTML and HTTP. For 10 points, name this inventor of the World Wide Web.

Michelangelo painted the ceiling of this chapel in the Vatican between 1508 and 1512. Its fresco The Creation of Adam shows two fingers nearly touching. New popes are chosen in conclave inside it. For 10 points, name this papal chapel.

This Roman temple is topped by a concrete dome with a round opening called the oculus. The emperor Hadrian rebuilt it around 126 CE. The artist Raphael is buried there. For 10 points, name this well-preserved temple in Rome.

The Treasury, or Al-Khazneh, is carved into the rose-colored sandstone cliffs of this ancient city in Jordan. The Nabataeans built it, and visitors enter through a narrow canyon called the Siq. It appeared in an Indiana Jones film. For 10 points, name this archaeological site.

Suryavarman II built this temple in Cambodia in the twelfth century. It features five towers that resemble lotus buds and miles of carved reliefs. It was originally Hindu and later became Buddhist. For 10 points, name this temple complex near Siem Reap.
Jorn Utzon designed this performing arts center whose roof resembles sails. It stands on Bennelong Point in Sydney Harbour and opened in 1973. For 10 points, name this building in Australia.

Construction began on this tower in 1173, and the soil under one side soon began to sink. Galileo is said to have dropped balls from it. It is a freestanding bell tower of a cathedral in Tuscany. For 10 points, name this tilted tower.
This Roman city was buried by ash when Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE. Excavations found plaster casts of victims. Its nearby sister town was Herculaneum. For 10 points, name this city near Naples.

El Castillo, a step pyramid dedicated to the feathered serpent Kukulcan, stands at this Maya site in the Yucatan. The pyramid casts a serpent-shaped shadow at the equinoxes. A large ball court is also here. For 10 points, name this archaeological site.

This hilltop palace and fortress in Granada, Spain, was built by the Nasrid rulers. Its Court of the Lions has a fountain supported by twelve stone lions. It is a masterpiece of Moorish architecture. For 10 points, name this complex.

This set of annual awards was created through the will of a Hungarian-American newspaper publisher. Columbia University administers it. Categories include journalism, fiction, poetry, and music. For 10 points, name this prize first awarded in 1917.
The Soviet Union launched this first artificial satellite on October 4, 1957. It beeped as it circled the Earth. Its launch began the space race. For 10 points, name this satellite.

This telescope was launched aboard Space Shuttle Discovery in 1990. Its main mirror had a flaw that was fixed during a 1993 repair mission. It is named for an astronomer who showed that the universe contains many galaxies. For 10 points, name this orbiting observatory.

This ancient network of trade routes connected China with the Mediterranean. Silk, spices, and ideas traveled along it. Cities such as Samarkand and Kashgar grew rich from it. For 10 points, name this system.

Antonio Stradivari of Cremona, Italy, made string instruments prized for their sound. Some of his violins sell for millions of dollars. They were made in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. For 10 points, name this family of famous violins.

Between 1892 and 1954, millions of immigrants were processed at this small island in New York Harbor. It is now a museum. Statue of Liberty is a short ferry ride away. For 10 points, name this island.

This Albanian-born nun founded the Missionaries of Charity in Calcutta. She worked among the poor and dying and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979. The Catholic Church canonized her in 2016. For 10 points, name this woman.

This Jewish teenager hid with her family in a secret annex in Amsterdam during World War II. Her diary was published after her death at Bergen-Belsen. Her father Otto survived. For 10 points, name this author of The Diary of a Young Girl.
This British primatologist began studying chimpanzees at Gombe Stream in Tanzania in 1960. She observed them using tools. She worked with Louis Leakey. For 10 points, name this scientist.

This French explorer co-invented the Aqualung with Emile Gagnan and sailed the research ship Calypso. He made documentaries including The Silent World. His work promoted ocean conservation. For 10 points, name this undersea explorer.
