text: Two feuding families, the Montagues and Capulets, are at the center of this play set in Verona. The title lovers meet at a masked ball and are secretly married by Friar Laurence. A plan involving a sleeping potion goes wrong, and both lovers die. For 10 points, name this tragedy by William Shakespeare.

In this play the ghost of a murdered king appears to his son on the battlements of Elsinore. The prince feigns madness, stages a play within a play, and mistakenly kills Polonius. It contains the soliloquy "To be, or not to be." For 10 points, name this tragedy by William Shakespeare.

Three witches tell a Scottish general that he will become king, spurring him on to murder. His wife urges him on and later sleepwalks, trying to wash imaginary blood from her hands. Birnam Wood appears to move to Dunsinane Hill in this play. For 10 points, name this Shakespeare tragedy.

Elizabeth Bennet rejects a first proposal from Mister Darcy, in part because of his pride and because of lies told by George Wickham. Her sister Jane falls in love with Mister Bingley, and Lydia elopes with Wickham. For 10 points, name this novel by Jane Austen.

Ebenezer Scrooge is visited by the ghost of his dead partner, Jacob Marley, and then by three spirits representing past, present, and future. Scrooge's clerk, Bob Cratchit, has a sickly son named Tiny Tim. For 10 points, name this Charles Dickens novella.

Pip is helped by a secret benefactor after he meets an escaped convict named Abel Magwitch on the marshes. He later visits the eccentric Miss Havisham and falls in love with her ward Estella. For 10 points, name this novel by Charles Dickens.

This novel's title character becomes a governess at Thornfield Hall, where she falls in love with Mister Rochester. A mysterious laugh in the attic turns out to come from Rochester's first wife, Bertha Mason. For 10 points, name this novel by Charlotte Bronte.

A young scientist builds a creature from body parts and brings it to life in a laboratory. The creature, abandoned by its maker, learns language by watching a family and then seeks revenge. Mary Shelley wrote this novel as part of a ghost story contest. For 10 points, name this novel.

A group of boys stranded on an island elect Ralph as their leader, but Jack leads a rebellion. Piggy's glasses are used to start a signal fire, and Simon is killed during a frenzy. For 10 points, name this novel by William Golding.

Winston Smith works at the Ministry of Truth, rewriting history, and secretly begins a love affair with Julia. He is arrested and tortured in Room 101 by O'Brien. Big Brother watches the citizens of Oceania. For 10 points, name this dystopian novel by George Orwell.

The pig Squealer spreads propaganda, and the sheep chant "four legs good, two legs bad." Napoleon drives out his rival Snowball, and the workhorse Boxer is sold to a knacker after working himself to exhaustion on a windmill. A commandment is altered to say "but some animals are more equal than others." For 10 points, name this allegorical novella by George Orwell.

The hero of this Old English poem defeats the monster Grendel and Grendel's mother, then dies fighting a dragon as king of the Geats. The poem is set in Heorot, the hall of Hrothgar. For 10 points, name this epic poem.

A group of pilgrims tell stories to pass the time on a trip from the Tabard Inn to Canterbury. Characters include the Wife of Bath, the Miller, and the Pardoner. For 10 points, name this work in Middle English by Geoffrey Chaucer.

This Romantic poet wrote that poetry is "the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings" in the preface to Lyrical Ballads. He also wrote "Tintern Abbey" and the poem about wandering "lonely as a cloud" and seeing daffodils. For 10 points, name this friend of Coleridge.

Heathcliff is brought to a house on the Yorkshire moors and falls in love with Catherine Earnshaw, who marries Edgar Linton instead. Nelly Dean narrates much of this novel. For 10 points, name this novel by Emily Bronte.

In this play Puck mistakenly puts a love potion on the eyes of Lysander, and Titania falls in love with Bottom, who has been given a donkey's head. Oberon and Titania quarrel over a changeling boy. For 10 points, name this Shakespeare comedy.

This epic poem begins by invoking a Heavenly Muse to sing of "man's first disobedience." It features Satan declaring "Better to reign in Hell than serve in Heaven" and ends with Adam and Eve leaving Eden. Written by a blind poet, it is in twelve books. For 10 points, name this epic by John Milton.

The title character in this satire visits the flying island of Laputa, where scientists neglect practical matters, and meets the immortal but miserable Struldbrugs. He ends up preferring the company of intelligent horses called Houyhnhnms to humans. The author also wrote "A Modest Proposal." For 10 points, name this satire by Jonathan Swift.

This author created a detective who lives at 221B Baker Street and is assisted by Doctor Watson. His villain Professor Moriarty fought the detective at the Reichenbach Falls. For 10 points, name this author of The Hound of the Baskervilles.

Jim Hawkins finds a map in the chest of Billy Bones and sails on the Hispaniola in search of buried loot. The cook Long John Silver turns out to be a pirate and the leader of a mutiny. For 10 points, name this adventure novel by Robert Louis Stevenson.

Algernon pretends to be named Ernest to attract Cecily, while Jack uses the same name to court Gwendolen. Lady Bracknell famously asks "A handbag?" on learning where Jack was found as a baby. For 10 points, name this play by Oscar Wilde.

Marlow narrates a journey up the Congo River to find the ivory trader Kurtz, whose last words are "The horror! The horror!" This novella is told on a boat on the Thames. For 10 points, name this work by Joseph Conrad.

Angel Clare abandons his bride after she confesses she bore a child outside of marriage; she is later hanged after murdering Alec. This novel is set in Wessex and is subtitled "A Pure Woman." For 10 points, name this novel by Thomas Hardy.

This Middle English poem begins when a green giant enters Camelot at New Year and proposes a beheading game. The hero is later tempted by the wife of Lord Bertilak. For 10 points, name this poem about a knight of King Arthur's court.
answer: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight

text: In this dystopia, babies are grown in hatcheries and conditioned to accept their castes, and the drug soma keeps citizens happy. John the Savage is brought from a reservation to London. For 10 points, name this novel by Aldous Huxley.

This modernist author's novels include Mrs Dalloway and To the Lighthouse, and her long essay argues that a woman needs money and a room of her own to write fiction. She was a member of the Bloomsbury Group. For 10 points, name this author of Orlando.

Bilbo Baggins is recruited by Gandalf to join a company of thirteen dwarves, including Thorin Oakenshield. He finds a ring in a cave while riddling with Gollum and helps recover treasure from Smaug. For 10 points, name this prequel to The Lord of the Rings by J. R. R. Tolkien.

This Romantic poet wrote the long satirical poem Don Juan and the autobiographical Childe Harold's Pilgrimage. He was described as "mad, bad, and dangerous to know" and died during the Greek War of Independence. For 10 points, name this poet.

In this play, Iago convinces the Moorish general that his wife Desdemona has been unfaithful, using a lost handkerchief as evidence. Cassio is demoted, and Roderigo is used as a pawn. For 10 points, name this Shakespeare tragedy.

Jonathan Harker travels to Transylvania to meet a count who is later shipped to England in boxes of earth. Abraham Van Helsing leads the hunt, and Mina Harker is menaced. For 10 points, name this vampire novel by Bram Stoker.

text: A deluded minor nobleman reads so many chivalric romances that he sets out as a knight-errant with a farmer named Sancho Panza as his squire. He attacks windmills he believes to be giants and calls a peasant woman, Dulcinea, his lady. For 10 points, name this novel by Miguel de Cervantes.
alternates: The Ingenious Gentleman Don Quixote of La Mancha

text: In this poem the narrator is guided by Virgil through nine circles of a place in which sinners are punished according to their sins. Its inscription over the gate says "Abandon all hope, ye who enter here." The poet ends up meeting the traitors Judas, Brutus, and Cassius in the ninth circle. For 10 points, name this first part of the Divine Comedy by Dante.

The ex-convict Jean Valjean is hunted for decades by the policeman Javert in this novel, which climaxes at a barricade during the June Rebellion of 1832. Valjean adopts the orphan Cosette, who falls in love with Marius. For 10 points, name this novel by Victor Hugo.

A pilot stranded in the Sahara meets a small boy who has traveled from an asteroid and who cares for a single rose. He also befriends a fox, who teaches him that "what is essential is invisible to the eye." For 10 points, name this novella by Antoine de Saint-Exupery.

After the murder of an old pawnbroker, a former student named Raskolnikov is slowly worn down by guilt and by the detective Porfiry Petrovich. He confesses at the urging of the pious Sonya. For 10 points, name this novel by Fyodor Dostoevsky.

Pierre Bezukhov fights a duel with Dolokhov and later befriends the peasant Platon Karataev as a prisoner of the French. Prince Andrei is wounded at Austerlitz, and Natasha nearly elopes with Anatole Kuragin. The story covers the Napoleonic wars in Russia. For 10 points, name this very long novel by Leo Tolstoy.

Gregor Samsa wakes up to discover he has been turned into a giant insect. His family becomes increasingly resentful, and he dies after his father throws apples at him. For 10 points, name this novella by Franz Kafka.

The title scholar makes a pact with the devil Mephistopheles, and he falls in love with the young Gretchen. Dissatisfied with the limits of human knowledge, he wagers that he will never say to a moment "Stay, you are so beautiful." For 10 points, name this dramatic poem by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe.

The title character in this novel leaves her husband Karenin for Count Vronsky and throws herself under a train. A parallel plot follows the landowner Konstantin Levin and his courtship of Kitty. For 10 points, name this novel by Leo Tolstoy.

Nora Helmer forges a signature to save her husband's life, and then leaves him at the end of this play. Torvald calls her his "little squirrel," and she slams the door as she walks out. For 10 points, name this play by Henrik Ibsen.

Meursault attends his mother's funeral without crying and later shoots an Arab on a beach in Algiers. He is sentenced to death partly because of his apparent indifference. For 10 points, name this novel by Albert Camus.

A cadet with a large nose writes love letters for the handsome Christian to the beautiful Roxane. This play by Edmond Rostand ends with the hero dying while reciting a poem. For 10 points, name this title poet-swordsman.

Dr. Pangloss insists that this is "the best of all possible worlds" despite earthquakes and Inquisition burnings. The young hero is expelled from the castle of Baron Thunder-ten-tronckh for kissing Cunegonde. At the end, he decides "we must cultivate our garden." For 10 points, name this satire by Voltaire.

Edmond Dantes is imprisoned in the Chateau d'If after being falsely accused of treason. After escaping with the help of the Abbe Faria, he finds a hidden treasure and takes revenge on Danglars, Fernand, and Villefort. For 10 points, name this novel by Alexandre Dumas.

Charles Bovary's wife, Emma, has affairs with Rodolphe and Leon and runs up debts with the merchant Lheureux. She eventually poisons herself with arsenic. For 10 points, name this realist novel by Gustave Flaubert.

The monk Alyosha, the intellectual Ivan, and the sensualist Dmitri are three sons of the lecherous Fyodor Pavlovich, who is murdered. In this novel the "Grand Inquisitor" is a poem told by Ivan. For 10 points, name this last novel by Fyodor Dostoevsky.

The swindler Chichikov travels around Russia buying up serfs who have died but are still counted on tax rolls. This unfinished novel by Nikolai Gogol is subtitled "A Poem." For 10 points, name this work whose title refers to deceased serfs.

This Danish author wrote fairy tales including "The Ugly Duckling," "The Snow Queen," and "The Emperor's New Clothes." He also wrote about a mermaid who gives up her voice to gain legs. For 10 points, name this author.

In this play by a French dramatist, the title religious hypocrite is welcomed into the home of Orgon, who wants him to marry his daughter. Elmire exposes the impostor by hiding her husband under a table. For 10 points, name this comedy by Moliere.

Seven young women and three young men flee plague-stricken Florence to a villa in this work, where each tells a story every day for ten days. For 10 points, name this collection of one hundred tales by Giovanni Boccaccio.

Paul Baumer narrates this novel about a group of German schoolboys who enlist after a patriotic speech by their teacher, Kantorek. Paul is killed on a day when the army report says there was nothing new. For 10 points, name this World War I novel by Erich Maria Remarque.
answer: All Quiet on the Western Front

text: Josef K. is arrested one morning without being told what he is charged with. He is led to a quarry and killed "like a dog" after dealing with a nearly inaccessible court. For 10 points, name this unfinished novel by Franz Kafka.

This novel in verse follows a bored aristocrat who rejects the love of Tatyana and later kills his friend Lensky in a duel. The title character, a dandy, later regrets his rejection when she is married. For 10 points, name this work by Alexander Pushkin.

The Gaev family loses its estate to the businessman Lopakhin, who has it cut down for summer cottages. The sound of an axe is heard as the family leaves. For 10 points, name this play by Anton Chekhov.

A carpenter carves a puppet from a piece of wood, and it comes to life. Whenever the puppet lies, his nose grows longer, and he is swallowed by a giant whale. For 10 points, name this character, the creation of Carlo Collodi.

A man named Govinda accompanies a young Brahmin on his journey, but then the hero meets the Buddha and decides to find his own path. He eventually becomes a ferryman and learns from a river. For 10 points, name this novel by Hermann Hesse.

This multi-volume work begins with the narrator dipping a madeleine into tea, which triggers memories of Combray. It follows Swann's love for Odette and the narrator's love for Albertine. For 10 points, name this work by Marcel Proust.
alternates: A la recherche du temps perdu

text: A young man falls in love with Lotte, who is engaged to Albert, and he shoots himself with a pistol borrowed from Albert. This novel in letters brought its young author fame and inspired a wave of suicides. For 10 points, name this work by Goethe.

This poet wrote a collection of poems called "Flowers of Evil" and translated Edgar Allan Poe into French. He also wrote the poem "Correspondances" and introduced the figure of the flaneur. For 10 points, name this French poet.

The title doctor falls in love with Lara, who is also loved by Komarovsky, and writes poems during the Russian Revolution. The novel's publication was suppressed in the Soviet Union, and its author won the Nobel Prize in 1958. For 10 points, name this novel by Boris Pasternak.

text: Okonkwo, a wrestler and farmer in the village of Umuofia, kills a messenger and accidentally kills a clansman, leading to his exile. When he returns, missionaries have transformed his community, and he hangs himself. For 10 points, name this novel by Chinua Achebe.

The Buendia family lives in the town of Macondo, which is founded by Jose Arcadio Buendia. Colonel Aureliano Buendia fights in civil wars, and the last of the family reads Melquiades's parchments as the town is blown away. For 10 points, name this novel by Gabriel Garcia Marquez.

A woman tells a story every night to a king who has been executing his brides after one night. She saves herself by leaving each tale unfinished at dawn. Stories in this collection include "Aladdin" and "Sinbad the Sailor." For 10 points, name this collection.

This epic poem begins with an invocation of the Muse and follows a king of Ithaca who spends ten years trying to return home after the Trojan War. He blinds the Cyclops Polyphemus and listens to the Sirens tied to a mast. For 10 points, name this epic attributed to Homer.

This epic begins with the wrath of a Greek hero, who withdraws from battle after a quarrel with Agamemnon. His friend Patroclus is killed wearing his armor, and he kills Hector in revenge. For 10 points, name this epic attributed to Homer about the Trojan War.

Dasaratha's wife Kaikeyi demands that his eldest son be exiled for fourteen years. Rama's brother Lakshmana accompanies him, and Hanuman leaps over the sea to find the kidnapped Sita in Lanka. It is traditionally ascribed to Valmiki. For 10 points, name this Sanskrit epic attributed to Valmiki.

This enormous Sanskrit epic is about a war between the Pandavas and the Kauravas, and includes a dialogue between Arjuna and Krishna on the battlefield of Kurukshetra. For 10 points, name this epic, which contains the Bhagavad Gita.

Often called the world's first novel, this work by Murasaki Shikibu follows a prince of the Heian court and his many romances. Written in the early eleventh century, it also follows his son Kaoru. For 10 points, name this Japanese work whose title character is "shining."

This author renounced his knighthood in 1919 after the Amritsar massacre. He wrote the novel The Home and the World and the songs that became the national anthems of India and Bangladesh. He won the 1913 Nobel Prize for a collection of "Song Offerings." For 10 points, name this author.

This poet served as consul in Burma and as ambassador to France under Salvador Allende. He lived at Isla Negra and appears as a character in the film Il Postino. He wrote the collection Residence on Earth and the epic Canto General. For 10 points, name this poet.
This Nigerian author was the first African to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1986. His plays include Death and the King's Horseman and A Dance of the Forests. For 10 points, name this author.

This Argentine writer's short stories include "The Garden of Forking Paths," "The Library of Babel," and "The Aleph." His story collections include Ficciones and Labyrinths, and he was blind in his later years. For 10 points, name this author.

In this Chinese novel, a monk named Tripitaka travels to India to obtain Buddhist scriptures, accompanied by Pigsy, Sandy, and a monkey who can transform in seventy-two ways. For 10 points, name this novel, whose Monkey King is Sun Wukong.

This Qing dynasty novel follows the decline of the Jia family and the love triangle among Jia Baoyu, Lin Daiyu, and Xue Baochai. Cao Xueqin wrote the first eighty chapters. For 10 points, name this classic of Chinese literature, also known as The Story of the Stone.

Saleem Sinai is born at the stroke of midnight on the day India becomes independent and has telepathic powers connecting him to other children born in that hour. For 10 points, name this novel by Salman Rushdie.

This Mesopotamian epic follows a king of Uruk and his friend Enkidu, who is created by the gods. After Enkidu's death, the hero seeks immortality from Utnapishtim, a survivor of a flood. For 10 points, name this epic.

The Trojan Aeneas flees the burning city and has a tragic affair with the queen of Carthage, Dido. He then travels to Italy, where his descendants will found Rome. For 10 points, name this Latin epic by Virgil.

The seer Tiresias tells the king that he himself is the cause of a plague. A shepherd from Corinth reveals that the king was left on a mountain as a baby, after solving the riddle of the Sphinx. Jocasta hangs herself, and the king puts out his own eyes. For 10 points, name this play by Sophocles.

In this tragedy, the title princess of Colchis kills her own children to take revenge on her husband Jason, who plans to marry Glauce. She then escapes in a chariot drawn by dragons. For 10 points, name this play by Euripides.

In this Chilean novel, the Trueba family is led by Esteban and his wife Clara, who has clairvoyant powers. The granddaughter Alba is tortured after a military coup. For 10 points, name this first novel by Isabel Allende.

This Egyptian author's novels include Midaq Alley and the Cairo Trilogy, which follows the family of Al-Sayyid Ahmad Abd al-Jawad. He won the 1988 Nobel Prize in Literature. For 10 points, name this author.

This Japanese author wrote Norwegian Wood, Kafka on the Shore, and The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle. His novels blend realism with magic and often feature cats, wells, and jazz. For 10 points, name this author.
This Persian epic by Ferdowsi recounts the history of Persian kings, including the hero Rostam, who unknowingly kills his own son Sohrab. For 10 points, name this national epic of Iran.

This author wrote the Masnavi and the Diwan of Shams of Tabriz. A Persian poet and Sufi mystic, he founded the Mevlevi order, known for whirling dervishes. For 10 points, name this thirteenth-century poet.
In this South African novel, Reverend Stephen Kumalo travels to Johannesburg to search for his son Absalom, who has killed a white man. For 10 points, name this novel by Alan Paton.

In this black-and-white work, the author is sent to school in Vienna as a teenager and later returns home to marry. A young girl wears a headscarf to school after the fall of the Shah. Its author describes growing up in Iran during the Islamic Revolution and the Iran-Iraq War. For 10 points, name this graphic memoir by Marjane Satrapi.

Women of Athens and Sparta go on a sex strike to force their husbands to end the Peloponnesian War. The heroine leads the women who seize the Acropolis, and the men eventually give in. For 10 points, name this comedy by Aristophanes.

This Roman poet, who was exiled to Tomis by Augustus, wrote the Art of Love and a poem of fifteen books, which retells myths of transformations from creation to the deification of Julius Caesar. For 10 points, name this author of Metamorphoses.
A young man named Juan Preciado goes to the town of Comala to look for his father, only to find a town of whispering ghosts. For 10 points, name this novel by Mexican author Juan Rulfo.
This Lebanese-American writer's book of twenty-six prose poems is spoken by Almustafa, who is leaving the city of Orphalese after twelve years. For 10 points, name this author of The Prophet.

In this dystopian novel, Offred is a handmaid in the Republic of Gilead. Her role is to bear children for the Commander and his wife Serena Joy. For 10 points, name this novel by Canadian author Margaret Atwood.

text: A pig named Wilbur is saved from slaughter when a barn spider spins words like "SOME PIG" in her web. The girl Fern befriends the pig, and the rat Templeton helps the spider. For 10 points, name this children's novel by E. B. White.

An orphan raised by the Dursleys learns on his eleventh birthday that he is a wizard and is sent to Hogwarts. His friends Ron and Hermione help him fight the dark wizard Voldemort, who gave him a lightning-shaped scar. For 10 points, name this series by J. K. Rowling.

Four siblings named Peter, Susan, Edmund, and Lucy enter a magical land through a wardrobe. They help the lion Aslan defeat the White Witch, who has made it always winter but never Christmas. For 10 points, name this fantasy series by C. S. Lewis.

A girl follows a talking White Rabbit down a hole and encounters a Cheshire Cat, a Mad Hatter, and a Queen who says "Off with her head." For 10 points, name this novel by Lewis Carroll, which was followed by a sequel about a looking glass.

This author wrote about a mischievous feline in a tall striped hat and about a Grinch who steals Christmas. His real name was Theodor Geisel, and he also wrote Green Eggs and Ham. For 10 points, name this children's author.

Meg Murry travels through a tesseract with her brother Charles Wallace to rescue her father from the evil force IT. Three strange guides named Whatsit, Who, and Which help the children. For 10 points, name this novel by Madeleine L'Engle.
Jonas lives in a community without pain or color and is chosen as the Receiver of Memory. He later runs away with a baby named Gabriel. For 10 points, name this dystopian novel by Lois Lowry.

In this novel, the desert planet Arrakis is the only source of the spice melange. Paul Atreides becomes the leader of the Fremen and is called Muad'Dib. The Bene Gesserit and the Harkonnens oppose his house. For 10 points, name this science-fiction novel by Frank Herbert.

Arthur Dent is saved from the destruction of Earth by his friend Ford Prefect, who is writing an entry for a guidebook. The answer to the ultimate question of life, the universe, and everything is 42. For 10 points, name this comic science-fiction novel by Douglas Adams.
answer: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy

text: A boy genius named Andrew Wiggin is trained at Battle School to fight an alien race called the Formics, or buggers. His sister Valentine and his brother Peter are also very intelligent. For 10 points, name this novel by Orson Scott Card.

This form of Japanese poetry normally contains seventeen syllables, arranged in three lines of five, seven, and five. Matsuo Basho was a master of this form, which usually refers to a season. For 10 points, name this poetic form.
This poem has fourteen lines. The Petrarchan form is divided into an octave and a sestet, while the Shakespearean form ends in a rhyming couplet. For 10 points, name this poetic form.

Edward Lear popularized this form in his Book of Nonsense, and the poet Ogden Nash wrote many. Its first, second, and fifth lines rhyme and are longer than its third and fourth. It is often bawdy and begins with a line such as "There once was a man from Nantucket." For 10 points, name this form.

A Jewish girl hides in the Secret Annex above her father's business in Amsterdam with her family and four others. She is given a red-checked book on her thirteenth birthday. For 10 points, name this diary kept from 1942 to 1944 by Anne Frank.
answer: The Diary of a Young Girl

text: This memoir by an escaped slave describes his time with the cruel overseer Covey and his fight with him. The author later became an abolitionist and editor of The North Star. For 10 points, name this autobiography by Frederick Douglass.
answer: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
alternates: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave

text: This memoir recounts the author's time in Auschwitz and Buchenwald with his father Shlomo, whom he loses shortly before liberation. The author won the 1986 Nobel Peace Prize. For 10 points, name this memoir by Elie Wiesel.

Haymitch Abernathy mentors two tributes from District 12 who must survive a televised battle in an arena. The hero wears a mockingjay pin and forms an alliance with Rue, a young girl from District 11. She volunteers to replace her sister Primrose. For 10 points, name this young-adult novel by Suzanne Collins.

This mystery writer created the Belgian detective Hercule Poirot and the elderly spinster Miss Marple. She wrote And Then There Were None and Murder on the Orient Express. For 10 points, name this British author.
This ancient Greek storyteller is credited with fables such as "The Tortoise and the Hare" and "The Boy Who Cried Wolf." Each fable ends with a moral. For 10 points, name this author.

Jacob and Wilhelm collected German folk tales such as "Hansel and Gretel," "Rapunzel," and "Snow White." Their collection was published in 1812. For 10 points, give the surname shared by these two brothers.

Perseus Jackson learns that he is the son of Poseidon and attends Camp Half-Blood. His friends include Annabeth and Grover. For 10 points, name this author of the Lightning Thief and the series Percy Jackson and the Olympians.

This author wrote I, Robot and the Foundation series. He formulated the Three Laws of Robotics, the first of which states that a robot may not injure a human being. For 10 points, name this science-fiction author.
Ged, a wizard from the island of Gont, releases a shadow while studying at Roke. This book, by Ursula K. Le Guin, begins the Earthsea series. For 10 points, name this fantasy novel.

Co-written with Alex Haley, this book follows a man's life from being a hustler to becoming a minister in the Nation of Islam. He later made a pilgrimage to Mecca and was assassinated in 1965. For 10 points, name this autobiography.

In this graphic novel, Jews are drawn as mice, Germans as cats, and Poles as pigs. The author interviews his father Vladek about surviving Auschwitz. For 10 points, name this Pulitzer Prize-winning work by Art Spiegelman.

Rorschach, Doctor Manhattan, and Ozymandias are among the retired superheroes in this graphic novel. Alan Moore wrote it and Dave Gibbons illustrated it. For 10 points, name this twelve-issue series, published by DC Comics.

This novel by William Goldman features Westley, who is known as the Dread Pirate Roberts. Inigo Montoya, the swordsman, says "Hello, my name is Inigo Montoya." For 10 points, name this fairy tale about Buttercup.
A small bear lives in Hundred Acre Wood with a donkey named Eeyore, a pig named Piglet, and a boy named Christopher Robin. He loves honey. For 10 points, name this character created by A. A. Milne.

A boy named Max is sent to bed without supper after misbehaving in a wolf suit. His bedroom turns into a forest, and he sails to an island where he becomes king of the creatures there, who roar their terrible roars. When he returns, his supper is still hot. For 10 points, name this picture book written and illustrated by Maurice Sendak.
This ancient Chinese military treatise attributed to Sun Tzu has thirteen chapters. It advises that the supreme excellence is to subdue the enemy without fighting. For 10 points, name this classic.

text: This hero was raised on the island of Seriphos after his mother Danae was set adrift in a chest. He used a mirrored shield from Athena and a curved sword from Hermes on a quest. He later rescued Andromeda from a sea monster. For 10 points, name this Greek hero who beheaded Medusa.

This monster had snakes for hair and turned anyone who met her gaze to stone. She was one of three Gorgon sisters but the only mortal one. Pegasus sprang from her blood after her beheading. For 10 points, name this monster killed by Perseus.

This musician charmed Charon and Cerberus with his lyre while searching the Underworld for his wife Eurydice. He was told not to look back until they reached the surface, but he did anyway. He was later torn apart by Maenads. For 10 points, name this Thracian poet.

This goddess was abducted by Hades while picking flowers. Her mother's grief caused the seasons to change when she had to spend part of each year below the earth after eating pomegranate seeds. For 10 points, name this daughter of Demeter and queen of the Underworld.

This Titan was punished by being chained to a rock where an eagle ate his liver every day. He had angered Zeus by stealing a gift from the gods for humans. For 10 points, name this Titan who gave humanity fire.

After Epimetheus accepted her as a wife, this woman opened a jar given by the gods. Out flew all the evils of the world, leaving only hope inside. She was created by Hephaestus at the order of Zeus. For 10 points, name this first woman in Hesiod's account.

This Athenian hero sailed to Crete with a group of youths and maidens as tribute. With help from Ariadne's thread, he found his way out of a maze after killing its inhabitant. His father Aegeus threw himself into the sea after he forgot to change his sails. For 10 points, name this slayer of the Minotaur.

This beast with the head of a bull and the body of a man lived at the center of a Labyrinth. It was the son of Pasiphae and a bull sent by Poseidon. For 10 points, name this creature slain by Theseus.

This king of Ithaca came up with the idea of the Trojan Horse. After the war he spent ten years trying to get home, blinding the Cyclops Polyphemus on the way. His wife Penelope waited for him. For 10 points, name this hero of an epic by Homer.

This greatest Greek warrior at Troy was dipped in the River Styx by his mother Thetis. He sulked in his tent after a quarrel with Agamemnon over Briseis. He was killed by an arrow to his heel. For 10 points, name this hero of the Iliad.

This prince of Troy was the eldest son of Priam and the husband of Andromache. He killed Patroclus in battle and was then killed in a duel outside the city walls. His body was dragged behind a chariot. For 10 points, name this Trojan defender slain by Achilles.

This Trojan escaped his burning city carrying his father Anchises on his back. He later landed in Carthage, where he abandoned a queen who killed herself. For 10 points, name this son of Venus and the hero of Virgil's epic.

This goddess of wisdom and war sprang fully grown from the head of Zeus. Her symbols include the owl and the olive tree, and she won the contest to be patron of a city that took her name. For 10 points, name this goddess associated with the Parthenon.

This twin brother of Artemis drove the sun across the sky in later tradition. He was the god of music, prophecy, and healing, and was worshiped at Delphi. For 10 points, name this Greek god of the lyre.

This god of the sea carried a trident and caused earthquakes. He lost a contest with Athena over the patronage of Athens and was the father of Polyphemus. For 10 points, name this brother of Zeus and Hades, called Neptune by the Romans.

This messenger god wore winged sandals and carried a caduceus. He was the son of Zeus and Maia and was the guide of souls to the Underworld. For 10 points, name this god who was called Mercury in Rome.

This god of wine and revelry was born from the thigh of Zeus after his mother Semele died. He was accompanied by satyrs and Maenads and carried a staff topped with a pine cone called a thyrsus. For 10 points, name this god known as Bacchus in Rome.

This god of war was the son of Zeus and Hera and was disliked by many other gods. He was caught in a net by her husband Hephaestus while with his lover. For 10 points, name this Greek god whose Roman counterpart is Mars.

This goddess of love was said to have risen from the sea foam near Cyprus. She was married to Hephaestus but had an affair with Ares, and she was the mother of Eros. For 10 points, name this goddess called Venus by the Romans.

This son of Zeus was invited to dine with the gods but tested them by serving up his own son Pelops as a meal. His punishment in the Underworld was to stand in water beneath a fruit tree, with both the water and fruit receding whenever he reached for them. For 10 points, name this king whose name gives us an English verb meaning to tease.

This beautiful youth fell in love with his own reflection in a pool and wasted away. The nymph Echo had loved him in vain. A flower is named for him. For 10 points, name this figure from Ovid's Metamorphoses.

This swift huntress refused to marry any man who could not beat her in a footrace. Hippomenes won by dropping golden apples that she stopped to pick up. She also drew first blood in the Calydonian boar hunt. For 10 points, name this Greek heroine.

This craftsman built the Labyrinth for King Minos of Crete and also made a wooden cow for Pasiphae. Imprisoned by Minos, he escaped the island using wings made of feathers and wax, which cost the life of his son. For 10 points, name this legendary Athenian inventor.

This hero led the Argonauts on a quest for the Golden Fleece. He was aided by the sorceress Medea, whom he later abandoned for Glauce. For 10 points, name this Thessalian prince who sailed on the Argo.

This king of Thebes unknowingly killed his father Laius and married his mother Jocasta. He solved the riddle of the Sphinx and later blinded himself on learning the truth. For 10 points, name this tragic hero of a Sophocles play.

This king of Corinth was condemned to eternally push a boulder up a hill only to watch it roll down again. He had cheated death more than once. For 10 points, name this figure whose name describes a futile task.

This Titan was forced to hold up the sky on his shoulders as punishment after the war with the Olympians. The Hesperides were his daughters, and Heracles briefly took his place while he fetched golden apples. For 10 points, name this Titan, whose name is given to a book of maps.

This monstrous dog with three heads guarded the gates of the Underworld, fawning on those who entered but devouring any who tried to leave. The Roman poet Virgil says Aeneas drugged him with a honey cake, and Orpheus lulled him with music. Capturing him was the twelfth labor of Heracles. For 10 points, name this hound of Hades.

This daughter of Oedipus defied King Creon by burying her brother Polynices, who had been declared a traitor. Creon ordered her sealed in a cave, where she hanged herself. Her fiance Haemon killed himself after. For 10 points, name this title character of a Sophocles play.

text: This god hung for nine nights on a tree and sacrificed an eye at Mimir's well in exchange for wisdom. He rides an eight-legged horse and carries the spear Gungnir. His ravens Huginn and Muninn bring him news. For 10 points, name this one-eyed chief of the Norse gods.

This god wields a hammer and rides a chariot pulled by two goats. He is the son of Odin and fights the giants, and thunder is said to be the sound of his chariot. For 10 points, name this Norse god of thunder.
This trickster god is the father of Fenrir and Hel and gave birth to the horse Sleipnir after turning into a mare. He arranged the death of Baldr. For 10 points, name this Norse shapeshifting god.

This god was killed by an arrow made of mistletoe, thrown by his blind brother Hodr at the urging of Loki. His death was mourned by all of creation except one giantess. For 10 points, name this beautiful son of Odin and Frigg.

This god of war put his hand in the mouth of the wolf Fenrir as a pledge and lost it when the wolf realized he was being tricked. He is associated with justice and single combat. For 10 points, name this one-handed Norse god.

This watchman of the gods lives at the end of the rainbow bridge and has such keen senses that he can hear grass grow. He will blow the horn Gjallarhorn at the start of the final battle. For 10 points, name this guardian god.

This wife of Odin was the goddess of marriage and foresight. She tried to make all things swear not to harm her son Baldr but overlooked the mistletoe. For 10 points, name this Norse queen of the gods.

This giant ash tree connects the nine worlds in Norse cosmology. An eagle sits at its top, a serpent gnaws at its roots, and a squirrel runs up and down it carrying insults. For 10 points, name this world tree.
In this hall in Asgard, Odin gathers warriors who died bravely in battle. They fight each day and feast each night. For 10 points, name this Norse afterlife hall whose name means hall of the slain.

In this prophesied battle, Surtr will set the world aflame, Odin will be swallowed by Fenrir, and Thor will die after killing the world serpent. Afterward, the world will rise again from the sea. For 10 points, name this Norse end of the world.

This giant wolf, a son of Loki, was raised among the gods, but only Tyr dared feed him. The gods bound him with the ribbon Gleipnir after he broke two other chains. He is fated to break free at Ragnarok and swallow Odin. For 10 points, name this monstrous wolf.

This sea serpent grew so large that it encircled the world and bit its own tail. Thor once tried to catch it while fishing and will fight it at Ragnarok. For 10 points, name this child of Loki, also called the Midgard Serpent.
The dwarves Brokkr and Sindri forged this weapon, which has a short handle because Loki interfered during its making. It always returns to its owner. For 10 points, name this weapon of Thor.

This ribbon, forged by dwarves, bound the wolf Fenrir after he broke other chains. It was made from six impossible things, including the sound of a cat's footfall, the beard of a woman, and the roots of a mountain. For 10 points, name this magical fetter.

This burning rainbow bridge connects Midgard to Asgard and is guarded by the watchman Heimdall. Thor must wade through rivers instead of crossing it, since his weight and fire would break it. For 10 points, name this bridge in Norse myth.
This realm is the home of the Aesir gods. It is surrounded by a wall built by a giant in exchange for the sun, the moon, and the goddess Freya. For 10 points, name this Norse city of the gods.

These female figures, whose name means choosers of the slain, ride into battle and bring the dead to Valhalla, where they serve mead to the warriors. Brynhild is a famous example of one. For 10 points, name these warrior maidens in the service of Odin.

This giantess rules the realm of the dishonored dead, where she is half living flesh and half corpse. She is the daughter of Loki and the giantess Angrboda. For 10 points, name this Norse goddess of the underworld.

This goddess guarded the apples that keep the gods young. She was kidnapped by the giant Thjazi after Loki, who had been threatened, tricked her into leaving Asgard. For 10 points, name this wife of the poet Bragi.

This god of the Vanir is the twin brother of Freya and the father of Freyr. He is the god of the sea and ships and was sent to live among the Aesir as a hostage. For 10 points, name this Norse sea god, who was married to Skadi.
This god of the Vanir owns the ship Skidbladnir and a sword that fights by itself, which he gave up to win the giantess Gerd. For 10 points, name this Norse god of fertility, the brother of Freya.

This goddess of love and beauty owns the necklace Brisingamen and drives a chariot pulled by cats. She is the sister of Freyr, and she receives half of those slain in battle in her hall Folkvangr. For 10 points, name this Norse goddess.

This primeval giant was killed by Odin and his brothers Vili and Ve, and the world was made from his body. His blood became the seas, his skull the sky, and his bones the mountains. For 10 points, name this first being in Norse myth.

This primeval cow licked the salty ice of Ginnungagap, freeing Buri, an ancestor of the gods. She fed the giant Ymir with her milk, and her name means something like hornless cow of the void. For 10 points, name this cow in Norse cosmology.

This severed head was consulted by Odin for advice. He was killed by the Vanir during an exchange of hostages and is known for his wisdom. For 10 points, name this guardian of a well of knowledge beneath Yggdrasil.

This dwarf-made ring, owned by Odin, drips eight new rings every ninth night. Odin placed it on the funeral pyre of his son Baldr, but Baldr returned it from Hel through Hermod. For 10 points, name this golden ring.
This hero killed the dragon Fafnir and bathed in its blood. He was later betrayed and killed by Gunnar's family, and his wife was Gudrun. For 10 points, name this hero of the Volsunga saga.

This squirrel runs up and down Yggdrasil carrying insults between an eagle at the top and a serpent at the roots. It stirs up strife between creatures of the tree. For 10 points, name this messenger squirrel.

This dragon gnaws at the roots of Yggdrasil along with many other serpents. It also chews on the corpses of oath-breakers and murderers in the realm of the dead. For 10 points, name this Norse dragon.

This fire giant will come from Muspelheim with a flaming sword to burn the world at Ragnarok. He is said to guard that southern realm of fire from the beginning of time. For 10 points, name this giant, whose name means black.

text: This god was said to sail across the sky in a solar barque each day and through the Underworld each night, where he fought the serpent Apep. He was often shown with the head of a falcon topped by a sun disk. For 10 points, name this Egyptian sun god.

This Egyptian god of the dead was murdered by his brother Set, and his body was cut into pieces. His wife Isis reassembled him, and he became ruler of the Underworld. For 10 points, name this green-skinned god, the father of Horus.

This goddess used her magic to gather the scattered pieces of her husband Osiris. She hid her son Horus in the marshes of the Nile Delta to protect him from Set. For 10 points, name this Egyptian goddess of magic and motherhood.

This lion-headed Egyptian goddess was sent by Ra to punish humanity for rebelling against him. She was stopped only when the gods tricked her into drinking beer dyed red to look like blood. For 10 points, name this goddess of war and healing.

This god of chaos, storms, and the desert killed his brother Osiris and fought a long contest with his nephew for the throne. He is often shown with an animal head of uncertain type. For 10 points, name this Egyptian god.
This falcon-headed sky god lost an eye in battle with Set, and that eye became a symbol of protection. Pharaohs were considered his living embodiment. For 10 points, name this son of Isis and Osiris.
This ibis-headed Egyptian god of writing and wisdom recorded the results when the hearts of the dead were weighed. He was also associated with the moon and with scribes. For 10 points, name this god.

This Sumerian king of Uruk befriended the wild man Enkidu and later traveled in search of immortality after his friend died. He met Utnapishtim, who survived a great flood. For 10 points, name this hero of an ancient Mesopotamian epic.

This primeval goddess of salt water was split in two by Marduk, and her body formed the heavens and the earth. She had taken a monstrous form to avenge her mate Apsu. For 10 points, name this Babylonian dragon of chaos.
This Babylonian god became king of the gods after defeating Tiamat. He was the patron deity of the city of Babylon and is the hero of the Enuma Elish. For 10 points, name this god.

This Sumerian goddess descended through seven gates to the Underworld, losing an item of clothing at each. Her sister Ereshkigal killed her, but she was revived. For 10 points, name this goddess of love and war, whom the Akkadians called Ishtar.

This feathered serpent god of the Aztecs was also a god of wind and learning. He was said to have created humans from bones and his own blood. For 10 points, name this god whose Maya counterpart is Kukulkan.

This Aztec god of war and the sun was born fully armed from his mother Coatlicue. He killed his sister Coyolxauhqui, and he is associated with the founding of Tenochtitlan. For 10 points, name this patron deity of the Mexica.
This Aztec god of the night sky, whose name means smoking mirror, was the rival of Quetzalcoatl. He is often shown with a missing foot, replaced by an obsidian mirror. For 10 points, name this god.

This Hindu god is the preserver of the universe and has appeared in ten avatars, including Rama and Krishna. He is often depicted resting on the serpent Shesha. For 10 points, name this member of the Trimurti.

This Hindu god of destruction and transformation is depicted with a third eye and a crescent moon in his hair. He performs the cosmic dance of the Nataraja. For 10 points, name this god whose consort is Parvati.

This elephant-headed Hindu god is the remover of obstacles and the patron of scribes. He is the son of Shiva and Parvati and rides a mouse. For 10 points, name this god whose broken tusk he used to write the Mahabharata.

This prince of Ayodhya was exiled for fourteen years. His wife Sita was kidnapped by the demon king Ravana, and he rescued her with the aid of an army of monkeys. For 10 points, name this hero of the Ramayana.

This Hindu warrior goddess rides a lion or a tiger and holds weapons in each of her many arms. She was created by the gods to kill the buffalo demon Mahishasura. Her festival is celebrated during Navaratri. For 10 points, name this goddess.
This Hindu avatar of Vishnu acts as the charioteer of Arjuna and speaks the Bhagavad Gita on the battlefield. As a child, he was known for stealing butter. For 10 points, name this blue-skinned god.

This Irish hero's real name was Setanta, but he got his new name after killing the smith's hound and offering to take its place. He single-handedly defended Ulster during the Cattle Raid of Cooley. For 10 points, name this warrior of the Ulster Cycle.
This Irish hero gained knowledge by burning his thumb on the Salmon of Knowledge. He led the Fianna and was the father of the poet Oisin. For 10 points, name this legendary warrior.

This Japanese goddess of the sun hid in a cave after her brother Susanoo's misbehavior, plunging the world into darkness. The other gods lured her out with a mirror and a dance. For 10 points, name this ancestor of the imperial family.
This Japanese storm god, the brother of Amaterasu, was exiled from heaven. He slew the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi and found the sword Kusanagi in its tail. For 10 points, name this god.

This Chinese Monkey King studied under a Taoist master, gained a staff that could change size, and caused chaos in heaven. He later escorted the monk Xuanzang on a journey in the novel Journey to the West. For 10 points, name this trickster.
This Polynesian demigod used a magical fishhook to pull islands from the sea. He is also credited with slowing the sun and with stealing fire. For 10 points, name this Hawaiian and Maori hero.
This Hawaiian goddess of volcanoes and fire lives in the crater of Kilauea. She is known for her fiery temper and her feud with her sister Namaka. For 10 points, name this goddess.

This West African trickster takes the form of a spider and won all the world's stories from the sky god Nyame. For 10 points, name this folktale hero who traveled to the Caribbean with enslaved Africans.

In this Slavic folktale, a witch lives in a hut that stands on chicken legs. She flies in a mortar and steers with a pestle, and she is sometimes helpful, sometimes dangerous. For 10 points, name this figure of Russian folklore.

This creator god of the Inca rose from Lake Titicaca and fashioned the sun, the moon, and the stars. He made the first people from stone and later wandered the land disguised as a beggar. For 10 points, name this Andean deity.

text: This object was found in 1799 near a port in the Nile Delta by soldiers of Napoleon's army. It bears a decree issued in 196 BC in three scripts, including Greek and Demotic. Jean-Francois Champollion used it to decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs. For 10 points, name this slab of granodiorite now in the British Museum.

In 1215, rebellious barons forced King John of England to seal this document at Runnymede. Its clause 39 promised that no free man would be imprisoned except by lawful judgment of his peers. It is often cited as a foundation of constitutional limits on rulers. For 10 points, name this "Great Charter."

This man's best-known work, printed in Mainz in the 1450s, was a Bible with 42 lines per page. He combined a screw press with movable metal type cast in a hand mold. His workshop was financed by loans from Johann Fust. For 10 points, name this German printer.

This constructed language was published in 1887 in a booklet called the Unua Libro. Its creator, a Polish ophthalmologist, wanted it to be a neutral second language for everyone. Its name comes from its creator's pseudonym, Doktoro, meaning "one who hopes." For 10 points, name this most widely spoken constructed language.

This man lost his sight in a childhood accident in his father's leather workshop. At age 15 he adapted a military code called night writing, invented by Charles Barbier. The system he developed uses cells of six raised dots. For 10 points, name this Frenchman who created a reading system for the blind.

This inventor and painter was helped by Alfred Vail in refining his electromagnetic telegraph. In 1844 he sent the message "What hath God wrought" from the Capitol to Baltimore. His name is given to a code of dots and dashes. For 10 points, name this American.

This man's assistant Thomas Watson heard the first sentence spoken over his device: "Come here, I want to see you." He received a patent for his invention in 1876. He was born in Edinburgh and taught speech to deaf students in Boston. For 10 points, name this inventor of the telephone.

One of these two siblings made the first powered flight on December 17, 1903, lasting twelve seconds. They tested gliders and built a wind tunnel in their Dayton bicycle shop. Their craft was the Flyer, flown at Kitty Hawk. For 10 points, name these brothers, Orville and Wilbur.

Its original definition came from a French expedition that surveyed the arc from Dunkirk to Barcelona. It was meant to equal one ten-millionth of the distance from the equator to the North Pole through Paris. It is the base unit of length in the metric system. For 10 points, name this unit, about 39 inches long.

Originally, this man's temperature scale was inverted, with 100 as the freezing point of water and 0 as its boiling point. Carl Linnaeus helped reverse it after his death. He was an astronomer at Uppsala who also measured the shape of the Earth in Lapland. For 10 points, name this Swede who gives his name to a scale on which water freezes at zero.

On this scale, talc is rated 1 and gypsum is rated 2. Quartz is 7 and corundum is 9. A mineral that can scratch another has a higher number on it. For 10 points, name this scale of mineral hardness topped by diamond at 10.

Created by an Irish-born officer of the Royal Navy, this scale originally described the effect of wind on a sailing ship's canvas. Its levels run from 0, "calm," up to 12. Force 12 is a hurricane. For 10 points, name this scale of wind speed.

Developed in 1935 by a seismologist at the California Institute of Technology, this logarithmic scale measures earthquake size. Each whole-number step means ground motion ten times greater. It has largely been replaced by moment magnitude. For 10 points, name this scale named for Charles Richter.

Established by a bequest from a Hungarian-born newspaper publisher, this prize is administered by Columbia University. First awarded in 1917, its categories include journalism, letters, drama, and music. Winners get a certificate and a cash award. For 10 points, name this American prize that honors writers and journalists.

This system was devised in 1876 by a librarian at Amherst College. It divides knowledge into ten main classes, such as 500 for natural sciences and 800 for literature. Books on library shelves are arranged by its numbers. For 10 points, name this classification system created by Melvil Dewey.

This Swedish botanist's Systema Naturae first appeared in 1735. He standardized binomial nomenclature, giving each species a genus name and a species name. He called humans Homo sapiens. For 10 points, name this "father of taxonomy."

This man's first book, a speller with a blue cover, taught generations of American children to read. In 1828 he published a two-volume dictionary that simplified spellings such as "color" and "theater." He was a Connecticut-born lexicographer. For 10 points, name this author of An American Dictionary of the English Language.

A black basalt stele topped by a relief of the sun god Shamash records this ruler's laws. It was found at Susa in 1901 and is now in the Louvre. Its laws include "an eye for an eye" punishments. For 10 points, name this king of Babylon.

This alphabet is named for a Byzantine missionary, Saint Cyril, though his associate probably did not design it. It is used for writing Russian, Ukrainian, Bulgarian, and Serbian. Many of its letters, such as the one shaped like a backward N, derive from Greek. For 10 points, name this alphabet.

This man, who was not literate in English, invented a syllabary for his people's language around 1821. Each of its symbols stands for a syllable rather than a single sound. Within a few years, thousands of his people had learned to read and write. For 10 points, name this Cherokee silversmith.

The Polish Cipher Bureau first broke early versions of this device. At Bletchley Park, Alan Turing and others read its messages with help from electromechanical bombes. It scrambled letters using rotors, a plugboard, and a reflector. For 10 points, name this cipher machine used by Nazi Germany.

The notes to a paper translating a lecture by Luigi Menabrea include what is often called the first computer program. It was an algorithm to calculate Bernoulli numbers on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine. The author was the only legitimate child of Lord Byron. For 10 points, name this woman, the Countess of Lovelace.

In 1989, this British scientist working at CERN proposed a system of linked hypertext documents. He wrote the first web browser and server in 1990. He later founded the World Wide Web Consortium. For 10 points, name this inventor of the World Wide Web.

Introduced by a papal bull in 1582, this system dropped ten days that October. It was designed to fix drift in the date of Easter that the Julian system caused. Under its rule, a century year is a leap year only if divisible by 400. For 10 points, name this calendar used worldwide, named for Pope Gregory XIII.

An international conference in Washington in 1884 chose this English town's observatory as the zero of longitude. The prime meridian passes through the Royal Observatory there. Mean time at this location gives its name to a world time standard. For 10 points, name this London borough on the Thames.

This Swedish chemist made a fortune from dynamite and other explosives. His will set aside money to honor achievements in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature, and peace. The first prizes were given in 1901. For 10 points, name this man who established an annual set of prizes.

In 1901, this Italian engineer received a signal sent from Cornwall at his station on Signal Hill in Newfoundland. The signal was the letter S in Morse code. He shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics for work on wireless telegraphy. For 10 points, name this inventor of a radio system.

After graduating from Yale, this man built a machine at a Georgia plantation that separated cotton fibers from seeds. He patented it in 1794. Later he promoted the idea of interchangeable parts in making muskets for the government. For 10 points, name this American inventor of the cotton gin.

In 1913 at the Highland Park plant, this man's company introduced a moving assembly line. In 1914 he announced a wage of five dollars for an eight-hour day. His cheap Model T put millions of Americans on the road. For 10 points, name this founder of a Detroit car company.

This imaginary line mostly follows the 180th meridian, though it bends around island groups such as Fiji and Kiribati. A traveler crossing it heading west skips ahead one calendar day. It lies opposite the prime meridian. For 10 points, name this line where each new calendar day begins.

text: This thinker's works are mostly dialogues in which his teacher asks questions about virtue, justice, and knowledge. He founded a school in a grove near Athens around 387 BC that lasted for centuries. His most famous student was Aristotle. For 10 points, name this author of the Republic and Symposium.

This philosopher was born in Stagira and served as tutor to Alexander the Great. He founded the Lyceum, where he and his students walked while discussing ideas, earning them the name Peripatetics. He wrote on logic, biology, physics, ethics, and politics. For 10 points, name this student of Plato.

This philosopher founded a school in Athens called the Garden. He taught that pleasure is the highest good but defined it as freedom from bodily pain and mental disturbance. He argued that "death is nothing to us" because when we exist, death is not, and when death exists, we are not. For 10 points, name this Greek founder of a school of hedonism.

This thinker from Citium on Cyprus came to Athens, where he taught at a painted porch. He founded a school whose members taught that virtue is sufficient for happiness and that the universe is governed by divine reason. A shipwreck is said to have turned him toward philosophy, after which he studied with the Cynic Crates. For 10 points, name this founder of Stoicism, who shares a first name with a paradox-maker from Elea.

This philosopher from Ephesus held that fire is the basic element and that everything is in constant change. A quote attributed to him says that no one steps into the same river twice. He taught that the universe is governed by a rational principle and that opposites are in tension. For 10 points, name this "obscure" pre-Socratic philosopher.

This thinker from Elea wrote a poem in which a goddess describes the Way of Truth and the Way of Opinion. He argued that what exists cannot come into being or pass away and that change and plurality are illusions. His student Zeno devised paradoxes to defend his views. For 10 points, name this Eleatic philosopher of "being," who gave his name to a dialogue by Plato.

With his teacher Leucippus, this philosopher from Abdera proposed that reality consists of indivisible particles moving in empty space. He held that differences between objects come from the shape, size, and arrangement of these particles. He is called the "laughing philosopher." For 10 points, name this Greek atomist.

This man founded a religious and philosophical community at Croton and was said to have believed that the soul is reborn in different bodies. He taught that all things are numbers and that numerical ratios govern music. A theorem about the sides of a right triangle is named for him. For 10 points, name this Greek thinker.

This Milesian is often called the first Western philosopher. He said that all things come from water and is said to have predicted a solar eclipse. Plato reports a story that he fell into a well while gazing at the stars. For 10 points, name this first of the seven sages of Greece.

This pre-Socratic from Miletus was a student of Thales who held that the first principle of all things is the boundless, or apeiron. He is credited with drawing an early map of the world and with explaining cosmic order as a kind of justice between opposites. For 10 points, name this philosopher whose name follows the prefix "Anaxi-" and ends in "-mander."

This philosopher from Acragas claimed that all things are composed of fire, air, earth, and water, which are moved by two forces called Love and Strife. Legend says he died by leaping into the crater of Mount Etna. He wrote poems titled On Nature and Purifications. For 10 points, name this pre-Socratic who proposed four "roots" of matter.

This sophist from Abdera is remembered for the claim that "man is the measure of all things." He charged fees to teach rhetoric and virtue and is the title character of a Platonic dialogue. His relativism holds that things are for each person as they appear to that person. For 10 points, name this Greek sophist.

Called the "Second Sage" after Confucius, this Chinese philosopher argued that human nature is inherently good and that everyone has four moral "sprouts," including compassion. He said a person who sees a child about to fall into a well will naturally feel alarm. His sayings are collected in a book named for him. For 10 points, name this Confucian thinker.

This Chinese philosopher is the author of a book of stories and parables that includes a tale of a man who dreamed he was a butterfly and wondered whether the butterfly was dreaming it was the man. He championed spontaneity and the relativity of viewpoints. Along with Laozi, he is a foundational figure of Daoism. For 10 points, name this thinker.

This Stoic from Corduba wrote On the Shortness of Life and Letters to Lucilius. He was tutor and later adviser to a Roman emperor, who eventually ordered him to commit suicide in 65 AD. He argued that wise people should face death and misfortune with calm. For 10 points, name this Roman Stoic who tutored Nero.

This author of a series of private notes called the Meditations was the last of the Five Good Emperors of Rome. He wrote in Greek, reminding himself to accept fate and focus on his own character. He ruled from 161 to 180 and died campaigning on the Danube. For 10 points, name this Stoic emperor.

Born into slavery in Phrygia, this Stoic taught that some things are "up to us" while others are not. His lectures were recorded by his student Arrian in the Discourses and a short handbook, the Enchiridion. He taught in Nicopolis after being expelled from Rome. For 10 points, name this former slave and Stoic philosopher.

This thinker's pupil Porphyry compiled his lectures into six groups of nine treatises called the Enneads. He taught that all reality emanates from an ineffable first principle, and that the soul can return to it through contemplation. Intellect and Soul rank below that source. For 10 points, name this third-century founder of a Platonic school who wrote about "the One."

This philosopher is said to have traveled with Alexander the Great's army to India, where he encountered Indian ascetics. He taught that because we cannot know the true nature of things, we should suspend judgment and thereby achieve tranquility. A school of skepticism is named for him. For 10 points, name this founder of the oldest school of Greek skepticism from Elis.

This philosopher from Clazomenae introduced the concept of nous, or mind, as the force that orders the world. He taught that the sun is a fiery mass of metal and was prosecuted for impiety in Athens. Pericles was among his students and friends. For 10 points, name this pre-Socratic who was said to be the first philosopher to teach in Athens.

This ten-book dialogue is set at the Piraeus and has Socrates examine what justice is in a city and in a soul. It argues that the best city would be ruled by philosophers and divides the soul into reason, spirit, and appetite. Its censorship of poetry is a famous controversy. For 10 points, name this major work of Plato.

In this story, prisoners chained in an underground cavern see only shadows cast on a wall by a fire. One prisoner is freed and goes up into the light, finally seeing the sun, which represents the Form of the Good. When he returns, the others mock him. For 10 points, name this allegory from Book VII of Plato's Republic that illustrates education and knowledge.

This work is divided into ten books and discusses virtue as a mean between excess and deficiency, with courage lying between cowardice and rashness. Two books discuss friendship and its types. It argues that the highest human good is activity of the soul in accordance with virtue. For 10 points, name this ethical treatise by Aristotle.

In this dialogue, the title character is prosecuting his own father for murder when he meets Socrates outside the courthouse. Socrates asks whether the pious is loved by the gods because it is pious, or whether it is pious because it is loved by the gods. The conversation ends without a definition. For 10 points, name this Platonic dialogue that gave its name to a dilemma about morality and divine command.

In this work, a man tells the jury that he is a gadfly sent to sting the city of Athens. He says that "the unexamined life is not worth living" and explains that his inquiries began after the oracle at Delphi called someone wise. The accusers include Meletus. For 10 points, name this account of the defense speech of Socrates written by Plato.

The narrator in this dialogue tells Echecrates about the last day of Socrates, who is in prison awaiting execution. Socrates offers arguments for the immortality of the soul to Simmias and Cebes. The work ends with the drinking of hemlock. For 10 points, name this Platonic dialogue named for its narrator.

Plato's version of this idea says that the world we perceive is a copy of perfect, unchanging entities such as Beauty, Justice, and the Good. Objects in the physical world "participate" in these entities. Aristotle criticized this view, saying that they should be in things themselves. For 10 points, name this theory about a realm of abstract ideals.

Gorgias, Hippias, and Prodicus were members of this group of itinerant teachers in fifth-century Greece. They charged fees to teach rhetoric and skills for success in the city. Socrates criticized them for valuing persuasion over truth. For 10 points, name this group whose name is now used for people who use clever but misleading arguments.

This Greek term for the highest human good is often translated as "flourishing" or "happiness." Aristotle held that it consists of virtuous activity of the soul. Its name literally refers to having a good guiding spirit. For 10 points, give this Greek word that is central to the ethics of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle.

The Roman emperor Justinian is traditionally said to have closed this institution in 529 AD, ending nearly a millennium of philosophy there. It was founded near a grove named for the hero Akademos. Its later heads included Arcesilaus and Carneades, who adopted a skeptical outlook. For 10 points, name this school that took its name from the Athenian grove where Plato taught.

text: This thinker imagined a malicious demon who deceives him about everything. In Meditations on First Philosophy, he decides that the one thing he cannot doubt is his own existence as a thinking thing. He also invented analytic geometry, in which Cartesian coordinates are used. For 10 points, name this French philosopher who said "I think, therefore I am."

This philosopher argued that the mind begins as a blank slate, a "tabula rasa," and that all ideas come from experience. His Essay Concerning Human Understanding is a foundational text of empiricism. In his Two Treatises of Government, he argued that people have natural rights to life, liberty, and property. For 10 points, name this English philosopher.

This Scottish philosopher's Treatise of Human Nature argued that the self is nothing but a bundle of perceptions. He raised the problem of induction and the claim that one cannot derive an "ought" from an "is." Immanuel Kant said this thinker's work awakened him from his "dogmatic slumber." For 10 points, name this author of An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding.

This philosopher from Konigsberg wrote that he was awakened from his "dogmatic slumber" by Hume. He distinguished between the phenomenal world of appearances and the noumenal world of things in themselves. He formulated a moral law that tells us to act only on principles we could will to be universal. For 10 points, name this author of the Critique of Pure Reason.

In Leviathan, this English philosopher argued that life in the state of nature would be "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short." He said that people escape the war of all against all by surrendering their rights to an absolute sovereign. His book takes its name from a biblical sea monster. For 10 points, name this author of a work on political authority.

This Genevan philosopher began a book with the line "Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains." He argued that legitimate government rests on the general will and wrote the novel-treatise Emile on education. He also wrote an autobiography titled Confessions. For 10 points, name this author of The Social Contract.

This Victorian philosopher defended individual freedom in On Liberty and argued for the harm principle. He was educated rigorously by his father James and wrote The Subjection of Women. He refined an ethical theory by saying it is "better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied." For 10 points, name this British utilitarian thinker.

This English philosopher proposed the "felicific calculus" to measure pleasure and pain. He designed a circular prison called the Panopticon, in which a single guard could observe all inmates. His preserved body, called the Auto-Icon, is displayed at University College London. For 10 points, name this founder of modern utilitarianism.

This German philosopher wrote Thus Spoke Zarathustra and proclaimed that "God is dead." He introduced the idea of the Ubermensch and the thought experiment of eternal recurrence. His On the Genealogy of Morality contrasts master and slave morality. For 10 points, name this author of Beyond Good and Evil.

This Danish thinker wrote Fear and Trembling under the pseudonym Johannes de Silentio. In it, he discusses Abraham's willingness to sacrifice Isaac as a "teleological suspension of the ethical." He broke off an engagement to Regine Olsen. For 10 points, name this author of Either/Or, often called the father of existentialism.

This philosopher's Phenomenology of Spirit appeared in 1807, and his Philosophy of Right claims that "the owl of Minerva spreads its wings only with the falling of the dusk." He described history as the unfolding of freedom through a dialectical process. He taught at the University of Berlin. For 10 points, name this German idealist.

This philosopher's The World as Will and Representation argued that the world's inner essence is a blind, striving will. He taught that life is suffering and that relief comes from art and compassion. He was strongly influenced by the Upanishads and scheduled lectures at the same time as his rival Hegel in Berlin. For 10 points, name this German pessimist.

This philosopher's Ethics was written in the style of Euclid's geometry, with definitions, axioms, and propositions. He identified God with Nature in the phrase "Deus sive Natura" and held that only one substance exists. He was expelled from the Amsterdam Jewish community in 1656 and earned a living grinding lenses. For 10 points, name this Dutch rationalist.

This German philosopher believed that the universe consists of simple, indivisible substances called monads. He argued that this is "the best of all possible worlds" in his Theodicy. He also independently developed calculus alongside Newton. For 10 points, name this rationalist who proposed pre-established harmony.

This Irish bishop argued that "to be is to be perceived" and denied the existence of material substance. His Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous defend his idealism against skepticism. A California city and its university are named for him. For 10 points, name this empiricist who wrote A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge.

This German thinker wrote Das Kapital and, with Friedrich Engels, The Communist Manifesto. He developed historical materialism, which holds that economic conditions shape society. He ended the Manifesto with "Workers of the world, unite!" For 10 points, name this author who analyzed class struggle between bourgeoisie and proletariat.

This Austrian-born philosopher wrote the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, which ends: "Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent." His later work, published after his death as Philosophical Investigations, introduces language games and a private language argument. He taught at Cambridge. For 10 points, name this philosopher of language.

This British philosopher wrote Principia Mathematica with Alfred North Whitehead. He discovered a paradox about the set of all sets that do not contain themselves, and his "theory of descriptions" appeared in "On Denoting." He received the 1950 Nobel Prize in Literature. For 10 points, name this author of Why I Am Not a Christian.

This English statesman wrote the Novum Organum, which urged scientists to base conclusions on systematic observation and induction. He warned about "idols" that distort the mind and is credited with the phrase "knowledge is power." He served as Lord Chancellor under James I. For 10 points, name this author of New Atlantis.

This Florentine wrote that it is safer for a ruler to be feared than loved, if he cannot be both. His most famous book, dedicated to a member of the Medici family, discusses virtu and fortuna. He also wrote Discourses on Livy. For 10 points, name this author of The Prince.

This French Enlightenment writer satirized Leibnizian optimism in Candide. He wrote the Treatise on Tolerance after the Calas affair and used the slogan "crush the infamous thing" against religious fanaticism. He had a long relationship with Emilie du Chatelet. For 10 points, name this French author who used a pen name instead of his birth name, Francois-Marie Arouet.

This French thinker argued in The Spirit of the Laws that power should be divided among branches of government so that one power checks another. His ideas about separation of powers strongly influenced the framers of the United States Constitution. He also wrote the epistolary satire Persian Letters. For 10 points, name this Baron de La Brede.

This English writer's A Vindication of the Rights of Woman argued that women should be educated alongside men. Her earlier work, A Vindication of the Rights of Men, responded to Edmund Burke. She died shortly after giving birth to the author of Frankenstein. For 10 points, name this early feminist philosopher.

This Irish-born statesman wrote Reflections on the Revolution in France, warning that radical change would lead to chaos. He also wrote a treatise on the sublime and the beautiful. He is considered a founder of modern conservatism. For 10 points, name this British politician and thinker who defended tradition and prescription.

This Scottish philosopher's The Wealth of Nations describes how a pin factory shows the benefits of division of labor. He used the image of an "invisible hand" to explain how self-interested actions can benefit society. An earlier book, The Theory of Moral Sentiments, emphasizes sympathy. For 10 points, name this founder of classical economics.

This author spent a night in jail for refusing to pay a poll tax, an experience that led to his essay "Civil Disobedience." He lived for two years in a cabin near a pond in Concord, Massachusetts. He described the experience in a book subtitled Life in the Woods. For 10 points, name this transcendentalist author of Walden.

This Concord-based essayist wrote "Self-Reliance" and "The American Scholar," the latter called America's intellectual declaration of independence. His book Nature helped found the movement of transcendentalism. He mentored Henry David Thoreau. For 10 points, name this American writer who urged "trust thyself."

This French philosopher coined the word "sociology" and proposed the law of three stages: theological, metaphysical, and positive. His Course of Positive Philosophy argued that knowledge should be based on observation. He designed a "religion of humanity" in his later years. For 10 points, name this founder of positivism.

This English-born pamphleteer wrote Common Sense in 1776, urging American independence. He later wrote Rights of Man in defense of the French Revolution and The Age of Reason, which criticized organized religion. His series The American Crisis begins "These are the times that try men's souls." For 10 points, name this author.

This French writer edited a landmark multivolume reference work with Jean le Rond d'Alembert. He also wrote the dialogue Rameau's Nephew and the novel Jacques the Fatalist. He was a leading materialist of the Enlightenment. For 10 points, name this editor of the Encyclopedie.
