text: This Australian philosopher argued in "Famine, Affluence, and Morality" that if you could save a child drowning in a shallow pond at small cost to yourself, you ought to do so, and that distance should not matter. He wrote Animal Liberation, which criticized what he called speciesism. He teaches at Princeton and is associated with effective altruism. For 10 points, name this utilitarian ethicist.

This thinker's novel Nausea and play No Exit, which includes the line "Hell is other people," explore freedom. His major philosophical work, Being and Nothingness, describes the condition of denying one's own freedom as "bad faith." He declined the 1964 Nobel Prize in Literature. For 10 points, name this French existentialist and partner of Simone de Beauvoir.

This French philosopher wrote The Second Sex, which includes the line "One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman." She also wrote The Ethics of Ambiguity and the novel The Mandarins. She was the long-time partner of Jean-Paul Sartre. For 10 points, name this feminist existentialist.

This Algerian-born French writer used the myth of a man condemned to roll a boulder up a hill forever to illustrate the absurd condition. He wrote the novels The Stranger and The Plague and won the 1957 Nobel Prize in Literature. He famously wrote, "One must imagine Sisyphus happy." For 10 points, name this author of The Myth of Sisyphus.

In this thought experiment, parties choose the principles of a just society without knowing their own race, class, talents, or religion. It forms part of the "original position" in A Theory of Justice. John Rawls argued that people behind it would choose principles that protect the worst-off. For 10 points, name this device named for a covering that blocks sight of one's own social position.

In this thought experiment by John Searle, a man who does not know Chinese sits in a room manipulating symbols according to a rule book and passes out answers in Chinese. Searle used it to argue that running a program cannot by itself produce understanding. It is directed against "strong AI." For 10 points, name this thought experiment, named for a room.

Alan Turing proposed this test in the 1950 paper "Computing Machinery and Intelligence." A human judge converses by text with a hidden person and a hidden machine, and the machine passes if the judge cannot reliably tell them apart. Turing originally called it the "imitation game." For 10 points, name this test of machine intelligence.

This Dominican friar of the thirteenth century wrote the Summa Theologica, which contains the "Five Ways," arguments for God's existence. He united Christian doctrine with the philosophy of Aristotle and is called the "Angelic Doctor." He was born in Aquino. For 10 points, name this medieval Italian scholastic.

This bishop of Hippo wrote that he had been drawn to Manichaeism before being converted in Milan, where he heard sermons of Ambrose. His mother, Monica, prayed for his conversion. He developed the doctrine of original sin in debates with Pelagius. For 10 points, name this North African church father who wrote after the sack of Rome in 410.

This medieval rabbi, born in Cordoba, wrote the Guide for the Perplexed, which tries to reconcile Aristotelian philosophy with Jewish law. He also compiled the fourteen-volume law code Mishneh Torah and a list of thirteen principles of faith. He served as physician at the court in Cairo. For 10 points, name this scholar also known as the Rambam.

This Andalusian philosopher, called "the Commentator" in the Latin West, wrote extensive commentaries on Aristotle. He replied to al-Ghazali in The Incoherence of the Incoherence. He served as a judge in Seville and Cordoba. For 10 points, name this Muslim philosopher also known as Ibn Rushd.

This Persian philosopher was born near Bukhara and wrote the Book of Healing and the Canon of Medicine. He imagined a "floating man" who is suspended in the air and deprived of all sensation but still aware of himself. He argued that God is the "necessary existent." For 10 points, name this Islamic polymath also called Ibn Sina.

This man studied law in London and worked as a lawyer in South Africa, where he founded Tolstoy Farm. Back in India, he promoted homespun cloth called khadi and launched the Quit India movement in 1942. He was killed by Nathuram Godse in 1948. For 10 points, name this leader of Indian independence, who was called "Mahatma."

This text is part of the epic Mahabharata and takes the form of a dialogue on a battlefield at Kurukshetra. Arjuna hesitates to fight his kinsmen, and his charioteer Krishna teaches him about duty and detachment from the fruits of action. It presents several paths, including karma yoga and bhakti. For 10 points, name this Hindu scripture whose title means "Song of the Lord."

These ancient Indian texts, which conclude the Vedas, contain the phrase "tat tvam asi," or "you are that." They teach that the individual self is identical to the ultimate reality of the universe. Arthur Schopenhauer called them the solace of his life. For 10 points, name these philosophical texts, the basis of Vedanta.

In this game-theory scenario, two arrested suspects are separately offered a deal for betraying each other. Each does better by betraying no matter what the other does, yet both are worse off than if both had stayed silent. Albert Tucker named it. For 10 points, name this game theory scenario about cooperation and defection.

Garrett Hardin popularized this idea in a 1968 essay in Science. It describes how individuals acting in their own interest can deplete a shared resource, such as a pasture in which each herder adds more animals. An earlier 1833 pamphlet by William Forster Lloyd used the example of cattle grazing. For 10 points, name this concept in ethics and economics.

Cicero, Thomas Aquinas, and John Locke are major figures in this tradition. It claims that certain moral principles are built into human nature or reason and are universal. Martin Luther King Jr. invoked it when he argued that an unjust law is no law at all. For 10 points, name this theory that law should reflect universal moral truths.

Charles Sanders Peirce, William James, and John Dewey were founders of this American school of thought. It judges ideas by their practical effects and consequences. James described the truth of an idea as its "cash value." For 10 points, name this philosophy that emphasizes practical results.

This Russian-born novelist wrote Atlas Shrugged and The Fountainhead. She promoted a philosophy called Objectivism, which champions reason, individualism, and laissez-faire capitalism. Her essays collected in The Virtue of Selfishness defend egoism. For 10 points, name this author born Alisa Rosenbaum.

One version of this paradox says: "This sentence is false." If the sentence is true, then it is false, but if it is false, then it is true. Tradition ties it to Epimenides the Cretan, who said that all Cretans are liars. Alfred Tarski's work on truth was in part a response to it. For 10 points, name this paradox of self-reference.

Eubulides of Miletus is credited with this paradox, whose name comes from the Greek word for "heap." One grain of wheat is not a heap, and adding one grain never turns a non-heap into a heap, yet a large pile of grains is a heap. It is the standard example of the problem of vagueness. For 10 points, name this paradox.

This thought experiment describes a donkey placed exactly halfway between two identical bales of hay. Unable to choose, it starves. It is named for a fourteenth-century French priest and is used in debates about free will and rational choice. For 10 points, name this paradox about a hungry animal.

Robert Nozick presented this thought experiment in Anarchy, State, and Utopia. You are offered a chance to plug into a machine that would give you any experiences you desire, all indistinguishable from reality. Most people refuse, which Nozick took as evidence against hedonism. For 10 points, name this thought experiment.

This political philosophy opposes all forms of compulsory government and hierarchy. Its thinkers include Emma Goldman and Mikhail Bakunin, and its symbol is a circled A. Its Spanish version was prominent in the CNT during the 1930s. For 10 points, name this movement that advocates a stateless society.

This group of philosophers and scientists met in a city on the Danube in the 1920s and 1930s. Moritz Schlick led it, and Rudolf Carnap and Otto Neurath were members. They defended the principle that a statement has meaning only if it can be verified. For 10 points, name this group of logical positivists in Austria's capital.

In this thought experiment by Frank Jackson, a scientist raised in a black-and-white room knows every physical fact about the neurophysiology of color vision. When she steps out and sees a red tomato, she seems to learn something new. Jackson used it to argue against physicalism. For 10 points, name this thought experiment about a color scientist named for a woman.

This view holds that the right action is the one that best promotes the agent's own interests. It differs from psychological egoism, which claims that people in fact only act from self-interest. Thomas Hobbes is often read as a psychological egoist. For 10 points, name this ethical theory, in contrast with altruism.

This second-century Indian Buddhist founded the Madhyamaka, or Middle Way school. His Mulamadhyamakakarika argues that all phenomena are empty of inherent existence. He is considered a central figure of Mahayana. For 10 points, name this philosopher who developed the doctrine of sunyata, or emptiness.

David Chalmers popularized this thought experiment of a being that is physically identical to a normal person and acts the same, but has no inner conscious experience. He argues that if such a being is conceivable, physicalism is false. For 10 points, name this undead-themed philosophical being.

text: This man's first revelation is said to have come in a cave on Jabal al-Nour called Hira, where he often meditated. His early followers were persecuted by the Quraysh, and he lost his wife Khadijah and his uncle Abu Talib in the same "year of sorrow." In 622 he migrated to Yathrib, and he later returned to conquer his birthplace almost without bloodshed. For 10 points, name this final prophet of Islam, who received the Quran.

This city's Sacred Mosque contains a cube-shaped building toward which Muslims face when praying. It was the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad, and non-Muslims are forbidden to enter it. Pilgrims travel there during the Hajj each year. For 10 points, name this holy city in Saudi Arabia.

In 622 the Prophet Muhammad made a journey known as the Hijra to this city, then called Yathrib, after persecution in his hometown. His tomb lies beneath the green dome of the Prophet's Mosque here. The Constitution named for this city set up an agreement among its tribes. For 10 points, name this holy city of Islam in Saudi Arabia, second only to Mecca.

This holy month of the Islamic calendar involves fasting from dawn until sunset each day. It is the month in which the Quran was first revealed, and it ends with the festival of Eid al-Fitr. Muslims often break the fast with a meal called iftar. For 10 points, name this ninth month.

Pilgrims taking part in this event wear plain white garments called ihram and circle the Kaaba seven times. Other rites include running between the hills of Safa and Marwa and standing on the plain of Arafat. Every able Muslim who can afford it should do this at least once. For 10 points, name this annual pilgrimage to Mecca, one of the five pillars of Islam.

According to Muslim tradition, this cube-shaped structure was rebuilt by Ibrahim and his son Ismail. It is draped in a black cloth called the kiswah and holds the Black Stone in one corner. Muslims around the world face it during prayer. For 10 points, name this shrine at the center of the Sacred Mosque in Mecca.

Verses of this text are read in the original Arabic during daily prayers and memorized by people called hafiz. Its chapters are arranged roughly from longest to shortest, apart from the short opening one. The Uthmanic edition is the basis of every modern copy. For 10 points, name this scripture.

This event of 622 is the starting point of the Islamic calendar. Muhammad's cousin Ali is said to have slept in his bed to deceive pursuers while he left Mecca with Abu Bakr and hid in a cave. The travelers' destination was Yathrib. For 10 points, name this emigration of Muhammad and his followers to Medina.

A disputed succession after Muhammad's death in 632 split Islam into two major branches. The larger branch, which makes up roughly eighty-five to ninety percent of Muslims, accepted Abu Bakr as the first caliph. Its name refers to following the tradition of the Prophet. For 10 points, name this branch of Islam, contrasted with Shia.

This branch of Islam holds that leadership should have passed to Ali, Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law. Its followers commemorate the martyrdom of Husayn, and most of them live in Iran, Iraq, and Azerbaijan. They honor leaders called imams. For 10 points, name this second-largest branch of Islam.

This woman was the wife of Ali and the mother of Hasan and Husayn. She is sometimes given the title al-Zahra, "the radiant." Both Sunnis and Shia revere her, and one of the most successful Fatimid dynasties took her name. For 10 points, name this youngest daughter of Muhammad and Khadijah.

This man was Muhammad's close friend and father of his wife Aisha. After the Prophet's death he became the first of the Rashidun, or "rightly guided," caliphs. His short reign saw the Ridda Wars against tribes that broke away. For 10 points, name this first caliph, whose surname means "father of the virgin."

This caliph, the second of the Rashidun, ruled from 634 to 644 and oversaw conquests of Syria, Egypt, and Persia. He is credited with starting the Hijri calendar and with entering Jerusalem peacefully. He was assassinated by a Persian slave named Abu Lulu. For 10 points, name this successor of Abu Bakr.

This third caliph oversaw the compilation of a standard written version of the Quran. He belonged to the Umayyad clan and was married to two of Muhammad's daughters in turn. His murder in 656 led to the First Fitna, or civil war. For 10 points, name this Rashidun caliph, successor to Umar.

This man was Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, and he became the fourth caliph in 656. His supporters, the party of this man, gave the Shia branch its name. He moved the capital to Kufa and was killed there in 661. For 10 points, name this figure who is regarded as the first imam by Shia Muslims.

This title belonged to the political and religious successors of Muhammad, such as Abu Bakr and Umar. Later holders ruled from Damascus, Baghdad, Cairo, and Istanbul. The institution ended in 1924 when it was abolished by Mustafa Kemal Ataturk. For 10 points, give this title of the leader of the Muslim community.

These collections record the sayings and actions of Muhammad as reported by his companions. Compilers such as Bukhari and Muslim judged the chain of narrators for each one. Together with the Quran they are a key source of Islamic law. For 10 points, name these reports of the Prophet's words and deeds.

This term, meaning "the path to the water source," refers to Islamic religious law. It is derived from the Quran, hadith, consensus, and analogy, and it is interpreted by scholars called muftis. Four Sunni schools, including the Hanafi and Maliki, apply it. For 10 points, give this term for Islamic law.

This pillar of Islam requires Muslims to give a fixed portion of their savings, usually two and a half percent, to the needy. Its name means "purification." It is separate from voluntary charity called sadaqah. For 10 points, name this obligatory almsgiving.

Muslims perform this ritual five times a day facing Mecca, after performing ablution called wudu. It involves bowing and prostrating on a mat. The call to it is given by the muezzin. For 10 points, name this Islamic prayer, the second pillar of Islam.

The first pillar of Islam is a statement of faith beginning "There is no god but God." It adds that Muhammad is the messenger of God. Saying it with sincere belief makes a person a Muslim. For 10 points, name this declaration of faith.

This festival marks the end of Ramadan and is celebrated for three days. Muslims dress in new clothes, attend special prayers, and give a charity called zakat al-fitr. Sweets are exchanged among families. For 10 points, name this festival whose name means "breaking of the fast."

This festival honors Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son at God's command. It falls on the tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah, at the end of the Hajj, and families sacrifice a sheep or goat and share the meat. It is also called the "Greater Eid." For 10 points, name this festival of sacrifice.

On this night near the end of Ramadan, according to tradition, the first verses of the Quran were sent down to Muhammad. The Quran says it is better than a thousand months. Muslims often seek it on odd-numbered nights of the last ten days. For 10 points, name this "Night of Power."

Muslims worship in this kind of building, which often has a dome and a tall tower. Worshippers remove their shoes before entering the prayer hall. The Great Umayyad building in Damascus and the Blue one in Istanbul are famous examples. For 10 points, give this Islamic house of worship.

The muezzin traditionally gives the call to prayer from this feature of a mosque. These tall, slender towers are found at the Great Mosque of Samarra, which has a spiral one called the Malwiya. Many mosques have four or more. For 10 points, name this tower.

This feature of a mosque is a niche in the wall that indicates the direction of Mecca. It is often decorated with tile or calligraphy, and the imam stands in front of it to lead prayers. A nearby stepped pulpit is called a minbar. For 10 points, name this niche.

According to Islamic belief, this angel revealed the Quran to Muhammad. He is called Jibril in Arabic and is also said to have accompanied the Prophet on the Night Journey. Christians know the same angel as the one who announced Jesus's birth to Mary. For 10 points, name this archangel.

This shrine in Jerusalem is topped by a golden dome and stands over the rock from which Muhammad is said to have ascended to heaven. It was built by the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik around 691. It stands on the Temple Mount. For 10 points, name this Islamic shrine.

Practitioners of this mystical branch of Islam seek direct experience of God. Some orders use music, such as the Mawlawi order, whose members whirl in a ceremony called sama. Rumi is its best-known poet. For 10 points, name this tradition whose members are sometimes called dervishes.

The first dynasty of Muslim caliphs, founded by Muawiya in 661, ruled from Damascus. Its rule eventually reached Spain and the Indus. It was overthrown by the Abbasids in 750. For 10 points, name this dynasty, whose name comes from a clan of the Quraysh.

This dynasty built a capital called the "Round City" at Baghdad in 762 under al-Mansur. Its rule produced a "House of Wisdom" that translated Greek works during the reign of al-Mamun. Hulagu Khan ended its power in 1258. For 10 points, name this caliphal dynasty that replaced the Umayyads.

In 680 Husayn, grandson of Muhammad, was killed in this Iraqi city by the army of Yazid. Shia Muslims mourn his death on the day of Ashura, and pilgrims visit his shrine here. For 10 points, name this city, the site of the most important Shia martyrdom.

text: This man was born a prince in Lumbini, in present-day Nepal, and left his palace after seeing an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and an ascetic. He fasted for years before accepting a bowl of rice milk from a girl named Sujata. After meditating under a fig tree, he taught his first sermon at the Deer Park in Sarnath. For 10 points, name this founder of Buddhism.

Buddhism teaches that suffering exists, that it has a cause in craving, that it can end, and that a path leads to its end. The Buddha gave these in his first sermon after enlightenment. For 10 points, name this set of four central teachings.

This path consists of right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. It is the fourth of the Four Noble Truths. It is called the Middle Way between luxury and extreme asceticism. For 10 points, name this Buddhist path to the end of suffering.

Buddhists seek this state of liberation, whose name literally means "blowing out," in which the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion are extinguished. Reaching it ends the cycle of rebirth. The Pali form of this word is nibbana. For 10 points, name this goal of Buddhist practice.

The Buddha attained enlightenment while meditating beneath this kind of tree at Bodh Gaya. It is a species of fig, and descendants of the original are venerated in Sri Lanka and India. Buddhist pilgrims visit the site. For 10 points, name this tree, whose name means "awakening."

This branch of Buddhism, whose name means "School of the Elders," is dominant in Sri Lanka, Thailand, and Myanmar. It follows the Pali Canon and emphasizes the ideal of the arhat. For 10 points, name this branch, often contrasted with Mahayana.

This branch of Buddhism, whose name means "Great Vehicle," spread to China, Korea, and Japan. It emphasizes the ideal of the bodhisattva, who delays nirvana to help others. Pure Land and Zen belong to it. For 10 points, name this branch of Buddhism.

This school of Mahayana Buddhism, called Chan in China, emphasizes seated meditation known as zazen. It was brought to Japan by Eisai and Dogen, and its masters use riddles called koans. For 10 points, name this Japanese form of Buddhism.

This title is held by the spiritual leader of the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism, who is believed to be a reincarnation of his predecessor. The current holder fled Tibet in 1959 and settled in Dharamsala. For 10 points, give this title of the most famous Tibetan Buddhist leader.

This Tibetan school of Buddhism, whose name means "Diamond Vehicle," uses mantras, mandalas, and ritual practices. It arrived with Padmasambhava and Atisha. For 10 points, name this form of Buddhism practiced in Tibet and Bhutan, also called Tantric Buddhism.

This religion is practiced by roughly a billion people, mainly in India and Nepal. It has no single founder or scripture, but its texts include the Vedas and Upanishads. For 10 points, name this religion whose major gods include Vishnu and Shiva.

These oldest scriptures of Hinduism are written in Sanskrit and are divided into four collections, including the Rigveda. They contain hymns to deities such as Agni and Indra. For 10 points, name these sacred texts, from which the Upanishads emerged.

These philosophical texts end the Vedas and are called Vedanta, "the end of the Veda." They discuss the identity of atman and Brahman. Over 100 exist, and ten principal ones were commented on by Shankara. For 10 points, name these texts.

This text is a conversation set on the battlefield of Kurukshetra between a warrior and his charioteer. The warrior is Arjuna, who hesitates to fight his kin. It is part of the Mahabharata. For 10 points, name this "Song of God," a central Hindu scripture.

In Hinduism, this god is the creator in a trinity with Vishnu and Shiva. He is depicted with four faces and is often shown with a swan. For 10 points, name this god, not to be confused with the impersonal ultimate reality called Brahman.

This Hindu god preserves the universe and descends to earth in forms called avatars. His ten main incarnations include Rama and Krishna. He sleeps on the serpent Shesha. For 10 points, name this member of the Trimurti.

This Hindu god is depicted with a third eye, a trident, and the Ganges flowing from his hair. He is both destroyer and ascetic, and is worshipped in the form of the lingam. His wife is Parvati. For 10 points, name this member of the Trimurti.

This elephant-headed Hindu god is the remover of obstacles and the son of Shiva and Parvati. He is invoked at the start of ventures and rides a mouse. For 10 points, name this god, whose festival Ganesh Chaturthi is celebrated every year.

This Hindu god grew up among cowherds in Vrindavan, where he played the flute and danced with the gopis. He later killed his uncle Kamsa and founded the city of Dwarka. His charioteering for Arjuna is told in a famous scripture. For 10 points, name this eighth avatar of Vishnu.

This Hindu epic tells of a prince's fourteen-year exile, the abduction of his wife by a ten-headed king, and the aid of a monkey god in a battle at Lanka. It is attributed to the sage Valmiki, who is called the first poet. Dussehra honors its hero's victory. For 10 points, name this Sanskrit epic.

In this epic, Yudhishthira loses his kingdom in a game of dice to Duryodhana's side, and the five brothers are exiled for thirteen years. Bhishma lies on a bed of arrows, and Karna is killed when his chariot wheel sticks in the mud. A dog follows the victors to heaven at the end. For 10 points, name this Sanskrit epic attributed to Vyasa.

This festival of lights, celebrated in October or November, honors Lakshmi and Rama's return to Ayodhya. Families light clay lamps called diyas and set off fireworks. For 10 points, name this Hindu festival.
This spring festival of colors involves throwing colored powder and water. It celebrates the burning of Holika and Krishna's love for Radha. For 10 points, name this Hindu festival.

In Hindu and Buddhist thought, this concept holds that a person's actions have consequences that shape future lives. Good deeds produce good outcomes and bad deeds the opposite. For 10 points, name this principle of cause and effect.

In Hinduism, liberation from the cycle of birth and death is called this. It is the final goal of life, reached by realizing the unity of the self and Brahman. Jains and Buddhists call a similar state nirvana. For 10 points, give this Sanskrit term.

Hindus consider this river sacred and bathe in it at cities such as Varanasi and Haridwar. The goddess of the same name is said to have descended from heaven through Shiva's hair. For 10 points, name this river of northern India.
This religion was founded by Guru Nanak in the Punjab in the fifteenth century. Its scripture is the Guru Granth Sahib, and followers wear the five Ks. For 10 points, name this monotheistic religion.

This Chinese philosopher compiled maxims on filial piety, ritual, and the gentleman, which were collected in the Analects. He lived in the Spring and Autumn period, and his followers included Mencius. For 10 points, name this founder of Confucianism.

The Tao Te Ching is attributed to this legendary sage, said to have written it before leaving China on a water buffalo. For 10 points, name this figure traditionally regarded as the founder of Daoism.

This Japanese religion has no founder and venerates spirits called kami. Its shrines are marked by gateways called torii, and its priests perform purification rituals. For 10 points, name this indigenous religion of Japan.

This Indian religion's twenty-fourth tirthankara was Mahavira, who taught strict nonviolence. Its monks may wear white robes or go naked, and some sweep the ground before them to avoid harming insects. For 10 points, name this religion.

text: This religion's holy book, the Avesta, includes hymns called the Gathas. Its priests tend fires in temples, and it holds that the universe is a battle between good and evil. Its followers in India are known as Parsis. For 10 points, name this ancient Persian religion that worships Ahura Mazda.

This prophet is said to have received a vision of Ahura Mazda at about age thirty. He composed the Gathas and taught the dualism of truth and the lie. He is believed to have lived in ancient Iran. For 10 points, name this founder of a religion also called Mazdaism.

In Zoroastrian belief, this evil spirit, also called Ahriman, opposes creation through lies, disease, and death. Its name means "destructive spirit," and it is contrasted with Spenta Mainyu. At the end of time the Saoshyant is expected to defeat it. For 10 points, give this adversary of Ahura Mazda.

This man claimed that the angel Moroni led him to golden plates buried in a hill in upstate New York. He translated them as a scripture and founded a church in 1830. He was killed by a mob in Carthage, Illinois, in 1844. For 10 points, name this founder of the Latter-day Saint movement.

This scripture is divided into books named for figures such as Nephi, Alma, and Ether. Followers of the Latter-day Saint movement believe it was translated from golden plates. It describes Jesus visiting the Americas. For 10 points, name this scripture first published in 1830.

After Joseph Smith's death, this man led the Mormon pioneers west to the Great Salt Lake in 1847. He became the second president of the church and the first governor of Utah Territory. He had many wives. For 10 points, name this leader.

This city in Utah was founded by Mormon pioneers in 1847 and is the headquarters of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Temple Square is its center. For 10 points, name this state capital.

This religion was founded in nineteenth-century Persia and teaches the unity of God, religion, and humanity. Its Lotus Temple is in Delhi, and its holiest shrines are in Haifa and Acre. For 10 points, name this faith, founded by Baha'u'llah.

This Persian nobleman, born Mirza Husayn-Ali, declared himself a manifestation of God in 1863. He was exiled to Acre and wrote the Kitab-i-Aqdas. For 10 points, name this founder of the Baha'i Faith, whose name means "Glory of God."

This religion began in Jamaica in the 1930s and regards Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia as divine. Many followers wear dreadlocks and avoid meat, and the use of cannabis is a sacrament. For 10 points, name this movement associated with Bob Marley.

This religion, which blends West African Yoruba beliefs with Catholic saints, developed among enslaved people in Cuba. Practitioners honor spirits called orishas. For 10 points, name this religion, also known as Regla de Ocha.

This Afro-Caribbean religion was developed in Haiti and honors spirits called lwa. Its priests are called houngans and its priestesses mambos. For 10 points, name this religion, often misrepresented in films.

These priests of the ancient Celts served as judges, teachers, and religious leaders. Julius Caesar describes their sacrifices, and Roman sources say they venerated mistletoe and oak. For 10 points, name these ancient Celtic priests.

This Quaker movement founder wrote a journal and preached that the Inner Light of God is in each person. Born in Leicestershire in 1624, he was repeatedly imprisoned. For 10 points, name this founder of the Religious Society of Friends.

This Christian group, living mostly in Pennsylvania and Ohio, avoids modern technology and drives horse-drawn buggies. They follow an Anabaptist tradition named for a Swiss leader, Jakob Ammann. For 10 points, name this group.

This Christian denomination, founded after the Great Disappointment of 1844, observes Saturday as the Sabbath. It emphasizes health and was shaped by Ellen G. White. For 10 points, name this denomination, which runs Loma Linda University.

This denomination was named by Charles Taze Russell's followers and publishes The Watchtower. Members go door to door, refuse blood transfusions, and do not celebrate birthdays. For 10 points, name this group.

This Christian denomination was founded by Mary Baker Eddy, who wrote Science and Health. It teaches that illness is an illusion that prayer can heal, and it publishes a daily newspaper in Boston. For 10 points, name this church.

This tradition emphasizes the experience of the Holy Spirit, including speaking in tongues. It grew from the 1906 Azusa Street Revival in Los Angeles and is now one of the fastest-growing Christian movements. For 10 points, name this movement.

This prophet, born in Persia in the third century, taught a dualistic religion that blended Christian, Zoroastrian, and Buddhist elements. His religion spread from Rome to China before dying out. For 10 points, name this founder of Manichaeism.

This mystery religion of the Roman army worshipped a god who slew a sacred bull. Its followers met in underground temples called mithraea. For 10 points, name this religion, named for a god of Persian origin.

This religious group in northern Iraq venerates Melek Taus, the Peacock Angel, and prays facing the sun. Their holiest site is the valley shrine of Lalish. They are mostly Kurdish-speaking and have suffered massacres in 2014. Membership is traditionally limited to those born into it. For 10 points, name this religion.

This theological system of the Hellenistic era taught that the material world was created by a lesser being and that salvation comes through secret knowledge. The Nag Hammadi library contained its texts. For 10 points, name this movement, whose name comes from the Greek for "knowledge."

This monument in Wiltshire, England, is a ring of large standing stones. Some think it was used for astronomical purposes, and people gather there at the summer solstice. For 10 points, name this prehistoric monument.

This 1890 movement among Plains tribes, started by the Paiute prophet Wovoka, promised the return of the dead and the end of white expansion. Dancers wore shirts believed to be bulletproof. It was suppressed at Wounded Knee. For 10 points, name this ritual.

This Ethiopian emperor, born Tafari Makonnen, is revered as the returned Messiah by Rastafari. He ruled from 1930 until he was deposed in 1974, with a break during the Italian occupation. He addressed the League of Nations in 1936 after Mussolini's invasion, and he gave Jamaica's Rastas their name for him. For 10 points, name this man.

This word describes the belief that natural objects, such as rivers, rocks, and trees, have a spirit. Edward Tylor used it in the nineteenth century to describe early religion. For 10 points, give this term.

This religious figure, in many Siberian and Native cultures, enters trances to communicate with spirits and heal. The word comes from the Tungus language. For 10 points, name this kind of practitioner.

This Unitarian principle, found in Enlightenment Europe, holds that God created the universe but does not intervene in it. Thomas Jefferson and Benjamin Franklin held views of this sort. For 10 points, name this belief.

This nickname is commonly applied to members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, after a prophet-historian in their scripture. Members avoid coffee and alcohol and often serve two-year missions. For 10 points, give this nickname.

text: This theorem is proved by induction using the fact that a sum of two binomial coefficients equals a coefficient in the next row of a triangle. It gives the coefficient of x to the k in the expansion of the sum of x and y raised to the n as n choose k. For n equal to 4, the coefficients are 1, 4, 6, 4, 1. For 10 points, name this theorem about expanding powers of a sum of two terms.

The sum of these quantities for a polygon with n sides is 180 times n minus 2 degrees. This is why the three of them in a triangle sum to 180 degrees. A hexagon has six of them summing to 720 degrees. For 10 points, name these angles found inside a closed figure at the vertices.

This number, equal to 2 times 3 times 5 times 7, is the product of the first four primes. It is the smallest number divisible by each of 2, 3, 5, and 7. Half of it is 105. For 10 points, name this number, the product of the first four primes.

This mathematician proved that the number of primes is infinite in his Elements, and also gave an algorithm for the greatest common divisor of two numbers. He is called the father of geometry. For 10 points, name this Greek mathematician who wrote the Elements.

Conic sections include the parabola, the hyperbola, and this curve. It is defined as the set of points for which the sum of distances to two fixed foci is constant. A circle is a special case with both foci at the same point. For 10 points, name this oval-shaped conic section, the shape of planetary orbits.

This theorem states that in a right triangle the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides. A 3-4-5 triangle is a common example. For 10 points, name this theorem named for a Greek philosopher from Samos.

A function f is called one of these if f of negative x equals negative f of x, so its graph is symmetric about the origin. The sine function and x cubed are examples, while cosine is not. The product of two such functions is even. For 10 points, name this type of function, the counterpart to an even function.

This sequence begins 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. The ratios of consecutive terms approach the golden ratio. Each term is the sum of the two before it. For 10 points, name this sequence introduced to Europe in the Liber Abaci by a mathematician from Pisa.

In a set of numbers, this measure of center is found by listing the values in order and taking the one in the middle. For 1, 3, 5, 7, 100 it equals 5, unaffected by the outlier. For 10 points, name this statistic distinct from the mean and the mode.

This number, approximately 3.14159, is the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter. It is irrational and transcendental. It is celebrated on March 14. For 10 points, name this constant represented by a Greek letter.

This mathematician posed a "last theorem" in a margin of a copy of Arithmetica, claiming that no three positive integers satisfy a to the n plus b to the n equals c to the n for n greater than 2. A proof was finally given by Andrew Wiles. For 10 points, name this French lawyer and mathematician.

This function is defined for positive integers as the product of all positive integers up to n, and Euler extended it to the complex numbers with an integral. Zero of these is defined as 1. Five of these is 120. For 10 points, name this function written with an exclamation point.

The Pythagorean identity states that sine squared plus this function squared equals 1. It is the ratio of adjacent side to hypotenuse in a right triangle. Its graph is a sine wave shifted by a quarter period. For 10 points, name this trigonometric function abbreviated cos.
A polygon with five sides is called this. A famous United States military headquarters has this shape. Its interior angles each measure 108 degrees if it is regular. For 10 points, name this shape.

This operation on a function gives the slope of the tangent line at each point. For x squared, the result is 2x. It was developed independently by Newton and Leibniz. For 10 points, name this basic operation of calculus, whose reverse is integration.

The set of numbers 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, and 13 are examples of these numbers, which have exactly two positive divisors. Two is the only even one. For 10 points, name this type of number that is only divisible by one and itself.

These numbers are written as a plus b i, where i is the square root of negative one. They can be plotted on the Argand plane. The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra says polynomials factor completely over this set. For 10 points, name this extension of the real numbers.

Cardano published a formula for the roots of this kind of polynomial equation, which Tartaglia had shown him. The general form has a term in x cubed and its graph can have up to two turning points. Abel and Galois later showed no such formula exists for degree five. For 10 points, name this degree-three kind of equation.

The area of a circle with radius 5 is 25 pi. The distance across a circle through its center is called this. It equals twice the radius. For 10 points, name this length, a chord passing through the center.

The probability of two independent events both occurring is found by doing this operation to their separate probabilities. For example, getting two heads in a row on fair coin flips has probability one fourth. For 10 points, name this operation, repeated addition.

This mathematician is the namesake of a point set that is the intersection of the original unit interval after repeatedly removing middle thirds. He also introduced the theory that some infinities are larger than others, proving the reals are uncountable. For 10 points, name this German founder of set theory.

The set of numbers 1, 2, 3, and so on that we use to count are called these numbers. Together with zero they are the whole numbers. For 10 points, name these numbers, which contrast with the integers that include negatives.

A square matrix has this quantity, which for the two by two matrix with entries a, b, c, d equals a d minus b c. If it equals zero, the matrix has no inverse. For 10 points, name this scalar value of a matrix.

In probability, this theorem says that the probability of A given B equals the probability of B given A times the probability of A, all divided by the probability of B. It is used to update beliefs given evidence. For 10 points, name this theorem named for an English reverend.

The number of degrees in a full turn around a circle is this number. It is also the number of days approximately in a year in the old Babylonian calendar. For 10 points, name this number, equal to 6 times 60.

This type of sequence has a constant ratio between consecutive terms, such as 2, 6, 18, 54. The sum of infinitely many terms converges if the absolute value of the ratio is less than one. For 10 points, name this kind of sequence, distinct from an arithmetic one.

John Napier introduced this function to simplify multiplication into addition, and slide rules rely on it. It is the inverse of an exponential, so the base ten version of it applied to 1000 equals 3. The natural version uses the number e as its base. For 10 points, name this function written log.

This number is the smallest positive integer, and it is neither prime nor composite. It is the multiplicative identity, so multiplying any number by it leaves that number unchanged. Its reciprocal is itself. For 10 points, name this number, which comes after zero and before two.

This mathematician's namesake paradox concerns the set of all sets that do not contain themselves. He co-wrote Principia Mathematica with Alfred North Whitehead. For 10 points, name this British logician and philosopher.

In geometry, two triangles are called this if their corresponding angles are equal and their sides are in proportion, such as a triangle and an enlarged copy of it. Congruent triangles are a special case. For 10 points, name this term for triangles with the same shape.

text: This data structure is accessed in last-in, first-out order, and a call of this type is how recursion stores return addresses. Its two main operations are push and pop. Running out of room in one gives a famous overflow error. For 10 points, name this data structure that also shares its name with a pile of plates.

This algorithm repeatedly steps through a list, comparing adjacent items and swapping them if out of order. Larger values "bubble" to the end on each pass. It takes quadratic time in the worst case. For 10 points, name this simple sorting algorithm with a bath-time name.

This type of loop in programming repeats a block as long as a condition remains true. Unlike a for loop, it does not necessarily have a counter. An infinite one occurs when the condition never becomes false. For 10 points, name this loop that begins with a keyword meaning "during."

This British mathematician described an abstract machine with an infinite tape and a read-write head, and also worked at Bletchley Park breaking Enigma. A test named for him asks whether a machine can imitate a human in conversation. For 10 points, name this founder of theoretical computer science.

This program translates source code written in a high-level language into machine code before the program runs. GCC is a well-known example for C. Interpreters differ in that they execute code line by line. For 10 points, name this kind of program.

Brendan Eich created this language in ten days in 1995 for Netscape. It runs in web browsers and lets pages respond to clicks, and despite a similar name it is unrelated to a coffee-named language from Sun. Node.js lets it run on servers. For 10 points, name this language.

This search algorithm repeatedly halves the interval of a sorted array by comparing the target with the middle element. It runs in logarithmic time. It fails if the array is not sorted. For 10 points, name this search algorithm that is far faster than a linear scan for sorted data.

This computer component, often called the "brain" of a computer, executes instructions. Intel and AMD make most of the ones in desktop computers. Its abbreviation stands for "central processing unit." For 10 points, name this component, abbreviated CPU.

Tim Berners-Lee invented this system in 1989 while at CERN, combining hypertext, URLs, and HTTP. Browsers like Firefox and Chrome access it. It is often confused with the Internet itself. For 10 points, name this system of linked pages, abbreviated WWW.

This type of error occurs when a program runs but does not do what the programmer intended, such as an off-by-one mistake. The term supposedly comes from a moth found in the Harvard Mark II. For 10 points, name this kind of flaw, whose removal is debugging.

A variable that can hold only true or false is called this type, named for an English mathematician who developed algebraic logic. The operations AND, OR, and NOT act on these values. For 10 points, name this data type.

This sorting algorithm picks an element called the pivot and partitions the array into smaller and larger elements, then recurses. Its average time is n log n but its worst case is quadratic. Tony Hoare invented it. For 10 points, name this sorting algorithm sometimes called partition-exchange sort.

This protocol suite underlies the Internet, with one part breaking data into packets and another handling addressing. The second part's addresses come in versions four and six. For 10 points, name this suite, abbreviated by two sets of letters separated by a slash.

This kind of memory is volatile, losing its contents when power is turned off, and is used for programs that are currently running. A typical laptop has several gigabytes of it. For 10 points, name this memory, abbreviated RAM.

Ada Lovelace wrote what is often called the first computer program for this mechanical computer designed by Charles Babbage. It was never completed in his lifetime and was to use punched cards. For 10 points, name this proposed general-purpose machine, which had an "Analytical" name.

This protocol, abbreviated HTTP, is used for web browsing, with a secure version ending in S. Pages at addresses beginning with it are fetched by browsers. For 10 points, give the full name of this protocol, whose first word is for text that links.

In a computer, a process waiting for a resource held by another process that is waiting for its resource is in this state. The classic illustration is five philosophers with forks. For 10 points, name this standstill in concurrent computing.

This data structure holds a first-in, first-out sequence, like a line at a store. Its main operations are enqueue and dequeue. Breadth-first search uses one. For 10 points, name this data structure that shares its name with a waiting line.

This kind of software, such as Windows, macOS, or Linux, manages hardware and provides services for other programs. Android and iOS are mobile examples. For 10 points, name this basic software layer, abbreviated OS.

Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie created this operating system at Bell Labs in 1969. Its philosophy includes small tools connected by pipes and everything being a file. macOS and Linux are descended from or modeled on it. For 10 points, name this operating system.

This structure consists of nodes connected by edges and has no cycles, with one special node at the top. Binary examples have at most two children per node. Heaps and file systems are organized as these. For 10 points, name this hierarchical data structure that has a root and leaves.

This programming language, created by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs, was used to rewrite an early operating system there. Its object-oriented extension by Bjarne Stroustrup has plus signs in its name. For 10 points, name this one-letter language.

A set of step-by-step instructions to solve a problem or perform a computation is called this. The word comes from the name of a Persian mathematician, al-Khwarizmi. For 10 points, give this term used for sorting and searching procedures.
This type of attack tries every possible password or key until the correct one is found. Longer passwords make it exponentially harder. For 10 points, name this attack named for its lack of subtlety.

This design principle in programming involves hiding internal details of an object and exposing only a controlled interface. It is one of the pillars of object-oriented programming, along with inheritance and polymorphism. For 10 points, name this principle that bundles data and methods together.

This language, whose name contains a hot drink, was released by Sun Microsystems and is known for "write once, run anywhere." It is distinct from JavaScript. For 10 points, name this object-oriented language.

This function in programming calls itself with a smaller input until it reaches a base case. A classic example computes factorial this way. Fibonacci can also be computed this way, though inefficiently. For 10 points, name this technique, or the type of function using it.

A hash of a password is usually stored rather than the password itself because this property of the function makes it infeasible to recover the input. Algorithms like SHA-256 are examples. For 10 points, name this type of function mapping data of arbitrary size to a fixed-size value.

A computer virus differs from this self-replicating malware, which spreads across networks without attaching to a host file. The Morris one was one of the first on the Internet. For 10 points, name this malware named for a crawling creature.

This US Navy rear admiral led the team that developed the first compiler and contributed to COBOL, a language for business. She worked on the Harvard Mark I and UNIVAC. A Navy destroyer was named for her. For 10 points, name this computer scientist known as "Amazing Grace."

text: This scientist's three laws describe motion, and he also formulated universal gravitation. His book Principia was published in 1687. A unit of force is named for him. For 10 points, name this English physicist who supposedly was inspired by a falling apple.

This property of a material describes how much mass it has per unit volume. It is measured in grams per cubic centimeter, and water has a value of one. An object floats if it has less of this than the fluid it is in. For 10 points, name this quantity found by dividing mass by volume.

This is the SI unit of force, equal to a kilogram meter per second squared. It is named for a physicist who wrote a famous book called the Principia and formulated three laws of motion. A medium apple weighs roughly one of these. For 10 points, name this unit, abbreviated N.

The scientific method begins with a testable guess called this, which an experiment then supports or refutes. It is a proposed explanation for an observation. For 10 points, name this term, often described as an "educated guess."
This scientist developed the theory of evolution by natural selection after traveling on the HMS Beagle. He wrote On the Origin of Species in 1859. For 10 points, name this English naturalist.

This French chemist and biologist developed pasteurization and a vaccine for rabies. His swan-neck flask experiments disproved spontaneous generation. For 10 points, name this scientist who is a founder of germ theory.

Zero on this SI base temperature scale is absolute zero, and water freezes at 273.15 on it. It is named for a Scottish-Irish physicist, William Thomson, who became a baron and worked on thermodynamics. For 10 points, name this unit, abbreviated K.

These instruments, invented in the Netherlands around 1608 and improved by Galileo, make distant objects appear closer. Hubble is a famous orbiting one. For 10 points, name this instrument used by astronomers.

This type of variable in an experiment is the one that the experimenter deliberately changes to see its effect. The measured outcome is the dependent one. For 10 points, name this variable, whose name begins with a word meaning "free from control."

This English chemist at King's College London produced Photograph 51, an X-ray diffraction image of DNA. Her data were used by Watson and Crick, who later won a Nobel Prize. She also studied coal and the tobacco mosaic virus. For 10 points, name this scientist.

This prefix indicates a factor of one thousand in the metric system. It is used in the unit of distance often used for road trips outside the United States, and in the unit of mass equal to about 2.2 pounds. For 10 points, name this prefix abbreviated k.

This quantity, measured in grams or kilograms, describes how much matter is in an object. It stays the same on the Moon, whereas the related quantity weight changes with gravity. It is measured with a balance. For 10 points, name this quantity, symbol m.

This Austrian monk grew thousands of pea plants in a monastery garden in Brno. He observed that traits like seed shape appear in predictable ratios, such as three to one, in the second generation. He discovered dominant and recessive traits. For 10 points, name this father of genetics.

This German physicist developed the theories of special and general relativity and the photoelectric effect explanation. He won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics. For 10 points, name this scientist famous for E equals m c squared.

This device measures temperature and is found in many medicine cabinets. Common ones use a thin column of mercury or colored alcohol in a glass tube that rises as it gets warmer. A person with a fever has a reading above about 38 degrees Celsius. For 10 points, name this instrument.

This field studies rocks, minerals, fossils, and the structure of the Earth. Charles Lyell wrote the Principles of this science and argued for gradual change over long times, an idea called uniformitarianism. James Hutton is called its father. For 10 points, name this Earth science.

This term describes a substance made of only one type of atom, such as gold or oxygen. There are 118 known types listed on the periodic table. For 10 points, name this basic substance, which cannot be broken down chemically.

This unit of energy is named for an English brewer and physicist who measured the mechanical equivalent of heat. One of these equals a newton meter, and a watt is one of them per second. For 10 points, name this SI unit of energy.
This Greek scientist, from Syracuse, is credited with a principle about buoyancy and with the cry "Eureka." He also described the lever. For 10 points, name this ancient scientist.

This process takes place in chloroplasts using the green pigment chlorophyll. Plants convert sunlight, carbon dioxide, and water into glucose and release oxygen as a byproduct. The Calvin cycle is part of it. For 10 points, name this process by which plants make their own food.
This law states that for a given amount of gas at constant temperature, pressure is inversely proportional to volume. It is named for an Anglo-Irish chemist. For 10 points, name this gas law.

This scale, from 0 to 14, measures how acidic or basic a solution is. Lemon juice is low on it, pure water is at seven, and bleach is high. Litmus paper and universal indicator give a rough reading. For 10 points, name this scale, whose abbreviation has a lowercase p.

This Italian scientist used a telescope to discover four moons of Jupiter, the phases of Venus, and mountains on the Moon. He supported the Copernican model and wrote the Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems. He was tried by the Inquisition. For 10 points, name this scientist.

This Russian chemist created a periodic table in 1869 that arranged elements by atomic weight and left gaps for undiscovered elements. He predicted the properties of eka-aluminium, later found as gallium. Element 101 is named for him. For 10 points, name this scientist.

This is the layer of gases surrounding Earth, held in place by gravity. It is composed of about 78 percent nitrogen and 21 percent oxygen. Its lowest layer, the troposphere, is where weather occurs, and above it lies the stratosphere. For 10 points, name this layer.

This scientist, the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, shared the 1903 physics prize with her husband and Henri Becquerel. For 10 points, give the term for the emission of particles by unstable nuclei that they studied.
This type of energy is stored in an object because of its position, such as a book on a high shelf. It converts to kinetic energy when the object falls. For 10 points, name this energy.

This unit, equal to about 3.26 light-years, is used by astronomers for distances to stars. It is the distance at which a star shows a parallax angle of one arcsecond. Its name combines two words, parallax and second. For 10 points, name this unit.

This scientist's namesake principle states that it is impossible to know both the position and momentum of a particle exactly. He was a German physicist who helped develop quantum mechanics. For 10 points, name him.

This is the study of weather, which includes forecasting by tracking pressure systems and fronts. Practitioners use satellites, radar, and balloons to measure the atmosphere. Despite the name, it has nothing to do with meteors. For 10 points, name this atmospheric science.

text: Bluma Zeigarnik noticed that waiters remembered unpaid orders better than completed ones. That finding led to a namesake effect stating that people remember interrupted or incomplete tasks better than finished ones. Kurt Lewin was her advisor in Berlin. For 10 points, name this effect named for a Lithuanian-born psychologist.

This thinker's study of suicide divided it into egoistic, altruistic, anomic and fatalistic types. He called society a reality distinct from individuals, made of "social facts." His books include The Division of Labor in Society and The Elementary Forms of Religious Life. For 10 points, name this French founder of functionalist sociology.

This German sociologist wrote The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism. He described the "iron cage" of rationalization and defined the state as holding a monopoly on legitimate violence. For 10 points, name this author of Economy and Society.

This French thinker coined the word "sociology" and proposed the law of three stages: theological, metaphysical and positive. He founded positivism, which holds that society can be studied scientifically. For 10 points, name this man called the father of sociology.

This word, from a Greek root meaning "lawlessness," was used by Durkheim for a condition of normlessness in which social rules break down. Robert Merton later borrowed it for his strain theory of deviance. For 10 points, name this state of social instability, often seen in rapid economic upheaval.

This theory, developed from the ideas of George Herbert Mead and Herbert Blumer, holds that people create meaning through everyday face-to-face interactions using symbols such as language. For 10 points, name this micro-level perspective in sociology.

This American sociologist's book The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life compared social interaction to theater, with a "front stage" and "back stage." He also wrote Asylums and Stigma. For 10 points, name this scholar who developed the dramaturgical approach.

Charles Horton Cooley proposed this concept in which a person's self-image develops from imagining how others see and judge them. The term uses a piece of furniture found in a bathroom. For 10 points, name this "glass" concept of self.

In this kind of institution, like prisons, boot camps and mental hospitals, inmates are cut off from society and live under formal rules. Erving Goffman gave this name to such places. For 10 points, what term describes an institution that controls all aspects of its residents' lives?

Robert Merton distinguished two kinds of function: manifest functions, which are intended and recognized, and these, which are unintended and unrecognized. A university's role as a place to meet marriage partners is an example. For 10 points, name this counterpart to manifest functions.

This German thinker co-wrote The Communist Manifesto with Friedrich Engels. His conflict theory describes class struggle between the bourgeoisie and the proletariat. For 10 points, name this author of Das Kapital.

Marx used this term for the process by which workers in capitalism become estranged from the products of their labor, from the labor process, from other people and from themselves. For 10 points, name this concept, a word also used for feeling distant or cut off.

This sociologist wrote The Philadelphia Negro, an empirical study of a city's Black community. He coined the term "double consciousness" in The Souls of Black Folk and co-founded the NAACP. For 10 points, name this scholar who also edited the journal The Crisis.

Howard Becker popularized this theory of deviance, which says that deviance is not an act itself but a label applied by society to a person. Edwin Lemert distinguished primary from secondary deviance within it. For 10 points, name this theory, which says that being tagged an outsider can fuel further deviance.

Thorstein Veblen coined this phrase in The Theory of the Leisure Class for lavish spending on goods to display social status, such as luxury cars or designer watches. For 10 points, name this two-word term for showy buying.

Ferdinand Tonnies contrasted Gemeinschaft with this term for impersonal, contract-based society typical of big cities. The first term means "community." For 10 points, name this German term meaning "society."

This term refers to the ranking of people in a hierarchy based on wealth, power, and prestige. Caste and class systems are two examples. For 10 points, name this term, taken from the layers of rock in geology.

In a caste system, social position is determined this way, which means a person is born into a status and cannot change it through effort. For 10 points, what term, also used for status inherited from parents, describes such a "ascribed" system?

Pierre Bourdieu used this term for non-financial assets like education, taste and manners that help people gain status. He paired it with habitus in studying class reproduction. For 10 points, name this form of "capital," which includes knowing which fork to use at a formal dinner.

Robert Putnam's book Bowling Alone argued that this resource, consisting of networks, trust and civic participation, had declined in the United States. For 10 points, name this kind of "capital" provided by relationships among people.

This author argued in The Sociological Imagination that personal troubles must be linked to public issues and historical context. He also wrote The Power Elite. For 10 points, name this American sociologist, first name C. Wright.

This American social reformer co-founded Hull House in Chicago, a settlement house that aided immigrants. She shared the 1931 Nobel Peace Prize. For 10 points, name this woman, a pioneer of social work.

William Graham Sumner coined this word for the belief that one's own culture is superior and the standard for judging others. For 10 points, name this attitude, which differs from cultural relativism.

Sumner also distinguished two kinds of norms: these everyday customs, such as table manners, are not strictly enforced, while the second type has strong moral weight. For 10 points, name these casual customs, a counterpart to mores.

This sociologist's thesis, which holds that "if men define situations as real, they are real in their consequences," is named for him and his wife Dorothy. He co-wrote The Polish Peasant in Europe and America. For 10 points, name this Chicago sociologist, first name William I.

George Ritzer applied Weber's idea of rationalization to the fast food industry and coined this term built on the name of a restaurant chain. It stresses efficiency, calculability, predictability and control. For 10 points, name this "process" named for the golden arches.

Edwin Sutherland proposed this theory, which says that people learn criminal behavior from others in intimate groups, along with attitudes favorable to breaking the law. For 10 points, name this theory about learning crime, whose name contrasts with isolation.

This sociologist, a leader of the Chicago School, studied human ecology and the "marginal man." His collaborator Ernest Burgess proposed the concentric zone model of the city. For 10 points, name this man, first name Robert E.

text: Max Weber, Karl Marx and Emile Durkheim are often called the three founders of this field. It studies human society, social relationships and institutions. For 10 points, name this social science, a word coined by Auguste Comte.

This term refers to the process by which people learn the norms, values and behaviors of their society, through family, schools and peers. For 10 points, name this lifelong process of social learning.

In this research method, a sociologist studies a group by living among its members and taking part in their activities. It is also widely used by anthropologists. For 10 points, name this method of fieldwork, called participant observation.

These groups, such as family and close friends, involve intimate, face-to-face relationships and strong emotional ties. Charles Horton Cooley named them. For 10 points, what term describes these small, intimate groups that contrast with secondary groups?

Georg Simmel wrote an essay about this figure, someone who arrives today and stays tomorrow, combining nearness and remoteness. He also wrote about the metropolis and mental life. For 10 points, name this outsider type who is both in and out of a group.

This author's Street Corner Society was a participant-observation study of Italian-American men in Boston's North End. He spent years living in the neighborhood he described. For 10 points, name this sociologist, first name William Foote.

This French thinker's book The Spirit of the Laws argued that government power should be divided among legislative, executive and judicial branches. His ideas deeply influenced the framers of the United States Constitution. For 10 points, name this Enlightenment baron, a champion of the separation of powers.

This English philosopher's Two Treatises of Government argued that people have natural rights to life, liberty and property, and that people may overthrow a government that violates them. Thomas Jefferson drew on his ideas. For 10 points, name this author.

This philosopher's Leviathan described a "state of nature" in which life is "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short." He argued people should submit to an absolute sovereign for safety. For 10 points, name this English political theorist.

This Italian Renaissance diplomat wrote a handbook for rulers arguing that it is safer for a ruler to be feared than loved. It is dedicated to Lorenzo de Medici. For 10 points, name this author of The Prince.

This practice involves drawing electoral district boundaries to favor one party or group. It is named for a Massachusetts governor and a salamander-shaped district. For 10 points, name this manipulation of districts.

In the United States, this body, created in Article II of the Constitution, has 538 members, and a candidate needs 270 of its votes to win the presidency. For 10 points, name this system in which states choose the president through electors.

Maurice Duverger observed that this kind of electoral system, where the candidate with the most votes in a district wins, tends to produce a two-party system. It is also called first-past-the-post. For 10 points, name this voting rule that elects whoever gets the most votes, even without a majority.

Under this type of electoral system, used in Israel and many European countries, parties win legislative seats in proportion to the share of votes they receive. For 10 points, name this system, abbreviated PR, that encourages multiparty politics.

In this form of government, the executive branch is chosen from and accountable to the legislature, as in the United Kingdom and Canada. The head of government is a prime minister. For 10 points, name this system that contrasts with a presidential system.

In the United States Senate, this tactic allows a senator to delay a vote through extended speech. It can be ended through a vote called cloture, which currently requires three fifths of the Senate. For 10 points, name this delaying tactic.

In this 1803 Supreme Court case, Chief Justice John Marshall established the principle of judicial review. It involved William Marbury, who did not receive his commission as justice of the peace. For 10 points, name this case also named for the Secretary of State.

This German-born scholar, author of The Origins of Totalitarianism, also coined the phrase "the banality of evil" while covering Adolf Eichmann's trial. For 10 points, name this political theorist, first name Hannah.

This term for supreme authority within a territory was formalized in the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. Jean Bodin and Hobbes helped develop it. For 10 points, name this concept, the right of a state to govern itself without outside interference.

This 1949 alliance among Western powers, including the United States, Canada and several European countries, is based on a principle that an attack on one is an attack on all. For 10 points, name this military alliance headquartered in Brussels.

This international body has five permanent members with veto power: the United States, United Kingdom, France, Russia and China. For 10 points, name this United Nations body charged with keeping international peace.

Joseph Nye coined this term for the ability to shape what others want through culture, values and diplomacy rather than force or payment. It contrasts with hard power. For 10 points, name this kind of power.

Diplomat George Kennan's "Long Telegram" and X Article argued for this policy toward the Soviet Union, a strategy of preventing Communist expansion rather than rolling it back. For 10 points, name this Cold War policy adopted by the Truman administration.

This school of international relations, associated with Hans Morgenthau, holds that states act in their self-interest and seek power in an anarchic world. For 10 points, name this theory contrasting with liberalism.

This French aristocrat toured the young United States in the 1830s and wrote Democracy in America. He praised American civic associations but warned about the "tyranny of the majority." For 10 points, name this author.

This political philosopher wrote On Liberty, which defends individual freedom of speech and action unless it harms others. He also wrote Utilitarianism. For 10 points, name this English thinker, whose "harm principle" is named in the book.

In United States campaign finance, organizations of this type raise and spend money to elect or defeat candidates and are regulated by the Federal Election Commission. Super versions can raise unlimited sums but cannot coordinate with campaigns. For 10 points, name these groups, abbreviated PACs.

In this process held before general elections, voters or party members choose their party's nominee. A closed version limits participation to registered members of the party. For 10 points, name these elections, which include caucuses.

In this 1787 and 1788 series of eighty-five essays signed "Publius," Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay urged ratification of the Constitution. Number 10 warns about factions. For 10 points, name this series.

The writer of Federalist number 51 argued that "ambition must be made to counteract ambition," explaining this system in which each branch can limit the others. For 10 points, name this system, which includes the presidential veto.

In many countries, a government may hold this kind of direct vote in which citizens approve or reject a specific proposal, such as the 2016 United Kingdom vote on leaving the European Union. For 10 points, name this kind of direct vote.
This Greek philosopher's dialogue The Republic describes a just city ruled by philosopher-kings. His student Aristotle instead wrote Politics. For 10 points, name this teacher of Aristotle.
