text: In this work's scherzo, timpani play a prominent role, and the finale begins with a recitative for cellos and basses that rejects earlier themes. The finale sets lines by Friedrich Schiller for four vocal soloists and chorus. It premiered in Vienna in 1824, with its deaf composer on stage. For 10 points, name this symphony in D minor whose "Ode to Joy" became the anthem of the European Union.

This composer wrote the Coffee Cantata and the Saint Matthew Passion. While serving the prince of Cothen he wrote his Brandenburg-era instrumental music, and later he improvised a three-part ricercar for Frederick the Great that grew into The Musical Offering. His B minor Mass was never performed complete in his lifetime. For 10 points, name this Lutheran composer from Eisenach, whose sons included Carl Philipp Emanuel.

This composer's final work was a Requiem left unfinished at his death in 1791 and completed by his pupil Franz Xaver Sussmayr. He wrote The Magic Flute, Don Giovanni, and The Marriage of Figaro. Ludwig von Kochel cataloged his output. For 10 points, name this child prodigy from Salzburg.

A riot allegedly broke out at the 1913 Paris premiere of this composer's The Rite of Spring, which had choreography by Nijinsky. He also wrote the ballets The Firebird and Petrushka for Diaghilev. Later he adopted a neoclassical style in works like The Rake's Progress. For 10 points, name this Russian-born composer.

This French composer wrote Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun, inspired by a Mallarme poem. His opera Pelleas et Melisande and orchestral sketches La mer used whole-tone scales and blurred harmonies. His Suite bergamasque includes "Clair de lune." For 10 points, name this impressionist composer.

This composer wrote the operas Rigoletto, La traviata, and Il trovatore. His opera Aida was commissioned for a Cairo opera house. His chorus "Va, pensiero" from Nabucco became an Italian patriotic anthem. For 10 points, name this Italian composer of Otello and Falstaff.

This composer developed the leitmotif as a recurring theme linked to a character or idea. He built a festival theater at Bayreuth for his four-opera cycle about a cursed ring. His Tristan und Isolde uses a famous unresolved chord. For 10 points, name this German composer of The Ring of the Nibelung and "Ride of the Valkyries."

This Austrian composer died at age thirty-one but wrote over six hundred songs, including "Erlkonig," based on Goethe, and the cycle Winterreise. His Symphony No. 8 is called "Unfinished," and his Trout Quintet has a set of variations on his song. For 10 points, name this master of the Lied.

This composer's Piano Sonata No. 2 includes a funeral march as its third movement. He wrote a "Raindrop" prelude while staying on Majorca with George Sand. His heart was returned to Warsaw after his death in Paris in 1849. For 10 points, name this Polish piano composer of nocturnes and mazurkas.

This composer died in poverty in Vienna in 1741. His Gloria in D major and his collection L'estro armonico influenced Bach, who transcribed several of his concertos. Four violin concertos accompanied by sonnets depict the seasons. For 10 points, name this Italian Baroque composer.

This German-born composer moved to London and wrote the oratorio Messiah, whose "Hallelujah" chorus is traditionally heard standing. He also wrote Water Music for a royal barge party and Music for the Royal Fireworks. For 10 points, name this Baroque composer, George Frideric.

This composer wrote A German Requiem and the Academic Festival Overture. His four symphonies were slow in coming because he felt overshadowed by Beethoven. He championed his friend Robert Schumann's wife Clara. For 10 points, name this composer of Hungarian Dances and a famous lullaby.

This American composer wrote the ballets Rodeo, Billy the Kid, and Appalachian Spring, which quotes the Shaker tune "Simple Gifts." He wrote Fanfare for the Common Man. He studied with Nadia Boulanger in Paris. For 10 points, name this composer of the "Dean of American Music."

This work, premiered in 1924 by Paul Whiteman's band with its composer at the piano, opens with a clarinet glissando. It combined jazz idioms with classical forms. Its composer also wrote Porgy and Bess and An American in Paris. For 10 points, name this George Gershwin work whose title names a color.

This composer was denounced by Pravda in 1936 over his opera Lady Macbeth of the Mzensk District. His Symphony No. 5 was subtitled a "Soviet artist's response to just criticism." His Seventh Symphony, written during the siege of a city, is named for it. For 10 points, name this Soviet composer of the DSCH motif.

This composer's Piano Concerto No. 2 helped him recover after the failure of his first symphony. He wrote Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini and the symphonic poem Isle of the Dead. He left Russia after the 1917 revolution and settled in the United States. For 10 points, name this pianist-composer with famously large hands.

This Austrian composer led the Vienna Court Opera and wrote Das Lied von der Erde and Kindertotenlieder. His Symphony No. 2 is nicknamed "Resurrection" and ends with a choral finale. His wife Alma was a composer and later married Gropius. For 10 points, name this Late Romantic.

This composer's best-known work is a one-movement orchestral piece built on a repeated snare-drum rhythm and a gradually growing crescendo. He also wrote Pavane for a Dead Princess and Mother Goose Suite. His left-hand piano concerto was written for Paul Wittgenstein. For 10 points, name this French composer of Bolero.

This composer spent most of his career working for the Esterhazy princes. His Symphony No. 94 includes a sudden loud chord after a quiet theme and is called "Surprise." He wrote The Creation and many string quartets, earning the title "Father of the Symphony." He taught Beethoven. For 10 points, name this Austrian composer.

This musical form has three main sections: an exposition presenting contrasting themes in different keys, a development that manipulates them, and a recapitulation returning to the home key. It is typical for the first movement of a symphony or sonata. For 10 points, name this structure, which shares its name with a multi-movement instrumental genre.

This contrapuntal composition begins with one voice stating a subject that is answered by other voices in imitation at a different pitch. Bach's The Art of this form remained unfinished. Its name comes from the Latin word for "flight." For 10 points, name this polyphonic form.

This New Orleans trumpeter led the Hot Five and Hot Seven bands and recorded "West End Blues." He popularized scat singing and was nicknamed "Satchmo." His late hits included "Hello, Dolly!" and "What a Wonderful World." For 10 points, name this jazz musician.

This bandleader played at Harlem's Cotton Club and composed "Mood Indigo" and "Sophisticated Lady." His longtime collaborator Billy Strayhorn wrote "Take the 'A' Train." He also wrote the extended work Black, Brown and Beige. For 10 points, name this jazz pianist and composer, Duke.

This trumpeter's 1959 album Kind of Blue is based on modal improvisation and features John Coltrane and Bill Evans. He also recorded Birth of the Cool and electric albums such as Bitches Brew. For 10 points, name this jazz innovator.

This saxophonist recorded the harmonically dense Giant Steps and a suite in four parts that begins with "Acknowledgement." His playing in the 1950s was described as "sheets of sound." He also recorded "My Favorite Things" on soprano saxophone. For 10 points, name this jazz musician who made A Love Supreme.

This group from Liverpool made Sergeant Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band and Abbey Road. They appeared on The Ed Sullivan Show in 1964. Producer George Martin worked with them, and members included John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, and Ringo Starr. For 10 points, name this British band.

This composer wrote Eugene Onegin and the ballet Swan Lake. His 1812 Overture calls for cannon fire. His Symphony No. 6, subtitled "Pathetique," ends with a slow movement and premiered nine days before his death in 1893. His patron was Nadezhda von Meck. For 10 points, name this Russian composer.

This Russian composer was a member of The Five, the "Mighty Handful." His opera Boris Godunov deals with the tsar's guilt. A piano suite of his depicts walking through a gallery of Viktor Hartmann's paintings, with the "Promenade" theme linking movements. For 10 points, name this composer of Pictures at an Exhibition and Night on Bald Mountain.

This Hungarian composer collected folk songs with Zoltan Kodaly and used them in his work. He wrote Mikrokosmos, a set of 153 piano pieces, and the opera Duke Bluebeard's Castle. He fled to the United States before World War II and wrote a Concerto for Orchestra. For 10 points, name this composer.

This Austrian composer developed a method of composing using all twelve chromatic pitches in a fixed row. He used Sprechstimme in Pierrot lunaire and wrote Verklarte Nacht. With Berg and Webern, he formed the Second Viennese School. He fled the Nazis and settled in Los Angeles. For 10 points, name this composer.

text: This Swedish director's The Seventh Seal depicts a knight, Antonius Block, playing chess with Death. His Persona stars Liv Ullmann and Bibi Andersson, and Wild Strawberries follows an aged professor on a road trip. He often worked with cinematographer Sven Nykvist and shot on Faro Island. For 10 points, name this director.

This Italian director's 8 1/2 follows a filmmaker named Guido, played by Marcello Mastroianni, who struggles with creative block. La Dolce Vita includes a scene in the Trevi Fountain. His composer was Nino Rota. For 10 points, name this director of La Strada and Amarcord.

This director's 1960 debut feature has Jean-Paul Belmondo as a petty criminal who imitates Humphrey Bogart and Jean Seberg as an American student in Paris. He wrote criticism for Cahiers du cinema before directing Contempt and Weekend. His editing used jump cuts. For 10 points, name this French New Wave filmmaker of Breathless.

This director's first feature follows the delinquent Antoine Doinel, played by Jean-Pierre Leaud, and ends with a freeze frame on a beach. He also directed Jules and Jim and Day for Night. He wrote an essay attacking the "tradition of quality" in French cinema. For 10 points, name this director of The 400 Blows.

Associated with critics at Cahiers du cinema such as Eric Rohmer, Jacques Rivette, and Claude Chabrol, this film movement emerged in the late 1950s. It favored location shooting, handheld cameras, and a personal style influenced by the "auteur theory." It broke with the studio-bound tradition of French cinema. For 10 points, name this movement whose name translates as "Nouvelle Vague."

Directors such as Roberto Rossellini and Vittorio De Sica led this postwar movement in Italy. Rome, Open City and Bicycle Thieves used location shooting, natural light, and many nonprofessional actors. Its films depicted the poverty and hardship of ordinary people after World War II. For 10 points, name this Italian film movement.

This film movement of the 1920s Weimar Republic used distorted sets, harsh shadows, and painted-on lighting. Examples include The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari by Robert Wiene and Murnau's Nosferatu. It influenced later film noir and horror films. For 10 points, name this German style.

In this 1958 film, a detective with acrophobia is hired to follow a woman who seems possessed by a dead ancestor. James Stewart plays Scottie Ferguson, and Kim Novak plays both Madeleine and Judy. The film is famous for a camera effect that simultaneously tracks backward and zooms forward. For 10 points, name this Alfred Hitchcock film set in San Francisco.

This effect named for a Soviet filmmaker shows how viewers derive meaning from editing. A neutral close-up of an actor's face was cut together with a bowl of soup, a coffin, and a woman, and audiences read different emotions into the same face. It is a cornerstone of montage theory. For 10 points, name this film editing effect named for Lev.

This French term, meaning "placing on stage," names everything visible in the frame: sets, costumes, lighting, actor positions, and props. Critics at Cahiers du cinema analyzed it in the work of auteurs. It is often contrasted with montage. For 10 points, name this term for visual composition within a shot.

This director pioneered cross-cutting for last-minute rescues in his Biograph shorts. His epic Intolerance interweaves four stories across different eras, and his earlier 1915 film is both a landmark in technique and notorious for racism. He co-founded United Artists. For 10 points, name this American silent film director, D. W.

This Bengali director's debut Pather Panchali began a trilogy about a boy named Apu, followed by Aparajito and The World of Apu. He also made Charulata. He won an honorary Oscar shortly before he died in 1992. For 10 points, name this Indian director from Calcutta.

This Japanese director's Tokyo Story follows an elderly couple visiting their children. He often placed the camera at a low height, as if viewing from a tatami mat, and used "pillow shots" of still objects between scenes. He often cast Setsuko Hara. For 10 points, name this director of Late Spring.

This Soviet director made Solaris, Stalker, and Mirror. His book Sculpting in Time outlines his view of the long take as shaping time. His first feature, Ivan's Childhood, won the Golden Lion in Venice in 1962, and his Andrei Rublev depicts a medieval icon painter. For 10 points, name this director.

This German director's Aguirre, the Wrath of God and Fitzcarraldo both starred the volatile Klaus Kinski. During the making of the latter, a steamship was hauled up a hill in the Peruvian jungle. His documentaries include Grizzly Man and Cave of Forgotten Dreams. For 10 points, name this director.

This Soviet filmmaker's 1929 work Man with a Movie Camera uses double exposures, split screens, and freeze frames to portray a day in the life of a city. He developed the "Kino-Eye" theory and led the Kinoks group. For 10 points, name this documentary pioneer, born David Kaufman.

This American filmmaker's 1922 documentary follows an Inuk hunter and his family in northern Quebec. Parts were staged, which sparked debate over documentary ethics. He later made Man of Aran and Louisiana Story. For 10 points, name this man who made Nanook of the North.

This term names the live recording of everyday sounds such as footsteps and door slams that are added to film in post-production. A studio stage may feature surfaces such as gravel and wood. Coconut shells are classically used to simulate horse hooves. It is named for a Universal Studios sound pioneer, Jack. For 10 points, give this term for sound-effects artistry.

This Italian composer scored Sergio Leone's Dollars trilogy, including The Good, the Bad and the Ugly, with coyote-like howls and whistling. He also wrote the music for Once Upon a Time in the West and The Mission. He won a competitive Oscar for The Hateful Eight. For 10 points, name this composer.

This composer scored Alfred Hitchcock's Psycho using only string instruments, with shrieking violins in the shower scene. He also scored Citizen Kane, North by Northwest, and Taxi Driver. A theremin features in his score for The Day the Earth Stood Still. For 10 points, name this American film composer.

This photographer ran the gallery 291 and edited the journal Camera Work, promoting the Photo-Secession. His 1907 picture The Steerage shows passengers on an ocean liner. His series Equivalents consists of photographs of clouds. For 10 points, name this photographer who was married to Georgia O'Keeffe.

This French photographer co-founded the Magnum agency in 1947 and coined the idea of the "decisive moment." His image Behind the Gare Saint-Lazare shows a man leaping over a puddle. He used a small Leica rangefinder. For 10 points, name this photojournalist, Henri.

This photographer's square-format images include Identical Twins, Roselle, New Jersey. She photographed giants, nudists, and people on society's margins, often at close range. She died by suicide in 1971, a year before a posthumous Venice Biennale showing. For 10 points, name this American photographer.

This artist's Untitled Film Stills, made from 1977 to 1980, show her posing as various female stereotypes from imaginary movies. She often acts as her own model, costumed and made up. She is associated with the Pictures Generation. For 10 points, name this American photographer.

This American artist in Paris made rayographs by placing objects directly on photographic paper. His Le Violon d'Ingres adds f-holes to a woman's back. He associated with Dada and Surrealism and collaborated with Marcel Duchamp. For 10 points, name this American Dada and Surrealist photographer.

This Hungarian-born photographer's blurred images of troops landing at Omaha Beach on D-Day survive only in a few frames. He photographed The Falling Soldier during the Spanish Civil War and co-founded Magnum. He was killed by a landmine in Indochina in 1954. For 10 points, name this war photographer.

This New York photographer with a studio on Broadway photographed Lincoln before a Cooper Union speech. During the Civil War, his teams captured battlefield scenes, including Antietam and Gettysburg. His staff included Alexander Gardner. For 10 points, name this documenter of the Civil War, Mathew.

This American cartoonist created the comic strip Little Nemo in Slumberland. His 1914 animated film features a dinosaur that interacts with him on stage in vaudeville. He also made The Sinking of the Lusitania. For 10 points, name this animator of Gertie the Dinosaur.

This Japanese artist founded Mushi Production and created Astro Boy, the first popular anime TV series. His Kimba the White Lion is a precursor of Disney's later hit with a lion. He is called the "God of Manga." For 10 points, name this creator.

This German animator made The Adventures of Prince Achmed in 1926, one of the earliest surviving feature-length animated films. She cut out figures from black paper and filmed their silhouettes on glass lit from below. Her husband Carl Koch collaborated. For 10 points, name this pioneer of silhouette animation, Lotte.

text: This architect designed the Queen's House at Greenwich and the Banqueting House in Whitehall. He laid out the Covent Garden piazza and designed masque sets for Ben Jonson. After visiting Italy, he introduced the Palladian style to England. For 10 points, name this seventeenth-century English architect.

After a fire in 1194, this Gothic cathedral southwest of Paris was rebuilt with flying buttresses and tall stained-glass windows. A labyrinth is inlaid in the floor of its nave. Its two unmatched spires differ in style. For 10 points, name this French cathedral whose blue glass is much admired.
alternates: Cathedral of Our Lady of Chartres

text: This architect designed the Salk Institute in La Jolla, with its central courtyard opening toward the Pacific. His Kimbell Art Museum in Fort Worth uses cycloid vaults to diffuse light. He designed the National Assembly in Dhaka and spoke of "silence and light." For 10 points, name this American architect of the Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad.

This German architect and his partner Adolf Meyer designed the glass-walled Fagus Factory. He founded the Bauhaus and designed its Dessau building. After emigrating to America he taught at Harvard and designed his own house in Lincoln, Massachusetts. For 10 points, name this modernist.

This Finnish-born American designed the Gateway Arch in Saint Louis and the TWA Flight Center at Kennedy Airport. His Tulip chair is a classic of mid-century furniture. He designed the main terminal at Dulles Airport and was the son of another architect. For 10 points, name this architect, Eero.

This architect designed the Glass House in New Canaan, Connecticut, and was the first winner of the Pritzker Prize. He collaborated with Mies on the Seagram Building and designed the AT&T Building with its Chippendale-style top. He curated MoMA's 1932 International Style exhibition. For 10 points, name this American architect.

This Italian architect and his British partner Richard Rogers designed the Pompidou Centre, with color-coded pipes on the exterior. He also designed the Shard in London and the Kansai International Airport terminal. For 10 points, name this architect, Renzo.

This British architect designed the glass dome of the Reichstag in Berlin and the HSBC building in Hong Kong. His 30 Saint Mary Axe in London is nicknamed the Gherkin. He also designed the Millau Viaduct and Apple Park. For 10 points, name this architect, Norman.

Le Corbusier's Unite d'Habitation and Boston City Hall exemplify this style. Its name comes from the French for "raw concrete." It features exposed concrete, massive forms, and repeating modular elements. Alison and Peter Smithson helped name it. For 10 points, name this style of postwar architecture.

This style flourished from about 1890 to 1910 and used sinuous plant-like lines. Victor Horta's Hotel Tassel in Brussels is an early example. Hector Guimard designed its cast-iron entrances to the Paris Metro. Mackintosh designed the Glasgow School of Art in this style. For 10 points, name this decorative style, "the new art."

Borromini's San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane is an example of this style, with undulating walls and oval plans. It flourished after the Council of Trent, emphasizing drama, movement, and light. Versailles and Bernini's work belong to this style. For 10 points, name this style that followed the Renaissance and preceded the Rococo.

This Loire Valley palace was begun under Francis I as a hunting lodge. It has a double-helix staircase often attributed to Leonardo da Vinci's ideas. Its roofline bristles with chimneys and turrets. For 10 points, name this large French chateau, whose name begins with C.

This building has a forest of columns supporting double-tiered red-and-white striped horseshoe arches. Begun by Abd al-Rahman I, it was converted into a cathedral after the Reconquista, with a Renaissance nave inserted into the center. For 10 points, name this former mosque in an Andalusian city.

This temple complex was built by the Khmer king Suryavarman II and dedicated to Vishnu. Its five towers rise in a quincunx and reliefs show the churning of the ocean of milk. It was later used by Buddhists. For 10 points, name this Cambodian temple.

This Buddhist monument in Java was built under the Sailendra dynasty. Nine stacked platforms are topped with a central stupa surrounded by seventy-two smaller bell-shaped stupas. Its galleries show relief carvings of the life of the Buddha. For 10 points, name this Indonesian monument.

On the spring and autumn equinoxes, the shadow of this pyramid's balustrade forms a serpent that appears to slither down its staircase. It stands at a Maya city in the Yucatan Peninsula near a large ball court. It has 91 steps on each of four sides plus a top platform. For 10 points, name this pyramid dedicated to Kukulcan.

This Nabataean capital in Jordan is entered by walking through a narrow canyon called the Siq. Its most famous facade, Al-Khazneh, or "the Treasury," is carved out of rose-colored sandstone. It appears in Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade. For 10 points, name this "rose-red city."

Ivan the Terrible commissioned this church in Moscow to commemorate the capture of Kazan. It has nine chapels grouped around a central tower, and its onion domes are brightly colored. It stands at the edge of Red Square. For 10 points, name this Russian Orthodox cathedral.
alternates: Cathedral of Saint Basil the Blessed

text: Construction of this bell tower in the Piazza dei Miracoli began in 1173, and it began leaning because of soft ground. It was stabilized in a project completed in 2001. Legend says Galileo dropped weights from it. For 10 points, name this tower in an Italian city.

After a fire in 1834 destroyed the old building, this architect rebuilt the Palace of Westminster in Gothic Revival style. Augustus Pugin designed the interiors and the clock tower, which houses Big Ben. He also designed the Reform Club in the style of an Italian palazzo. For 10 points, name this British architect, Charles.

This architect directed the construction of the "White City" at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition. He designed the Flatiron Building in New York and Union Station in Washington. He is associated with the Plan of Chicago and the line "Make no little plans." For 10 points, name this American architect, Daniel.

This New York park was laid out by Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux in the 1850s under the Greensward Plan. It has sunken transverse roads that carry cross-town traffic out of sight. Bethesda Terrace and Sheep Meadow are features. For 10 points, name this park in Manhattan.

This president designed his home at Monticello and the Rotunda of the University of Virginia, based on the Pantheon. He modeled the Virginia State Capitol on the Maison Carree in Nimes. He also wrote the Declaration of Independence. For 10 points, name this third president and amateur architect.

This architect's book Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture answered Mies's maxim by saying "less is a bore." He co-wrote Learning from Las Vegas with Denise Scott Brown and Steven Izenour. He designed a house for his mother and the Sainsbury Wing of the National Gallery. For 10 points, name this postmodern architect.

This Finnish architect designed the Paimio Sanatorium and Villa Mairea, and Finlandia Hall in Helsinki. His bentwood furniture was produced by Artek, a company he co-founded. His wavy glass Savoy vase is a design icon. For 10 points, name this Scandinavian modernist, Alvar.

This self-taught Japanese architect, a former boxer, designed the Church of the Light with a cross-shaped slit in a concrete wall. He won the Pritzker Prize in 1995. His work uses exposed concrete and natural light. For 10 points, name this architect of the Church on the Water.

This Spanish architect and engineer designed the Turning Torso in Malmo and the Quadracci Pavilion at the Milwaukee Art Museum, whose wings open and close. His Oculus transit hub in New York has a winged form. He built the Alamillo Bridge in Seville. For 10 points, name this architect.

This Dutch architect's firm OMA designed the Seattle Central Library and the CCTV Headquarters in Beijing. He wrote Delirious New York. He won the Pritzker Prize in 2000. For 10 points, name this architect, Rem.

This Paris building by Charles Garnier was designed in the Beaux-Arts style after a competition won by its unknown young architect in 1861. Its Grand Staircase is lined with marble, and the auditorium ceiling was painted by Chagall. It is the setting of Gaston Leroux's The Phantom of the Opera. For 10 points, name this Paris opera house.

This palace complex in Beijing was built under the Yongle Emperor in the early fifteenth century and housed Ming and Qing emperors. Its central axis runs through the Meridian Gate to the Hall of Supreme Harmony. Its buildings have yellow glazed tile roofs. For 10 points, name this imperial palace.

text: In this play, Pozzo arrives leading Lucky on a rope, and a boy brings word that the one being awaited will not come today. Two tramps named Vladimir and Estragon wait by a barren tree, frequently saying "Nothing to be done." It was first written in French by Samuel Beckett and premiered in Paris in 1953. For 10 points, name this play about waiting for a man named Godot.

At the end of this 1879 play, the heroine slams the door on her husband Torvald Helmer after he reacts badly to her having forged a signature. Nora Helmer dances a tarantella at a Christmas party, and Krogstad blackmails her. For 10 points, name this play by Henrik Ibsen whose title names a dwelling and a toy.

The Moscow Art Theatre staged the first successful production of this dramatist's The Seagull, directed by Stanislavski. He also wrote Uncle Vanya, Three Sisters, and The Cherry Orchard. He trained as a physician and wrote many short stories. For 10 points, name this Russian author.

Willy Loman is a traveling salesman who has hallucinations of his brother Ben, and his sons are Biff and Happy. His wife Linda says "attention must be paid" to him. The play ends with his funeral after a car crash suicide. For 10 points, name this 1949 Arthur Miller play.

Marlon Brando played Stanley Kowalski in the 1951 film of this play, set in New Orleans on Elysian Fields Street. Stella's sister Blanche DuBois ends by saying that she has "always depended on the kindness of strangers." It premiered on Broadway in 1947. For 10 points, name this Tennessee Williams play named for a form of transportation.

This Polish director founded the Laboratory Theatre in Wroclaw and wrote Towards a Poor Theatre. He stripped away costumes, sets, and lighting to focus on the actor's physical and spiritual work. His actor Ryszard Cieslak starred in The Constant Prince. For 10 points, name this theater practitioner.

This French writer called for a "Theatre of Cruelty" that would assault the audience's senses, as set out in his book The Theatre and Its Double. He broke with the Surrealists and spent years in asylums such as Rodez. He was inspired by Balinese theater. For 10 points, name this French theorist.

Martin Esslin coined this label in 1961 for a group of dramatists including Ionesco, Genet, and Pinter. Its plays often feature illogical dialogue, circular plots, and characters in meaningless situations. Camus's essay on Sisyphus supplied its philosophical background. For 10 points, name this movement in postwar theater.

This Athenian tragedian wrote Medea, The Trojan Women, and The Bacchae. He was often accused of making his gods into dei ex machina to resolve plots. He wrote about women's psychology in plays such as Hippolytus. For 10 points, name this contemporary of Sophocles.

This Elizabethan playwright wrote Tamburlaine the Great and The Jew of Malta. His Doctor Faustus has the line "Was this the face that launched a thousand ships?" He was stabbed in a tavern in Deptford in 1593. For 10 points, name this playwright who developed blank verse before Shakespeare.

This French playwright, born Jean-Baptiste Poquelin, wrote Tartuffe and The Misanthrope. He died in 1673 after collapsing during a performance of his play The Imaginary Invalid. His company performed at the Palais-Royal under Louis XIV's patronage. For 10 points, name this comic dramatist.

Nicknamed "the Divine," this French actress starred in Phedre and Victorien Sardou's La Tosca and played the male roles of Hamlet and L'Aiglon. She had her leg amputated in 1915 but kept performing. She appeared with the Comedie-Francaise. For 10 points, name this actress, Sarah.

This American actor played Hamlet for one hundred consecutive nights in 1864 and 1865 in New York. He founded The Players club in Gramercy Park. His brother assassinated Abraham Lincoln. For 10 points, name this nineteenth-century Shakespearean actor, Edwin.

This French-born choreographer worked for decades in Saint Petersburg and led the Imperial Ballet. He choreographed The Sleeping Beauty, La Bayadere, and Raymonda. He collaborated with Lev Ivanov on Swan Lake and The Nutcracker. For 10 points, name this "father of classical ballet."

This dancer was famous for his enormous leaps and for the role of the Golden Slave and for Le Spectre de la rose. He choreographed Afternoon of a Faun, which shocked Paris with an erotic gesture in 1912. He later suffered a mental breakdown and was institutionalized. For 10 points, name this Ballets Russes star, Vaslav.

This American dancer rejected the formal ballet technique, dancing barefoot in loose Greek-style tunics. She founded schools in Germany and Russia and died in 1927 when her long scarf caught in a car's wheel. She was a pioneer of modern dance. For 10 points, name this dancer, Isadora.

This choreographer founded his own company in 1953 and used chance procedures influenced by I Ching to decide the order of movements. He collaborated with composer John Cage and artist Robert Rauschenberg. He first danced with Martha Graham. For 10 points, name this American choreographer, Merce.

This choreographer's style includes bowler hats, white gloves, turned-in knees, and isolated hip movements. He directed the film version of Cabaret and choreographed Chicago and Pippin on Broadway. His semi-autobiographical film All That Jazz won awards. For 10 points, name this man who created "Steam Heat" in The Pajama Game.

This choreographer's Fancy Free, about three sailors on leave, was expanded into the musical On the Town. He staged the dances of West Side Story and was ballet master of the New York City Ballet. He later testified before the House Un-American Activities Committee. For 10 points, name this American choreographer, Jerome.

This dancer defected from the Soviet Union in 1961 at Le Bourget airport in Paris. A famous partnership with Margot Fonteyn at the Royal Ballet began soon afterward. He later directed the Paris Opera Ballet. For 10 points, name this Kirov dancer, Rudolf.

This Latvian-born dancer defected in 1974 while on tour in Toronto. He became a principal at American Ballet Theatre and later directed it. He also appeared in the film The Turning Point and in television's Sex and the City. For 10 points, name this dancer, Mikhail.

This German choreographer led the Tanztheater Wuppertal, merging dance and theater. Her works include Cafe Muller and a 1975 version of The Rite of Spring on a stage covered with peat. Wim Wenders made a 3-D documentary film about her in 2011. For 10 points, name this choreographer, Pina.

This classical Indian dance from Tamil Nadu uses elaborate hand gestures called mudras and the half-sitting position araimandi. It grew out of temple dance performed by devadasis and was revived in the twentieth century by Rukmini Devi Arundale. For 10 points, name this dance form whose name is traditionally broken into bhava, raga, tala, and natya.

This Chinese theater form combines singing, mime, acrobatics, and martial arts. Performers wear colored face paint, and roles are divided into sheng, dan, jing, and chou. Mei Lanfang was a famed male performer of female roles. For 10 points, name this theater form associated with the capital.

In this Indonesian art, a dalang manipulates flat leather puppets behind a lit white screen, accompanied by a gamelan orchestra. Stories are often drawn from the Ramayana and Mahabharata. It is especially associated with Java and Bali. For 10 points, name this shadow puppet theater whose name means "shadow" in Javanese.

This Saint Petersburg jeweler made a series of jeweled eggs for the Russian imperial family as Easter gifts, beginning with the Hen Egg. Each held a "surprise." Carl Peter made the series for Alexander III and Nicholas II. For 10 points, name this house of jewelers.

This American designer developed Favrile glass, an iridescent glass used in vases and lamps. His leaded-glass lamps, such as the Wisteria lamp, are collector's items. He decorated the Seventh Regiment Armory and created Laurelton Hall. He was the son of a famous New York jeweler. For 10 points, name this Art Nouveau artist, Louis Comfort.

This English potter developed Jasperware, with white classical reliefs on a blue background. He produced Queen's Ware and made copies of the Portland Vase. He was an abolitionist who made an anti-slavery medallion. His grandson was Charles Darwin. For 10 points, name this founder of a Staffordshire pottery company.

A 2002 exhibition at the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, brought national attention to the quilts of this small Alabama community along a river. Quilters such as Annie Mae Young and members of the Pettway family made improvisational geometric designs. The community was formerly a cotton plantation. For 10 points, name this community whose quilts are held in museums.

This work of embroidered wool on linen is about seventy meters long. It depicts the lead-up to the Norman Conquest and includes a scene of Halley's Comet, a Latin text, and a border with animals. Its main scenes show the Battle of Hastings. For 10 points, name this medieval work, named for a Norman town.

text: Cairo, Illinois, sits at the confluence where the Ohio River joins this river. Its headwaters are at Lake Itasca in Minnesota, and it passes Saint Paul, Saint Louis, and Memphis. Its delta lies south of New Orleans. For 10 points, name this river that empties into the Gulf of Mexico.

This river is formed by the confluence of the Allegheny and Monongahela Rivers at Pittsburgh. It forms the southern border of Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois. Cincinnati and Louisville lie on its banks. For 10 points, name this river that meets the Mississippi at Cairo, Illinois.

Its headwaters lie at Three Forks, Montana, where the Jefferson, Madison, and Gallatin Rivers meet. Lewis and Clark followed it upstream, passing the site of Great Falls. It flows past Omaha and Kansas City before joining the Mississippi north of Saint Louis. For 10 points, name this river nicknamed the "Big Muddy."

Elephant Butte Reservoir in New Mexico is on this river, which also flows through Albuquerque. Big Bend National Park is carved by a great loop of it. Ciudad Juarez lies across it from El Paso. For 10 points, name this river that forms much of the Texas-Mexico border.

The Glen Canyon Dam impounds Lake Powell on this river, and the Hoover Dam impounds Lake Mead. It begins in the Rocky Mountains of Colorado and carves the Grand Canyon. Its modern delta is in Mexico near the Gulf of California. For 10 points, name this river of the American Southwest.

The Grand Coulee Dam and Bonneville Dam are on this river, which is joined by the Snake River. It forms much of the border between Washington and Oregon. It enters the Pacific Ocean near Astoria. For 10 points, name this river of the Pacific Northwest.

Its source is Lake Tear of the Clouds in the Adirondack Mountains. The Palisades line its western bank, and it flows past Albany and West Point. It meets the Atlantic at New York Harbor, and the Erie Canal connects to it. For 10 points, name this river that names a school of landscape painters.

Spiral Jetty, an earthwork by Robert Smithson, juts into this lake. It is a shrinking remnant of the ancient Lake Bonneville and has no outlet. Antelope Island lies in it, and brine shrimp live in its extremely salty water. For 10 points, name this lake in Utah near a namesake city.

The Kissimmee River feeds this lake, which is encircled by the Herbert Hoover Dike. Its overflow historically drained south into the Everglades. Towns such as Clewiston and Belle Glade lie on its shores. For 10 points, name this large lake in south central Florida.

Badwater Basin, at 282 feet below sea level, is the lowest point in North America and lies in this place. Furnace Creek is a settlement within it. It is a national park in the Mojave Desert region of California and Nevada. For 10 points, name this extremely hot and dry valley.

The Susquehanna River is the largest tributary of this estuary. Annapolis and Baltimore lie on it, and the Bay Bridge crosses it in Maryland. The Delmarva Peninsula separates it from the Atlantic. For 10 points, name this large bay famous for its blue crabs.

The Appalachian Trail runs from Springer Mountain in Georgia to Mount Katahdin in Maine along this range. Mount Mitchell in North Carolina is its highest peak. The Blue Ridge and the Great Smoky Mountains are parts of it. For 10 points, name this mountain system of the eastern United States.

The Unangan people are native to this volcanic chain, where Shishaldin and Makushin are active volcanoes. Dutch Harbor is a major fishing port here. Japan invaded Attu and Kiska in 1942. For 10 points, name this Alaskan island chain that separates the Bering Sea from the Pacific.

Old Faithful is a geyser in this national park, which sits on a large volcanic caldera. It lies mostly in Wyoming and extends into Montana and Idaho. It was established in 1872. For 10 points, name this national park, known for bison and geysers.

The Pilgrims first landed at Provincetown on this Massachusetts peninsula. A canal cuts across its base, and Hyannis lies on its southern coast. It is shaped like a bent arm, and glaciers formed its many kettle ponds. For 10 points, name this peninsula east of Boston.

Mauna Kea and Kilauea are volcanoes on the largest island of this state. Honolulu is on its island of Oahu, and Maui is the second largest island. It was admitted to the Union in 1959. For 10 points, name this Pacific island state.

Paradise is a visitor area on this peak, which has more glaciers than any other mountain in the contiguous United States. It is a stratovolcano in the Cascade Range. Tacoma lies near its base. For 10 points, name this mountain in Washington State.

Gary, Indiana, and Green Bay, Wisconsin, lie on its shores, and the Sleeping Bear Dunes rise from its eastern side. The Door Peninsula separates it from Green Bay. The Straits of Mackinac connect it to Lake Huron, and Chicago sits at its southwestern corner. For 10 points, name this Great Lake.

Its civil divisions are called parishes rather than counties. Baton Rouge is the capital, and Lake Pontchartrain is north of New Orleans. The United States acquired it in a purchase from France in 1803. For 10 points, name this state with a Cajun culture.

Center-pivot irrigation drawn from this aquifer turned the High Plains into farmland. It underlies parts of eight states, including Nebraska, Kansas, and Texas. Pumping has depleted it faster than rainfall recharges it. For 10 points, name this large underground water source beneath the Great Plains.

This transform fault marks the boundary between the Pacific Plate and the North American Plate. The 1906 San Francisco earthquake occurred along it. The Carrizo Plain shows its trace, and the town of Parkfield sits on it. For 10 points, name this California fault.

Marjory Stoneman Douglas called this wetland a "river of grass." Sawgrass marshes and mangroves here are home to alligators and the Florida panther. It lies southwest of Miami and shares a region with Big Cypress. For 10 points, name this Florida national park.

Saguaro cacti are the signature plants of this desert. It spans southern Arizona and northwestern Mexico, with Phoenix and Tucson in it. The Gulf of California borders it on the south. For 10 points, name this desert.

Daniel Boone blazed the Wilderness Road through this pass in the Cumberland Mountains. It lies where Kentucky, Tennessee, and Virginia meet. Settlers used it to cross the Appalachians to the west. For 10 points, name this historic mountain passage.

Utah, Colorado, Arizona, and New Mexico meet at a single point in this region. A monument marks the exact spot, and visitors can stand in four states at once. The Navajo Nation manages the site. For 10 points, name this region of the Southwest.

This peninsula is shared by Delaware, Maryland, and Virginia. Its name is a blend of those three states. The Chesapeake Bay lies to its west and the Atlantic Ocean to its east. For 10 points, name this peninsula.

Joshua trees grow in this desert, which lies mostly in southeastern California. Barstow and Las Vegas lie near it, and the national preserve here includes Kelso Dunes. Death Valley lies on its northern edge. For 10 points, name this desert.

Seattle and Tacoma lie on this inlet of the Pacific Ocean. The Strait of Juan de Fuca connects it to the ocean, and the Olympic Peninsula forms its western shore. It was named for a lieutenant on George Vancouver's expedition. For 10 points, name this Washington sound.

Emerald Bay is part of this lake in the Sierra Nevada. It is famous for its clarity and straddles the border of California and Nevada. The Truckee River flows out of it. For 10 points, name this large alpine lake.

This peak in the Alaska Range rises 20,310 feet and is the tallest mountain in North America. It lies in a national park of the same name. It was officially renamed in 2015 from a name honoring a president. For 10 points, name this Alaskan mountain.

text: Lake Nasser, created by the Aswan High Dam, lies on this river. Its two main branches, the Blue and the White, meet at Khartoum. Luxor and Cairo lie along it. For 10 points, name this river that empties into the Mediterranean Sea in a large delta.

The Rio Negro meets the Solimoes near Manaus to form the main stem of this river. Its basin holds the world's largest tropical rainforest. It rises in the Andes of Peru and crosses Brazil. For 10 points, name this South American river.

Annapurna and Kangchenjunga are among the peaks of this range, which formed from the collision of India with Eurasia. It runs through Nepal, Bhutan, and Tibet. Mount Everest is its best-known summit. For 10 points, name this mountain range of Asia.

The Tuareg are traditional nomads of this desert, which stretches across Libya, Algeria, and Egypt. The Atlas Mountains lie to its northwest. The Sahel borders it on the south. For 10 points, name this largest hot desert, in northern Africa.

Irkutsk lies near this lake in southern Siberia. Its outflow is the Angara River. The nerpa, a freshwater seal, lives in it, and it holds the greatest depth of any lake. For 10 points, name this Russian lake.

Its source is near Donaueschingen in the Black Forest of Germany. It flows through Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest, and Belgrade. The Iron Gates gorge lies on it, and its delta in Romania meets the Black Sea. For 10 points, name this European river.

Aconcagua is the highest peak of this mountain range, which runs along the western edge of South America. Machu Picchu is among the Inca ruins in it. It passes through Chile, Argentina, Peru, and Bolivia. For 10 points, name this range.

Uhuru Peak is the summit of this volcano, which has three cones named Kibo, Mawenzi, and Shira. Glaciers on its snowy top lie near the equator. It is in Tanzania. For 10 points, name this tallest mountain in Africa.

The Rock of Gibraltar looms over this narrow waterway. Spain lies to its north and Morocco to its south. It links the Atlantic Ocean to the Mediterranean Sea. For 10 points, name this strait, whose name is the same as a British territory.
This strait divides the European and Asian parts of Istanbul. It links the Black Sea with the Sea of Marmara. Two suspension bridges span it. For 10 points, name this Turkish strait.

This river rises on the Tibetan Plateau and forms part of the border between Laos and Thailand. Phnom Penh sits where it meets the Tonle Sap. Its delta in southern Vietnam is a major rice-growing area. For 10 points, name this river of Southeast Asia.

Varanasi is the holiest city on this river for Hindus. It begins at the Gangotri Glacier and flows across northern India. It joins the Brahmaputra in Bangladesh to form a vast delta on the Bay of Bengal. For 10 points, name this sacred river.

This structure lies in the Coral Sea off the coast of Queensland. It consists of thousands of individual reefs and islands. Cairns is a common starting point for visitors. For 10 points, name this reef system off Australia.

The Perito Moreno Glacier and Torres del Paine are in this region at the southern end of South America. It is shared by Argentina and Chile. Tierra del Fuego lies at its southern tip. For 10 points, name this windswept region of steppe.

Chile contains this desert, among the driest places on Earth outside the polar regions. It was once a major source of nitrate mining. The ALMA observatory sits at high elevation in it. For 10 points, name this South American desert.

The Jordan River flows into this lake, which borders Israel and Jordan. Its shoreline is the lowest land elevation on Earth. Its salinity is so high that swimmers float easily. For 10 points, name this lake.

Lemurs live only on this island, whose capital is Antananarivo. The Mozambique Channel separates it from the African mainland. Baobab trees line a famous avenue here. For 10 points, name this large island nation in the Indian Ocean.

Thingvellir National Park here marks where the Mid-Atlantic Ridge rises above sea level. Reykjavik is its capital, and the Vatnajokull ice cap covers much of it. Eyjafjallajokull is a volcano here. For 10 points, name this North Atlantic island country.

Kinshasa and Brazzaville face each other across this river. Boyoma Falls and Livingstone Falls interrupt its course. It crosses the equator twice. For 10 points, name this river of central Africa, which flows through a rainforest to the Atlantic.
The Lorelei is a rock on this river in Germany. It begins in the Swiss Alps and passes Basel and Cologne. It reaches the North Sea at Rotterdam. For 10 points, name this European river.
Speke named this lake for a queen. Uganda, Kenya, and Tanzania share it, and Jinja lies where the Nile leaves it. Entebbe is on its shore. For 10 points, name this largest lake in Africa.

Baku lies on the shore of this sea, and the Volga River flows into it. Azerbaijan, Iran, Turkmenistan, Kazakhstan, and Russia border it. It is the largest enclosed inland body of water. For 10 points, name this sea.

Challenger Deep lies in this trench in the western Pacific. It is near the island of Guam. It formed where the Pacific Plate subducts beneath another plate. For 10 points, name this deepest known part of the ocean.

Gatun Lake and the Culebra Cut are parts of this waterway, which opened in 1914. A system of locks lifts ships over the isthmus. It links the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. For 10 points, name this canal.
Ferdinand de Lesseps led the building of this canal, which opened in 1869. Port Said lies at its northern end. It links the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea. For 10 points, name this Egyptian canal.

Its capital Nuuk was once called Godthab. Thule Air Base, a United States military installation, lies in its northwest. An ice sheet covers most of this autonomous territory of the Kingdom of Denmark. For 10 points, name this large Arctic island.

The Yangtze, Yellow, and Mekong Rivers all begin on this high region. Lhasa lies on it, and it is called the Roof of the World. Qinghai Lake is at its northeastern edge. For 10 points, name this high plateau in central Asia.

Sossusvlei lies in this desert, which has some of the tallest dunes in the world. Welwitschia plants grow here, and the Skeleton Coast lies at its northern edge. It runs along the Atlantic coast of southwestern Africa. For 10 points, name this desert in Namibia.

Yekaterinburg lies at the eastern foot of these mountains. Magnitogorsk is an industrial city on them. They are traditionally taken as part of the boundary between Europe and Asia. For 10 points, name this Russian mountain range.

The Uros people live on floating islands of reeds in this lake. Puno, Peru, is on its shore, and the lake lies on the Altiplano. Bolivia and Peru share it, and it is a very high-altitude lake. For 10 points, name this lake of the Andes.

text: In 1676 this Virginia planter led frontiersmen against Native Americans without the approval of Governor William Berkeley. His followers burned Jamestown. He died of dysentery and the revolt collapsed. For 10 points, name this rebellion, named for its leader.

In 1735 Andrew Hamilton won the acquittal of a New York printer on charges of seditious libel by arguing that truth is a defense. The case helped establish freedom of the press. The defendant published the New-York Weekly Journal. For 10 points, name this printer, tried for criticizing Governor William Cosby.

At a 1754 congress in this New York city, Benjamin Franklin proposed a plan of colonial union and published the "Join, or Die" cartoon. Delegates from seven colonies approved it, but no colonial legislature accepted it. For 10 points, name this plan, named for the city.

After the French and Indian War, King George III issued this 1763 order forbidding colonial settlement west of the Appalachian crest. It angered colonists and speculators. For 10 points, name this royal proclamation.

Roger Sherman of Connecticut proposed this 1787 deal at the Constitutional Convention, creating a House based on population and a Senate with equal representation. It resolved the dispute between the Virginia and New Jersey Plans. For 10 points, name this compromise.
In this 1787 essay James Madison argued that a large republic would control the dangers of faction. It is the best-known of the Federalist Papers. For 10 points, name this essay, numbered ten.

President John Adams sent diplomats to France in 1797, but agents later called X, Y, and Z demanded a bribe. The affair led to an undeclared naval conflict. For 10 points, name this diplomatic incident.

In this late 1814 meeting in Connecticut, Federalist delegates from New England discussed grievances over the War of 1812 and possibly secession. News of the Battle of New Orleans made them look unpatriotic. For 10 points, name this convention named for a city.

South Carolina declared the 1828 and 1832 tariffs void in this 1832 crisis. John C. Calhoun provided the theory, and Andrew Jackson threatened force. Henry Clay brokered a compromise tariff. For 10 points, name this crisis over states' rights.

Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott organized this 1848 gathering at a Wesleyan chapel, where Frederick Douglass spoke in favor of voting rights for women. Delegates signed a Declaration of Sentiments with eleven resolutions. For 10 points, name this first women's rights convention, held in a New York town.

In 1846 a Pennsylvania congressman proposed this amendment to a military appropriations bill to ban slavery in any land acquired from Mexico. The House passed it repeatedly but the Senate did not. For 10 points, name this proviso.

In 1858 Stephen Douglas defended popular sovereignty in debates against Abraham Lincoln across Illinois. At Freeport Douglas stated what became known as his Freeport Doctrine. For 10 points, name this series of debates in a Senate race.

On April 12, 1861 Confederate forces under P. G. T. Beauregard fired on this island fort in Charleston harbor. Major Robert Anderson surrendered after thirty-four hours. For 10 points, name this opening engagement of the Civil War.

In this deal after the disputed 1876 election, Democrats accepted Rutherford B. Hayes as president in return for the removal of federal troops from the South. It effectively ended Reconstruction. For 10 points, name this compromise.

In this 1896 case the Supreme Court upheld a Louisiana law requiring separate railroad cars for Black and white passengers. Justice John Marshall Harlan dissented. The "separate but equal" doctrine came from it. For 10 points, name this case.
In 1894 Eugene V. Debs led the American Railway Union in this strike against a Chicago sleeping-car company. President Grover Cleveland sent federal troops. For 10 points, name this strike.

William Jennings Bryan electrified the 1896 Democratic convention with a speech opposing the gold standard. He said, "You shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold." For 10 points, name this speech.

This 1904 corollary to a doctrine stated that the United States could intervene in Latin America to prevent European intervention. Theodore Roosevelt used it regarding the Dominican Republic. For 10 points, name this corollary to the Monroe Doctrine.

In January 1917 Germany's foreign secretary Arthur Zimmermann sent a message to Mexico proposing an alliance. British intelligence intercepted it. For 10 points, name this telegram that helped bring the United States into World War I.

Two Italian immigrants were convicted of a 1920 robbery and murder in Massachusetts and executed in 1927. Their trial became a symbol of anti-immigrant bias and radical hysteria. For 10 points, name this pair, Nicola and Bartolomeo.

This 1930 act raised tariffs on over 20,000 imported goods. Economists blame it for deepening the Great Depression by prompting retaliation abroad. It was named for two Republican legislators. For 10 points, name this tariff law.
In 1932 about 17,000 World War I veterans camped in Washington, D.C., demanding early payment of bonuses. General Douglas MacArthur drove them out. For 10 points, name this protest group.

In this 1944 case the Supreme Court upheld the internment of Japanese Americans in a 6-3 decision. Justice Frank Murphy called the order racism. For 10 points, name this case, named for a man who defied the order.
This 1947 plan proposed by Secretary of State George C. Marshall gave billions of dollars in aid to rebuild Western Europe. The Soviet Union refused to participate. For 10 points, name this plan.

In 1950 this Wisconsin senator claimed he had a list of Communists in the State Department. The Army-McCarthy hearings damaged him, and the Senate censured him in 1954. For 10 points, name this senator.

In August 1964 North Vietnamese boats allegedly attacked the USS Maddox in a gulf off Vietnam. Congress passed a resolution letting President Lyndon Johnson use force in Southeast Asia. For 10 points, name this resolution named for a body of water.

In this 1966 case the Supreme Court ruled that police must inform suspects of their rights to remain silent and have an attorney. Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote the opinion. For 10 points, name this case.

In 1978 President Jimmy Carter hosted Egypt's Anwar Sadat and Israel's Menachem Begin at a presidential retreat in Maryland. The resulting agreements led to a 1979 peace treaty. For 10 points, name this series of agreements named for the retreat.
In this 1620 document signed aboard a ship off Cape Cod, the Pilgrims agreed to form a government and obey its laws. It was a precedent for self-government. For 10 points, name this compact.

This 1825 waterway linked the Hudson River to Lake Erie and lowered shipping costs to the Midwest. Governor DeWitt Clinton pushed for it, and critics called it "Clinton's Ditch." For 10 points, name this canal.

text: In January 1077 Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV stood barefoot in the snow for three days outside a fortress in northern Italy to seek forgiveness. Pope Gregory VII had excommunicated him during a dispute over who could appoint bishops. The fortress belonged to Matilda of Tuscany. For 10 points, name this castle whose name is a byword for submission to authority.

This 1204 crusade, supported by Venice under Doge Enrico Dandolo, never reached Egypt or the Holy Land. Instead its army sacked the capital of the Byzantine Empire. A Latin Empire was set up afterward. For 10 points, name this crusade numbered fourth.

From 1309 to 1377 the popes lived in this city in southern France instead of Rome. Clement V began the practice. The period was followed by the Western Schism. For 10 points, name this city, whose papal palace still stands.

This English dynastic conflict between the houses of Lancaster and York began in 1455. Richard III was killed at Bosworth Field in 1485, and Henry Tudor took the throne. For 10 points, name this series of civil wars named for flowers.

This Bohemian reformer and rector of Charles University was burned at the stake at the Council of Constance in 1415. His followers, the Hussites, fought crusades against them. He was inspired by John Wycliffe. For 10 points, name this man.

This Habsburg ruler was Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain as Charles I. He presided over the Diet of Worms and abdicated in 1556, dividing his lands between his son and brother. For 10 points, name this ruler, numbered five.

In August 1572 Catholic mobs in Paris killed thousands of Huguenots after the wedding of Henry of Navarre to Margaret of Valois. Catherine de Medici is often blamed. The massacre is named for the feast day on which it began. For 10 points, name this massacre.

This nobleman, called "the Silent," led the Dutch Revolt against Spain's Philip II. He was a Prince of Orange and was assassinated in Delft in 1584. For 10 points, name this man, the great-grandfather of the later English king.

In 1571 a Holy League fleet defeated Ottoman forces in this naval battle in the Gulf of Patras. Don John of Austria commanded the Christian ships, and Miguel de Cervantes was wounded. For 10 points, name this battle.

This series of treaties of 1713 and 1714 ended the War of the Spanish Succession. Philip V kept the Spanish throne but renounced the French one. Britain gained Gibraltar and Minorca. For 10 points, name these treaties named for a Dutch city.

Frederick the Great of Prussia survived this global conflict of 1756 to 1763, known in America as the French and Indian War. The Treaty of Paris ended it, and Britain gained Canada. For 10 points, name this war named for its length.

In 1772, 1793, and 1795 Russia, Prussia, and Austria divided this country, which disappeared from the map until 1918. Tadeusz Kosciuszko led a failed uprising in 1794. For 10 points, name this country.

Denis Diderot and Jean d'Alembert edited this Enlightenment work, published from 1751 to 1772 in many volumes. It aimed to gather all knowledge and was opposed by the Church. For 10 points, name this French reference work.

In June 1789 the National Assembly's deputies met on an indoor court in Versailles and swore not to disband until they had written a constitution. Jacques-Louis David sketched it. For 10 points, name this oath.

On November 9, 1799, Napoleon Bonaparte and Emmanuel Sieyes overthrew the Directory in this coup. The date is by the revolutionary calendar. For 10 points, name this coup named for a month, which began the Consulate.

Horatio Nelson was killed at this 1805 naval battle off the coast of Spain. The British victory over a French and Spanish fleet ended Napoleon's invasion hopes. For 10 points, name this battle named for a cape.
In August 1819 cavalry charged a peaceful crowd demanding parliamentary reform in Manchester, killing about fifteen. The name mocks Waterloo. For 10 points, name this massacre at Saint Peter's Field.

This 1832 act in Britain eliminated rotten boroughs and gave seats to growing industrial cities like Manchester. Earl Grey was prime minister. For 10 points, name this first major electoral law of its kind in the nineteenth century.
This 1846 repeal of tariffs on imported grain was achieved by Robert Peel with help from Whigs and Richard Cobden. It split the Conservative Party. For 10 points, name this British legislation.

In May 1848 delegates met in Saint Paul's Church in this city to draft a constitution for a united Germany. They offered the crown to Frederick William IV of Prussia, who refused. For 10 points, name this assembly named for a city.
In 1894 a Jewish French army captain was falsely convicted of treason and sent to Devil's Island. Emile Zola wrote "J'Accuse" to defend him. For 10 points, name this scandal named for the captain.
This radical government ruled Paris in the spring of 1871 after France's defeat by Prussia. It was crushed in the "Bloody Week" by troops from Versailles. For 10 points, name this government.

The Schlieffen Plan called for Germany to defeat France quickly by marching through this neutral country. Its invasion in 1914 brought Britain into World War I. For 10 points, name this small country whose capital is Brussels.
From February to December 1916 the French and Germans fought this longest battle of World War I, around a fortress on the Meuse. Philippe Petain became a hero there. For 10 points, name this battle.
In 1923 Adolf Hitler and the Nazis tried to seize power in Munich by marching from a beer hall. The attempt failed and he was jailed. For 10 points, name this unsuccessful uprising.

Pablo Picasso painted this huge black-and-white canvas in 1937 for the Spanish Republic's pavilion at the Paris World Exposition. It shows screaming figures, a bull, and a wounded horse. It responds to the German bombing of a Basque town during the Spanish Civil War. For 10 points, name this painting.
In August 1939 Germany and the USSR signed this treaty, which contained a secret protocol dividing Eastern Europe. It was named for two foreign ministers. For 10 points, name this pact.

In late May and early June 1940 hundreds of small civilian boats helped rescue over 300,000 British and French soldiers from a beach and harbor in northern France. German forces had trapped the army against the sea. Winston Churchill said that wars are not won by evacuations. For 10 points, name this evacuation.
In February 1945 Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin met at this Crimean resort to plan the postwar order. They agreed to divide Germany into occupation zones. For 10 points, name this conference.

In 1968 Alexander Dubcek introduced "socialism with a human face" in this country, but Warsaw Pact troops invaded in August. For 10 points, name this country and this reform period, called a "spring" in its capital.
This Polish electrician led the Solidarity movement at the Gdansk shipyard in 1980. He won the 1983 Nobel Peace Prize and became Poland's president in 1990. For 10 points, name this man.

text: Around 1200 BC groups known by this collective name, mentioned in Egyptian inscriptions at Medinet Habu, attacked the eastern Mediterranean. Ramses III repelled them. Their migrations coincided with the collapse of Ugarit and the Hittite Empire. For 10 points, name these raiders, whose label does not describe them as a single nation.

This Assyrian king assembled a library of clay tablets at Nineveh in the seventh century BC. It preserved the Epic of Gilgamesh. He fought a civil war against his brother in Babylon. For 10 points, name this last great king of Assyria.

This Lydian king, known for his wealth, was defeated by Cyrus the Great around 546 BC. He asked the oracle at Delphi whether he should attack Persia and was told a great empire would fall. For 10 points, name this man, whose name is a byword for wealth.

In 479 BC the Greek allies under the Spartan regent Pausanias crushed the last major Persian army on Greek soil at this battle in Boeotia. The Persian commander Mardonius died. For 10 points, name this land battle.
This Athenian reformer of 594 BC canceled debts, ended debt slavery, and divided citizens into four property classes. He is counted among the Seven Sages. For 10 points, name this lawgiver.

In 371 BC this Theban general broke Sparta's reputation for invincibility at Leuctra using an oblique formation. He also freed the Messenian helots. He died at Mantinea in 362. For 10 points, name this man.

In 338 BC this king of Macedon defeated Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea. He had reformed the army with the long pike called the sarissa. He was assassinated in 336 by one of his bodyguards. For 10 points, name this father of Alexander.
This Epirote king won costly battles against Rome at Heraclea and Asculum in the 270s BC. His name gives us a phrase for a victory that costs too much. For 10 points, name this king.
In 202 BC the Romans under Scipio defeated Hannibal at this battle near Carthage. Masinissa's Numidian cavalry helped. It ended the Second Punic War. For 10 points, name this battle.

These two brothers, tribunes of the plebs in the 130s and 120s BC, proposed land reforms and were killed by senatorial mobs. Their opponents included Scipio Nasica, who led senators wielding stool legs against Tiberius. Their mother Cornelia was the daughter of Scipio Africanus. For 10 points, name these Roman reformers.

This Roman general reformed the army in 107 BC by recruiting landless citizens and held the consulship seven times. His rival Sulla marched on Rome. For 10 points, name this uncle of Julius Caesar by marriage.
This Roman dictator in 82 BC issued proscription lists to eliminate enemies. He retired in 79 BC. He was first to march on Rome with an army. For 10 points, name this man who defeated Marius.
Crassus died in 53 BC in this disastrous battle against Parthian cavalry and horse archers in Mesopotamia. The Romans lost their legionary standards. For 10 points, name this battle.

In 48 BC Julius Caesar defeated Pompey at this battle in Greece. Pompey fled to Egypt, where he was killed. Caesar had about half as many men as his rival, and his troops broke the cavalry on the enemy flank. The battle took place on a plain near the Enipeus River. For 10 points, name this battle in Thessaly.
In AD 9 Arminius ambushed three Roman legions led by Publius Quinctilius Varus in this German woodland. Augustus is said to have cried, "Give me back my legions!" For 10 points, name this battle.
This queen of the Iceni led a revolt against Rome in AD 60 or 61. She burned Londinium and Camulodunum. She was defeated by Suetonius Paulinus. For 10 points, name this British queen.

This Roman emperor and Stoic philosopher wrote the Meditations while on campaign along the Danube. He was the last of the "Five Good Emperors." His son Commodus succeeded him. For 10 points, name this man.

In AD 212 an emperor of the Severan dynasty issued an edict extending Roman citizenship to nearly all free inhabitants of the empire. He killed his brother Geta. For 10 points, name this emperor, for whom a famous set of baths in Rome is named.

In AD 378 Emperor Valens was killed at this battle in Thrace by Gothic cavalry. It showed the weakness of the Roman army. The emperor had refused to wait for reinforcements from his nephew Gratian. Two-thirds of the eastern field army perished in the fighting. For 10 points, name this battle named for a city.

In 451 the Romans and Visigoths under Aetius defeated this ruler of the Huns on the Catalaunian Plains. He later invaded Italy and was turned back from Rome. For 10 points, name this "Scourge of God."

In AD 476 this Germanic general deposed the last western Roman emperor Romulus Augustulus. He ruled Italy as king. He sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople and nominally accepted the authority of Emperor Zeno. The deposed boy emperor was pensioned off in Campania. For 10 points, name this man.

This dynasty ruled much of the Yellow River valley from around 1600 BC. Its kings used oracle bones for divination and buried chariots in royal tombs at Anyang. For 10 points, name this dynasty that preceded the Zhou.

The Zhou kings justified overthrowing the Shang with this doctrine, saying that heaven grants the right to rule to a just ruler. The idea was used by the Duke of Zhou to defend the conquest of King Wu. It was later applied to explain the rise and fall of later dynasties, which supposedly lost it through misrule. For 10 points, name this Chinese concept.

This Chinese general and strategist, said to have served the state of Wu, wrote a treatise on war containing the line "all warfare is based on deception." For 10 points, name this author of The Art of War.

This Han emperor ruled from 141 to 87 BC, expanded Chinese territory, sent Zhang Qian west, and established Confucianism as state doctrine. For 10 points, name this emperor whose name means "martial."

This Bronze Age city in the Indus Valley had a Great Bath, a grid plan, and drains. It was excavated in the 1920s in what is now Pakistan. For 10 points, name this city whose name means "mound of the dead."

This founder of the Mauryan Empire took power around 321 BC after the Nanda dynasty. He later became a Jain monk. His adviser Kautilya wrote the Arthashastra. For 10 points, name this emperor, grandfather of Ashoka.
This capital of the Assyrian Empire on the Tigris was destroyed in 612 BC by a Babylonian and Median alliance. It lies across the river from modern Mosul. For 10 points, name this city.
